track.title: Finance Shared Services
track.tagline: Every team, one key word at a time, explained like you're 20

lessons.title: Accounts Payable & the P2P cycle
lessons.summary: Every rupee the company owes its suppliers flows through one team: AP.

term.meaning: Accounts Payable (AP) is the money a company owes to suppliers for goods and services it has received but not yet paid for, and P2P (Procure-to-Pay) is the end-to-end process from asking to buy something to paying for it.

sections.b: Think of ordering food for a hostel party on credit from the canteen uncle. Someone asks for food (requisition), you agree a price (purchase order), the food arrives (goods receipt), the uncle hands you a bill (invoice), you check it and pay at month end (payment). AP is the friend who keeps the notebook of who is owed what and makes sure nobody is paid twice or paid for food that never came. In a big company this notebook covers thousands of suppliers in dozens of countries.

• Receive invoices (email, supplier portal, e-invoice feed, paper scan) and digitise them with OCR
• Check each invoice against the PO and goods receipt, then post it to the ERP
• Chase approvers and buyers when something doesn't match
• Run scheduled payment runs and send remittance advice to suppliers
• Answer supplier queries ('where is my payment?')
• Book month-end accruals and reconcile the AP subledger to the GL

The Pune delivery unit needs 20 laptops. A requisition is raised in the ERP, Procurement creates PO 4500012345 for ₹14,00,000 + GST with Dell India. Laptops arrive and IT stores post a GRN. Dell's invoice lands in the AP mailbox, OCR reads it, the system matches PO-GRN-invoice and posts it. On the due date (Net 45) the payment run pays Dell ₹14,00,000 + GST minus TDS, and Dell gets a remittance email.

• No PO, no pay: invoices without a valid PO should be the exception and need extra approval
• Segregation of duties: the person who creates vendors should not post invoices or release payments
• Cut-off: invoices for services received in March must be accrued in March even if they arrive in April
• Auditors sample paid invoices and check approval, match and payment terms

lessons.action: Ask an AP colleague to walk you through one invoice from the moment it hits the mailbox to the moment it is paid, and note each system screen it touches.

quiz.q: What does P2P stand for?
quiz.why: P2P covers requisition, PO, receipt, invoice and payment.

quiz.q: A supplier invoice arrives for services that were delivered. In the balance sheet, until it is paid, the amount sits as…
quiz.why: Money you owe others is a liability.

quiz.q: Scenario: the same AP clerk can create a new vendor, post its invoice and release payment. What is the main problem?
options: No segregation of duties, so fraud is easy
The vendor will be paid late
The invoice will post in the wrong currency
quiz.why: One person controlling the whole chain can create a fake vendor and pay it.

lessons.title: Purchase order (PO) & GRN
lessons.summary: The PO is the promise to buy; the GRN is proof you actually got it.

term.meaning: A purchase order is the buyer's official document listing what is being bought, at what price, quantity and terms, and a goods receipt note (GRN) records that the goods or services were actually received.

sections.b: A PO is like the order you confirm on a food delivery app: item, quantity, price, address, all fixed before anything is cooked. The GRN is you tapping 'Received' when the rider hands over the bag. Without the order you can't argue about the price; without the 'Received' tap nobody knows whether you actually got the food. AP needs both before it can comfortably pay.

• Procurement creates the PO in the ERP (SAP ME21N / Oracle Purchasing) after approvals
• For goods, stores or the requester posts a goods receipt (SAP MIGO, movement type 101)
• For services, the requester confirms a service entry sheet or receipt in the system
• The GRN posting creates an accounting entry: Dr Expense/Inventory, Cr GR/IR clearing
• AP checks GRN exists before matching an invoice; missing GRNs are chased with the requester
• Open POs with no receipts are reviewed periodically and closed

PO 4500098765 to Tata Communications: 12 months of MPLS link at ₹50,000/month. Each month the network team posts a service receipt of ₹50,000. In June the June receipt is missing, so June's invoice goes on hold and AP emails the network manager to confirm the service was delivered and post the receipt.

• Retro POs (PO raised after the invoice) are a control breach and usually tracked as a KPI
• Receipts must be posted by someone who actually received the goods, not by AP to 'unblock' an invoice
• Partial deliveries: GRN quantity can be less than PO quantity; only the received quantity can be paid
• Check PO price, currency, tax code and payment terms; errors here flow straight into the invoice

lessons.action: Ask the AP team for a list of invoices on hold for 'GRN missing' and see which requesters they belong to.

quiz.q: What does a GRN prove?
options: That goods or services were actually received
That the supplier has been paid
quiz.why: GRN = goods receipt; it confirms delivery.

quiz.q: When a goods receipt is posted against a PO in SAP, which account is typically credited?
quiz.why: GR/IR holds the liability until the invoice arrives.

quiz.q: Scenario: a PO is for 100 chairs, the GRN shows 80 received, and the invoice bills 100. What should AP pay now?
quiz.why: You only pay for what was received; the rest waits for the remaining delivery.

lessons.title: 3-way match (and 2-way)
lessons.summary: Three documents, one truth: PO, GRN and invoice must agree before money leaves.

term.meaning: A 3-way match compares the purchase order, the goods receipt and the supplier invoice on quantity and price before the invoice is approved for payment; a 2-way match compares only the PO and the invoice.

sections.b: Imagine you ordered 3 pizzas at ₹300 each, the rider handed over 3 pizzas, and the bill says 3 × ₹300. Order, delivery and bill agree, so you pay. If the bill said 4 pizzas or ₹350 each, you'd stop and ask. A 3-way match is exactly that check, done by the ERP automatically for thousands of invoices. A 2-way match skips the delivery check and is used where receipt isn't practical, like a fixed monthly subscription.

• The ERP compares invoice quantity with GRN quantity and invoice price with PO price
• Small differences inside a tolerance (e.g. a few rupees or a small %) post automatically
• Differences above tolerance post with a payment block (SAP block reason, often price or quantity)
• AP routes the block to the buyer to either amend the PO, post the GRN or get a credit note
• Once resolved, the block is released (SAP MRBR) and the invoice enters the payment run
• Some companies add a 4-way match with quality inspection

PO: 500 licences × $20 = $10,000. GRN: 500 licences. Invoice: 500 × $21 = $10,500. Price variance $500 (5%) is above the $50 tolerance, so the invoice posts blocked for price. The buyer confirms the PO was wrong because the vendor's price list changed, amends the PO to $21 and AP releases the block.

• Tolerances are a control: set too wide, overbilling slips through; ask what yours are
• Never 'fix' a match by editing the GRN quantity to equal the invoice
• 2-way match should be limited to approved categories (utilities, rent, subscriptions)
• Touchless (auto-matched) rate is a key automation KPI

lessons.action: Ask AP which tolerance limits are configured in your ERP for price and quantity variances.

quiz.q: Which three documents does a 3-way match compare?
quiz.why: PO = what was ordered, GRN = what arrived, invoice = what is billed.

quiz.q: A 2-way match is most suitable for…
options: Raw materials stored in a warehouse
quiz.why: No physical receipt is practical, so PO vs invoice is enough.

quiz.q: Scenario: invoice price is ₹1,020 vs PO ₹1,000, tolerance is ₹50. What happens?
options: It posts without a block because it is within tolerance
quiz.why: A ₹20 difference is inside the ₹50 tolerance.

calc.problem: PO price ₹250/unit, invoice price ₹262/unit, 400 units. Tolerance is 3%. Does it block?
calc.answer: Yes, it blocks for price: 4.8% (₹4,800) is above the 3% tolerance.

lessons.title: Invoice parking, posting & blocked invoices
lessons.summary: Not every invoice goes straight to 'posted': some wait, some get stuck.

term.meaning: Parking saves an invoice in the ERP without creating accounting entries, posting records it in the books as a liability, and a blocked invoice is posted but stopped from being paid until an issue is fixed.

sections.b: Parking is like saving an email as a draft: it's there, but nobody has received it. Posting is pressing Send: now it's official in the books. A blocked invoice is like a parcel that reached the post office but is held at customs: it's in the system, it's counted, but it won't be delivered (paid) until someone clears it. Knowing which state an invoice is in tells you whether the company has recognised the cost and whether the supplier will get money.

• Park invoices that need extra info (missing approval, unclear cost centre) - SAP MIR7 / FV60
• Post complete invoices - SAP MIRO for PO invoices, FB60 for non-PO; Oracle 'Validate'
• Invoices with match errors post with payment blocks (price, quantity, manual block)
• Review the blocked-invoice report daily and chase owners
• Release blocks once resolved (SAP MRBR) so the payment run picks them up
• At month end, review parked invoices: they are not in the books, so they may need accruing

On 30 June, AP has 120 parked invoices worth ₹2.3 crore waiting for cost-centre approval. Because parked invoices don't hit the GL, the close team accrues the ₹2.3 crore for services received in June. Separately, a ₹5 lakh invoice from a facilities vendor is posted with a quantity block; once the admin team posts the missing GRN, the block auto-releases and it pays on the next run.

• Old parked invoices are a cut-off risk: expenses may be understated
• Blocked invoices that age past due date damage supplier relationships and can breach MSME rules in India
• Manual payment blocks should have a reason and owner; random blocks hide problems
• Who can release blocks is an SoD question: AP releasing its own blocks without evidence is an audit finding

lessons.action: Ask AP for today's blocked-invoice report and look at the top three block reasons.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a parked and a posted invoice?
options: Parked has no accounting entry yet; posted does
Parked is only for foreign vendors
Parked is paid; posted is not
quiz.why: Parking is a draft; posting updates the GL.

quiz.q: A posted invoice has a payment block. Which statement is true?
options: The liability is in the books but it won't be paid until the block is released
It is not in the books
quiz.why: Blocks stop payment, not recognition.

quiz.q: Scenario: on month-end day there are many parked invoices for services already received. What should the close team consider?
options: Accruing those costs because they are not yet in the GL
quiz.why: Expenses for services received belong in the period, even if the invoice is only parked.

lessons.title: Vendor payment run & payment terms
lessons.summary: When and how suppliers get paid is decided by terms and run in batches.

term.meaning: A payment run is a scheduled, automated batch that picks all approved, due invoices and creates payments, and payment terms (like Net 30 or 2/10 Net 30) define when an invoice is due and whether an early-payment discount applies.

sections.b: Payment terms are like the rule 'pay rent by the 5th'. Net 30 means you have 30 days from the invoice (or receipt) date to pay. '2/10 Net 30' is the landlord saying: 'pay within 10 days and I'll knock off 2%, otherwise pay full by day 30'. A payment run is like setting up all your bill payments to go once a week in one go, instead of paying each bill whenever you remember.

• Terms are stored on the vendor master and copied to the PO and invoice; the ERP calculates due dates
• On run days (say Tuesday and Friday) AP executes the proposal (SAP F110 / Oracle Payment Process Request)
• Review the proposal: exceptions, blocked items, large amounts, new or changed bank details
• Treasury/finance approves; payment files go to the bank (often via host-to-host or SWIFT)
• The bank confirms; remittance advices are emailed to vendors
• Capture early-payment discounts where cash allows; in India track MSME dues against the 45-day limit

Vendor Infra Solutions (MSME, Micro) invoices ₹4,00,000 on 1 Aug with terms Net 45. The due date is 15 Sep. The payment run on 12 Sep picks it up. Another vendor offers 2/10 Net 30 on ₹10,00,000; paying by day 10 saves ₹20,000.

• India MSMED Act: payments to registered micro/small enterprises are due within the agreed period, capped at 45 days (15 days if no agreement); late payment attracts compound interest and, under income-tax rules, the expense deduction can be deferred until paid - check current rules
• Last-minute bank detail changes before a payment run are a classic fraud red flag
• Paying too early wastes cash; paying late costs penalties and goodwill
• Payment proposals should be reviewed and approved by someone other than the person who prepared them

lessons.action: Ask AP to show you a payment proposal list from the last run and how they review it before approval.

quiz.q: What does '2/10 Net 30' mean?
options: 2% discount if paid within 10 days, otherwise full amount due in 30 days
Full amount due in 10 days, 2% penalty after 30
quiz.why: Classic early-payment discount terms.

quiz.q: In India, the MSMED Act caps the agreed payment period to micro and small suppliers at…
quiz.why: 45 days maximum where there is an agreement; 15 days if there isn't.

quiz.q: Scenario: a vendor's bank account was changed by email the day before the payment run. What should AP do?
options: Hold the payment and verify the change via call-back to a known contact
Pay half to old and half to new account
Ignore it, the system will catch it
Pay quickly before the due date
quiz.why: Bank-change requests right before payment are a top fraud pattern.

calc.problem: Terms 2/10 Net 30 on a $50,000 invoice. What is the discount, and roughly what annual return does taking it represent?
steps: You pay 20 days earlier (day 10 vs day 30)
calc.answer: $1,000 discount, roughly 37% annualised, so it is usually worth taking if cash is available.

lessons.title: Accruals & GR/IR (goods received not invoiced)
lessons.summary: If you've received it, you owe it, even if the bill hasn't come yet.

term.meaning: An accrual records an expense and a liability for goods or services received in a period whose invoice hasn't been posted yet, and the GR/IR (goods receipt / invoice receipt) account is the SAP clearing account that holds receipts awaiting invoices.

sections.b: Say you ate at a friend's café all month and he'll send the bill next week. Your real spend this month already happened, so an honest budget tracker writes it down now. That's an accrual. GR/IR is the 'waiting room' account: when goods arrive the cost goes in; when the invoice arrives it comes out. If the waiting room has old stuff sitting there, something's wrong.

• Goods receipts automatically credit GR/IR (Dr Expense, Cr GR/IR)
• Invoice posting debits GR/IR and credits the vendor (Dr GR/IR, Cr Vendor)
• At month end, run the GR/IR report: GR > IR means accrued liability, IR > GR means invoice before receipt
• For services without POs or receipts, collect manual accrual inputs from business owners
• Post manual accruals with auto-reversal on day 1 of next month
• Regroup GR/IR balances for the balance sheet (SAP F.19) and clean up old items

In March, a consulting firm delivered ₹8,00,000 of work under a PO; the receipt was posted but the invoice came on 10 April. On 31 March GR/IR shows ₹8,00,000 credit (GR not invoiced), which is the accrued liability. Separately, the marketing team confirms an un-PO'd event costing ₹3,00,000 in March; AP books a manual accrual Dr Marketing expense, Cr Accrued liabilities, reversing on 1 April.

• Accruals without evidence (emails, timesheets, receipts) are an audit finding
• Forgetting to reverse an accrual double-counts the expense next month
• Old GR/IR items (e.g. >90 days) often mean wrong receipts, wrong quantities or lost invoices
• Over-accruing to 'smooth' results is a misstatement; accrue on best estimate

lessons.action: Ask AP or the GL team for the GR/IR ageing report and see how many items are older than 90 days.

quiz.q: Why do we book accruals?
options: To record expenses in the period they are incurred, even without an invoice
quiz.why: Matching principle / accrual accounting.

quiz.q: A goods receipt is posted but no invoice yet. The GR/IR account shows…
options: A credit balance representing goods received not invoiced
A debit balance in the bank
quiz.why: GR credits GR/IR; the invoice will clear it.

quiz.q: Scenario: an April accrual from March wasn't reversed and the real invoice was also posted in April. What happened?
options: The expense is missing in March
The expense is double-counted in April
quiz.why: Accrual plus invoice in the same month counts the cost twice.

calc.problem: In March: receipts posted worth ₹12,00,000; invoices posted against those receipts ₹7,50,000. What is the GR-not-invoiced balance at month end?
calc.answer: ₹4,50,000 credit: goods received but not yet invoiced (an accrued liability).

lessons.title: TDS on vendor payments & GST input tax credit for AP
lessons.summary: In India, AP isn't just paying bills; it's also a mini tax department.

term.word: TDS on vendor payments & GST input tax credit for AP
term.meaning: TDS (Tax Deducted at Source) is income tax the payer deducts from certain vendor payments and deposits with the government, and GST input tax credit (ITC) lets the company offset GST paid on purchases against GST it collects on sales.

sections.b: TDS is like your employer cutting tax from your salary before crediting it: the government gets its share early. For vendors, the company does the same: cut a % from the payment and deposit it under the vendor's PAN. GST ITC is like a refund coupon: GST you paid on a laptop can be used to reduce the GST you owe the government on your own sales, but only if the paperwork is right and the supplier has reported the sale.

• Map each vendor and expense to the right TDS section and rate (e.g. contractors, professional/technical fees, rent) in the ERP withholding tax setup
• Deduct TDS when the invoice is credited or paid, whichever is earlier; deposit it monthly and file quarterly TDS returns; issue TDS certificates to vendors
• Apply lower-deduction certificates where a vendor has one; higher rates apply if PAN is missing
• For GST: check the invoice has supplier GSTIN, your GSTIN, HSN/SAC, place of supply and correct CGST/SGST or IGST
• Match purchase register to GSTR-2B before claiming ITC; chase vendors whose invoices are missing
• Reverse ITC if the vendor isn't paid within 180 days of the invoice date (re-claim when paid)

A Bangalore entity receives a ₹1,00,000 + 18% GST (₹18,000) technical services invoice from an Indian vendor. TDS is deducted on the base amount, not the GST (when GST is shown separately). At an assumed 2% rate, TDS = ₹2,000. Payment = ₹1,18,000 − ₹2,000 = ₹1,16,000. The ₹18,000 GST is claimed as ITC once it appears in GSTR-2B.

• TDS rates and section numbers change (India's new Income-tax Act, 2025 renumbered sections from April 2026) - always check current rules with the tax team
• Wrong section = short deduction = interest and disallowance of the expense
• Claiming ITC on invoices not in GSTR-2B or on blocked credits (e.g. certain personal-use items) creates tax exposure
• Foreign vendor payments may need withholding under tax treaties and Form 15CA/15CB - a specialist area

lessons.action: Ask the AP or tax team to show you how the withholding tax code is set on one Indian vendor in the ERP.

quiz.q: Who deposits TDS with the government?
options: The payer (the company paying the vendor)
quiz.why: TDS is deducted and deposited by the payer.

quiz.q: Before claiming GST ITC, AP commonly matches the purchase register to…
quiz.why: GSTR-2B shows supplier-reported invoices available for ITC.

quiz.q: Scenario: an invoice shows ₹50,000 fee + ₹9,000 GST separately. TDS (assume 10%) is generally computed on…
quiz.why: Where GST is shown separately, TDS is on the value excluding GST.

calc.problem: Invoice: ₹2,00,000 professional fee + 18% GST. Assume TDS at 10% on the fee. What does AP pay the vendor?
calc.answer: ₹2,16,000 to the vendor; ₹20,000 deposited as TDS; ₹36,000 GST claimable as ITC if conditions are met.

lessons.title: Duplicate invoice check & vendor fraud controls
lessons.summary: Paying the same bill twice is the most common, and most avoidable, AP leak.

term.word: Duplicate invoice check & vendor fraud controls
term.meaning: A duplicate invoice check stops the same invoice being posted or paid more than once, and vendor fraud controls are the checks that stop fake vendors, fake invoices or diverted payments.

sections.b: Imagine your flatmate and you both pay the electricity bill because it came by email and post. That's a duplicate payment. Now imagine a stranger sends you a convincing 'electricity bill' with his own bank account. That's vendor fraud. AP's job is to spot both: same invoice in disguise (extra space, different date, 'INV-001' vs 'INV001') and fake vendors that look real.

• ERP duplicate check flags invoices with same vendor + reference + amount + date (SAP config on vendor master)
• Run fuzzy duplicate analytics: similar numbers, same amount different vendor, same bank account on two vendors
• Validate new vendors (PAN/GSTIN/bank) before first payment; see master data lessons
• Watch red flags: round amounts, invoices just under approval limits, PO-less urgent payments, vendor address = employee address
• Recover duplicates found after payment: ask vendor for refund or credit note
• Report findings to controllership; feed lessons into rules

Vendor ABC Tech sends invoice 'INV/2026/1045' for ₹3,40,000 by email; the scanned copy comes later as 'INV-2026-1045'. The ERP exact-match check misses it because of the slashes vs hyphens. A weekly fuzzy-match script normalises the reference (removes symbols) and flags the pair before the payment run. One is reversed.

• Duplicate check should not be switchable off by AP users
• Invoices from multiple channels (email + portal + paper) multiply duplicate risk
• Business email compromise: fraudsters impersonate vendors and ask for 'new bank details'
• Auditors and internal audit often run recovery audits on 2-3 years of payments

lessons.action: Ask AP which fields the ERP duplicate check uses, and whether anyone runs a fuzzy duplicate report.

quiz.q: Which change most often lets a duplicate slip past an exact-match check?
options: The vendor being in another country
Small formatting differences in the invoice number
quiz.why: 'INV-001' vs 'INV001' look different to a strict match.

quiz.q: Which is a vendor-fraud red flag?
options: Vendor bank account is the same as an employee's
quiz.why: Shared bank accounts with employees suggest a fake vendor.

quiz.q: Scenario: you find a duplicate that was already paid last month. Best next step?
options: Ignore it because the period is closed
Pay the vendor a third time to balance
Contact the vendor for refund or credit note and log the root cause
quiz.why: Recover the money and fix the cause.

lessons.title: AP KPIs: DPO, first-time-right, invoice cycle time
lessons.summary: How do you know AP is doing well? You measure it.

term.word: AP KPIs: DPO, first-time-right, invoice cycle time
term.meaning: AP KPIs are numbers that track AP performance, such as DPO (how many days on average the company takes to pay suppliers), first-time-right (share of invoices processed without rework) and invoice cycle time (days from receipt to approval/posting).

sections.b: Think of a food delivery app's dashboard: average delivery time, % orders delivered right the first time, % late. AP has the same kind of dashboard. DPO says how long we hold on to suppliers' money (longer is good for our cash, too long annoys suppliers). First-time-right shows quality. Cycle time shows speed. Your recon automation work directly moves these numbers.

• Pull data from the ERP and invoice workflow tool (OCR/portal) monthly
• Track: DPO, invoices processed per FTE, touchless/auto-post rate, first-time-right %, cycle time, % paid on time, % paid late to MSMEs, duplicate payments found
• Publish a dashboard to finance leadership and the client entity CFOs
• Do root-cause analysis on bad KPIs (e.g. top reasons for blocks)
• Agree SLA targets with stakeholders and report breaches

In Q2, AP processed 60,000 invoices; 45,000 needed no correction (first-time-right 75%). Median cycle time dropped from 6 to 4 days after the OCR upgrade. DPO went from 48 to 52 days because more vendors moved to Net 60 terms.

• DPO formulas vary (purchases vs cost of goods sold, average vs closing AP); always state the formula
• A rising DPO can mean late payments, not smarter terms; check on-time payment % alongside
• KPIs can be gamed (e.g. posting invoices fast but leaving them blocked)
• Targets differ by company - check your SLA document

lessons.action: Ask for the latest AP KPI dashboard and find out exactly how DPO is calculated in your organisation.

quiz.q: DPO measures…
options: Average days to collect from customers
Average days taken to pay suppliers
quiz.why: Days Payable Outstanding.

quiz.q: First-time-right in AP means…
options: Invoices processed without rework or correction
Invoices paid on the first day
The first invoice of the month
quiz.why: It's a quality KPI.

quiz.q: Scenario: DPO rises sharply but on-time payment % drops. What's the likely story?
options: The company is paying late, not negotiating better terms
quiz.why: Late payments inflate DPO; check both together.

calc.problem: Closing AP balance $9,000,000. Annual purchases (cost basis) $60,000,000. Calculate DPO on a 365-day year.

lessons.title: AP reconciliation: vendor statement recon & GR/IR clearing
lessons.summary: AP recon proves the books agree with suppliers and with themselves.

term.word: AP reconciliation: vendor statement recon & GR/IR clearing
term.meaning: AP reconciliation matches what the company's books say it owes a vendor against the vendor's own statement, matches the AP subledger total to the AP control account in the GL, and clears matched GR/IR items so only genuine open receipts or invoices remain.

sections.b: Think of you and a friend who lend each other money. Each of you keeps your own note. Once a month you compare notes: 'I think I owe you ₹1,200', 'My note says ₹1,500'. The ₹300 difference is a 'break' and you find out why (a missed coffee, a payment in transit). Vendor statement recon is exactly that, but with hundreds of vendors and thousands of lines. GR/IR clearing is tidying your own notebook so receipts and their matching bills cancel out.

• Subledger vs GL: AP vendor balances total must equal the AP control (reconciliation) account; differences come from manual GL postings or interface failures
• Vendor statement recon: get statements (email/portal), compare line by line with ERP open items (SAP FBL1N)
• Typical breaks: invoice missing in our books, payment in transit, credit note not posted, duplicate on our side, TDS deducted but not shown by vendor, FX differences
• GR/IR: match receipts and invoices by PO line; clear matched items (SAP F.13 / MR11 for write-off of small differences)
• Raise actions for each break: post, chase vendor, or correct
• Sign off recon with preparer and reviewer, with ageing of unreconciled items

Vendor Infosol's statement says we owe ₹9,20,000; our ERP shows ₹7,80,000. Break analysis: (1) invoice ₹1,80,000 not received by AP (on hold in OCR inbox), (2) our payment of ₹50,000 on 30 June not yet shown on vendor's statement, (3) TDS ₹10,000 we deducted which the vendor shows as still due. 7,80,000 + 1,80,000 − 50,000 + 10,000 = 9,20,000. Reconciled. Automation: a recon tool ingests the statement PDF, matches on invoice number/amount, auto-tags TDS and in-transit payments, leaving only the missing invoice for a human.

• Recon must be done, reviewed and evidenced by a deadline (often a few working days after close)
• Unexplained 'plugs' or long-aged reconciling items are audit red flags
• Debit balances on vendors (we overpaid) should be recovered, not left
• Automation: matching rules (exact, 1-to-many, tolerance), normalising invoice numbers, auto-classifying TDS/FX breaks, and workflow for exceptions

lessons.action: Ask for last month's AP control-account reconciliation and one vendor statement recon, and list the break types you see.

quiz.q: AP subledger total must agree with…
options: The AP control/reconciliation account in the GL
quiz.why: Subledger detail vs GL control total.

quiz.q: A vendor shows an amount due that we already paid on the last day of the month. This break is…
quiz.why: The vendor simply hasn't recorded our payment yet.

quiz.q: Scenario: GR/IR has hundreds of small (₹1-₹10) differences that block clearing. What's a typical fix?
options: Post them to the bank account
Clear them within an approved small-difference tolerance (e.g. MR11) with documentation
quiz.why: Small differences are written off within approved limits, with an audit trail.

calc.problem: Our books: we owe the vendor ₹5,00,000. Vendor statement: ₹5,60,000. Breaks found: an ₹80,000 invoice on the vendor statement that is not in our books, and a ₹20,000 credit note the vendor issued (on their statement) that we haven't posted. Is it reconciled?
steps: Add the invoice missing in our books: +₹80,000 → ₹5,80,000
Deduct the vendor's credit note we haven't posted: −₹20,000 → ₹5,60,000
calc.answer: Yes: ₹5,00,000 + ₹80,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹5,60,000, fully explained. Actions: get and post the missing invoice and the credit note.

lessons.title: Order-to-Cash (O2C) cycle
lessons.summary: From a signed deal to money in the bank: that whole journey is O2C.

term.meaning: Order-to-Cash is the end-to-end process from receiving a customer order or contract, through delivering and billing, to collecting and applying the customer's payment.

sections.b: If P2P is you buying food, O2C is you running the canteen. A student orders (order), you cook and serve (delivery), you write the bill (invoice), they pay later (collection), and you tick their name off in your credit notebook (cash application). If any step breaks, you either work for free or chase people forever. In an IT-services company the 'order' is usually a contract or SOW, and the 'delivery' is people's hours or project milestones.

• Sales signs a contract/SOW; customer master and contract are set up in the ERP
• Delivery happens; billing raises invoices (see Billing team lessons)
• Invoices create receivables in the AR subledger
• Collections team sends statements and reminders, follows up on due and overdue items
• Payments arrive at the bank; cash application matches them to invoices
• Disputes and deductions are resolved; bad debts are provided for or written off

A US bank client signs a $1.2M SOW for 12 months of application support, billed monthly at $100,000, Net 45. The January invoice is raised on 2 Feb, due 19 Mar. On 15 Mar the client pays $100,000 by ACH; cash application matches it to the invoice using the remittance, and the AR balance for January drops to zero.

• Weak links upstream (wrong customer master, missing PO number on invoice) cause collection delays downstream
• Revenue recognition and billing are different things: revenue can be recognised before billing (unbilled)
• O2C KPIs: DSO, % overdue, dispute cycle time, unapplied cash
• Credit risk: check customer creditworthiness before taking on big contracts

lessons.action: Ask the collections team which three customers have the largest overdue balance and why.

quiz.q: Which step comes immediately after an invoice is sent in O2C?
quiz.why: After billing, AR is collected.

quiz.q: In IT services, the 'order' in O2C is usually…
options: A contract or statement of work (SOW)
quiz.why: Services companies sell under contracts/SOWs.

quiz.q: Scenario: invoices keep getting rejected because the customer's PO number is missing. Which part of O2C should be fixed?
options: Billing/master data upstream, so the PO number prints on the invoice
quiz.why: Root cause is upstream data, not collections effort.

lessons.title: Accounts receivable & ageing buckets
lessons.summary: AR is money customers owe you; ageing tells you how worried to be.

term.meaning: Accounts receivable (AR) is the amount customers owe the company for invoices issued, and an ageing report groups those unpaid invoices into buckets by how many days they are past their invoice or due date.

sections.b: Think of friends who owe you money. Someone who borrowed yesterday isn't a worry; someone who borrowed six months ago and stopped replying is. An ageing report puts every debt in a bucket: not yet due, 1-30 days overdue, 31-60, 61-90, 90+. The older the bucket, the lower the chance of getting paid and the louder the chasing.

• Run the AR ageing (SAP S_ALR_87012178 / FBL5N, Oracle Aging report) by entity, customer and currency
• Buckets usually: current, 1-30, 31-60, 61-90, 91-180, 180+ days past due
• Prioritise collections calls on large and old balances
• Review with business/account managers in weekly or monthly calls
• Feed the ageing into bad-debt provisioning
• Report overdue % and top overdue customers to leadership

Customer GlobalRetail Ltd has: €200,000 current, €80,000 in 1-30, €50,000 in 61-90 and €20,000 in 180+. The collector focuses first on the €50,000 (getting close to the risky zone) and the €20,000 (escalate to the account manager, check if disputed).

• Ageing can be by invoice date or due date; know which your report uses
• Unapplied cash and credit notes should be netted or shown clearly, or the ageing looks worse than reality
• Wrong customer payment terms in master data distort the ageing
• Auditors use ageing to challenge the bad-debt provision

lessons.action: Ask the collections team for the latest ageing report and note the % of AR that is over 90 days past due.

quiz.q: What does an ageing report show?
options: Unpaid invoices grouped by how long they've been outstanding
quiz.why: It buckets receivables by days outstanding/past due.

quiz.q: Which bucket is generally the highest risk?
quiz.why: The older the debt, the less likely it is collected.

quiz.q: Scenario: a customer appears 120 days overdue but actually paid; the cash sits unapplied. What is the fix?
options: Apply the cash to the invoice so the ageing is correct
quiz.why: Unapplied cash makes AR look overdue when it isn't.

calc.problem: Total AR ₹10 crore: current ₹6 crore, 1-30 ₹2 crore, 31-90 ₹1.2 crore, 90+ ₹0.8 crore. What % of AR is overdue, and what % is 90+?

lessons.title: Dunning (reminder levels)
lessons.summary: Polite, then firm, then serious: dunning is structured nagging.

term.meaning: Dunning is the systematic process of sending payment reminders to customers in escalating levels as their invoices become more overdue.

sections.b: Like your mum reminding you to clean your room: first a gentle 'hey, when you get time', then 'today, please', then 'no Wi-Fi until it's done'. Dunning levels work the same way: level 1 is a friendly reminder, level 2 a firmer note, level 3 may involve the account manager and a credit hold, and the final level could be legal action or an agency.

• Configure dunning procedures in the ERP (SAP F150 dunning run; Oracle collections strategies) with levels, intervals and templates
• Run dunning on a schedule, excluding disputed items and customers with promises to pay
• Send statements and letters by email, sometimes in the customer's language
• Escalate higher levels to account managers or business heads
• Block new orders or apply credit hold at higher levels (with business approval)
• Log every contact in the collections tool for audit and follow-up

Dunning procedure: Level 1 at 7 days overdue (friendly email), Level 2 at 21 days (firm email + call), Level 3 at 45 days (letter from finance head, credit hold), Level 4 at 90 days (legal/agency review). A UK customer's £60,000 invoice reaches Level 2; the collector calls, gets a promise to pay on the 25th, and marks it so the next run skips it.

• Never dun disputed items; it annoys customers and wastes effort
• Key strategic clients often have custom, softer dunning agreed with sales
• Wrong contact emails in customer master send reminders into the void
• Local laws differ on late-payment interest and collection practices - check per country

lessons.action: Ask a collector to show you a dunning letter template for each level and who receives escalations.

quiz.q: Dunning is…
quiz.why: It's the reminder process for overdue receivables.

quiz.q: Which items should normally be excluded from dunning?
quiz.why: Disputes go through the dispute process, not reminders.

quiz.q: Scenario: a customer at Level 3 gives a credible promise-to-pay date. What should the collector do?
options: Record the promise and pause dunning until that date
quiz.why: Track promises to pay and follow up if broken.

lessons.title: Cash application & remittance advice
lessons.summary: Money landed in the bank, but whose invoice does it pay? That's cash app.

term.meaning: Cash application is matching incoming customer payments in the bank to the specific open invoices they pay, using the remittance advice (the customer's note listing what the payment covers).

sections.b: Imagine five friends each send you money by UPI with no message. You know you got ₹4,500 in total but not who paid for which dinner. A remittance advice is the message 'this ₹1,200 is for Friday's pizza'. Cash application is ticking off the right dinners so everyone's balance is correct. Big customers pay hundreds of invoices in one transfer, so the remittance is gold.

• Load bank statements (MT940/CAMT.053/BAI2) into the ERP daily
• Auto-match payments using customer reference, invoice numbers, amounts (SAP auto cash / Oracle Lockbox)
• Read remittances from emails, portals or EDI 820; increasingly with OCR/AI
• Apply payments; handle partial payments, short payments and overpayments
• Park unidentified receipts in unapplied cash and research them
• Post bank charges and FX differences per policy

Client EuroBank pays €312,450 in one SEPA transfer. The remittance email lists 14 invoices totalling €312,500 and notes '€50 bank charges'. Cash app applies €312,450 to the 14 invoices and posts the €50 to bank charges (within the write-off tolerance), clearing them all.

• Applying cash to the wrong customer or invoice distorts ageing and dunning
• Small differences: follow write-off tolerance policy; bigger short-pays become deductions/disputes
• Auto-match rate is a key automation KPI
• Same-day application matters for accurate credit exposure and DSO

lessons.action: Ask cash application what % of receipts were auto-matched last month and the most common reason for manual matching.

quiz.q: A remittance advice tells you…
quiz.why: It explains what the payment is for.

quiz.q: Bank statement files used for cash app are commonly in which format?
quiz.why: Standard electronic bank statement formats.

quiz.q: Scenario: a payment arrives with no remittance and doesn't match any single invoice amount. Where does it go first?
options: Unapplied / unidentified cash while it's researched
quiz.why: Park it, then identify.

calc.problem: Customer pays $98,700 against three invoices of $40,000, $35,000 and $25,000. Write-off tolerance is $100. What happens?
calc.answer: Apply $98,700, and treat the $1,300 short-pay as a deduction to investigate (not a write-off).

lessons.title: Unapplied / on-account cash
lessons.summary: Money you've received but can't match is a mystery that makes AR lie.

term.meaning: Unapplied or on-account cash is customer money received and recorded in the books but not yet matched to specific invoices.

sections.b: Like finding ₹2,000 in your wallet and not knowing who gave it. You can't tick anyone's debt off, so your list still shows people owing you, while you're actually holding their money. In AR, unapplied cash means customers look overdue (and may get angry dunning letters) even though they've paid.

• Post unidentified receipts to an unapplied/suspense or on-account line on the customer if the customer is known
• Research using bank reference, payer name, amounts, customer emails, sales teams
• Apply once identified; refund if it's an overpayment or wrong-entity payment
• Report unapplied cash ageing weekly; target to clear within a few days
• Fix root causes: missing remittances, customers paying wrong entity, combined payments

On 28 June, $45,000 arrives from 'ACME HOLD' with reference 'JUNE PMT'. No customer called ACME HOLD exists, but ACME Corp has open invoices totalling $45,000. The collector emails ACME, who confirm ACME Holdings is their parent company paying on their behalf. Cash is applied, and a note is added to the customer master about the alternate payer.

• Large unapplied balances at month end distort DSO and ageing
• Unapplied cash sitting a long time may need to be shown as a liability (customer advance) - check policy
• Payments received in the wrong legal entity need intercompany handling
• Unclaimed balances may have escheat/unclaimed-property rules in some countries

lessons.action: Ask for the unapplied cash report and see how old the oldest unapplied receipt is.

quiz.q: Unapplied cash means…
options: Cash received but not matched to invoices
quiz.why: Money in, but not yet linked to invoices.

quiz.q: A side-effect of high unapplied cash is…
options: Customers look overdue and may be wrongly dunned
quiz.why: AR ageing stays inflated.

quiz.q: Scenario: a customer paid the Indian entity for an invoice raised by the UK entity. What's needed?
options: Intercompany settlement or refund to move the cash to the right entity
quiz.why: Cash and invoice must sit in the same entity.

lessons.title: Disputes & deductions
lessons.summary: Sometimes customers don't pay because they don't agree. Now what?

term.meaning: A dispute is when a customer refuses or delays paying an invoice because they disagree with it, and a deduction is when they pay less than the invoice amount and keep the difference for a claimed reason.

sections.b: Like a restaurant bill where you say 'we never ordered that dessert'. You pay the rest and refuse the dessert (deduction) or refuse to pay until it's sorted (dispute). Collections can't just push harder; someone has to check whether the customer is right and either fix the bill or prove it.

• Log disputes with reason codes (pricing, rate, hours, PO missing, quality, duplicate) in the dispute module (SAP FSCM Dispute Management / Oracle)
• Route to the owner: billing, delivery manager, sales
• Gather evidence: SOW, timesheets, approvals, delivery acceptance
• Resolve by credit note (customer right), re-invoice, or evidence sent (customer wrong)
• Track dispute ageing and value; escalate stale ones
• Analyse root causes and feed back to billing

A Dutch client pays €90,000 against a €100,000 invoice, saying 'rate for two consultants should be €500/day, not €600'. The collector opens a dispute 'Rate mismatch', the billing team checks the SOW amendment and finds the client is right. A €10,000 credit note is issued and the invoice closes.

• Unlogged disputes hide in 'overdue' and spoil DSO analysis
• Credit notes need approval; don't let collections issue them alone
• Track dispute root causes: most are billing errors that should be prevented
• Disputed amounts may need a provision if unlikely to be collected

lessons.action: Ask collections for the top three dispute reason codes this quarter.

quiz.q: A deduction is when…
options: The customer pays less than the invoice and keeps the difference
quiz.why: Short payment with a reason.

quiz.q: Who usually resolves a 'wrong rate' dispute?
quiz.why: Billing checks what the contract says.

quiz.q: Scenario: the customer's claim is valid. How is the invoice corrected?
options: Delete the invoice in the ERP
quiz.why: Credit notes are the clean, auditable correction.

lessons.title: DSO (Days Sales Outstanding)
lessons.summary: How fast do customers pay? DSO answers in one number.

term.meaning: DSO is the average number of days it takes a company to collect payment after a sale, calculated roughly as receivables divided by revenue times the number of days.

sections.b: If you lend friends money for dinners and they pay back in 10 days on average, your 'DSO' is 10. If it creeps to 60, you're basically funding their lifestyle. For an IT-services company, a high DSO means it has done the work and paid its engineers but is waiting a long time for cash. Many such companies track DSO closely, sometimes split into billed and unbilled.

• Calculate DSO monthly per entity, customer, vertical (formula per company policy)
• Split into billed DSO (invoiced AR) and unbilled DSO (work done, not invoiced)
• Explain movements: big collections, delayed billing, disputes
• Set collection targets to hit DSO goals at quarter end
• Report to CFO and investor-relations teams (DSO is often discussed in results)
A US entity: AR $30M, quarterly revenue $45M (90 days). DSO = 30 ÷ 45 × 90 = 60 days. Unbilled revenue $9M adds 9 ÷ 45 × 90 = 18 days, so total DSO including unbilled = 78 days.

• Different formulas (simple, count-back, average AR) give different answers; be consistent
• Revenue spikes or one-off collections can distort DSO
• Factoring or early settlement deals can lower DSO artificially - disclose them
• Billed DSO falling while unbilled rises may mean billing is delayed

lessons.action: Ask what DSO your organisation reported last quarter and whether it includes unbilled revenue.

quiz.q: DSO roughly equals…
quiz.why: AR relative to sales, expressed in days.

quiz.q: Higher DSO generally means…
options: Customers are taking longer to pay
quiz.why: More days of sales stuck in receivables.

quiz.q: Scenario: billed DSO improved but total DSO worsened. Most likely cause?
options: Unbilled revenue grew because billing is delayed
quiz.why: Unbilled is the gap.

calc.problem: AR ₹240 crore; annual revenue ₹1,460 crore. Compute DSO on a 365-day year.

lessons.title: Credit limits & credit hold
lessons.summary: How much can a customer owe us before we stop and think?

term.meaning: A credit limit is the maximum amount a customer is allowed to owe at once, and a credit hold blocks new orders, deliveries or invoices when the customer exceeds that limit or is badly overdue.

sections.b: Like your credit card limit: the bank lets you spend up to ₹1 lakh, then blocks the card until you pay. Companies do the same for customers. If a client already owes $5M and starts slipping, you don't want to keep putting more engineers on their project without someone senior saying yes.

• Assess new customers: financials, credit ratings, payment history, country risk
• Set and approve credit limits per policy (higher limits need higher approval)
• ERP checks exposure (AR + open orders/unbilled) against limit (SAP credit management UKM / FD32 older)
• When exceeded, orders/billing documents go on credit block; credit team reviews and releases or holds
• Review limits periodically and after events (downgrade, big overdue)
• For high-risk countries, consider advance payment, LC or credit insurance

A Middle East customer has a $2M limit. AR is $1.7M and a new $500,000 order would take exposure to $2.2M. The order goes on credit block; the credit manager sees $600,000 is 90+ overdue and holds the order until a payment arrives. Next week $800,000 is received and the block is released.

• Overriding credit holds without documented approval is an audit point
• Exposure should include unbilled WIP in services businesses, not just invoiced AR
• Stale credit limits (set years ago) give false comfort
• Strategic clients may be exempted - make sure exemptions are approved and listed

lessons.action: Ask who approves credit-limit changes in your organisation and what the approval matrix is.

quiz.q: A credit limit is…
options: The maximum amount a customer may owe at once
quiz.why: It caps exposure.

quiz.q: Credit exposure for a services company should ideally include…
options: Open AR plus unbilled work and open orders
quiz.why: Unbilled work is also at risk.

quiz.q: Scenario: a customer is over limit with large 90+ overdue invoices. A salesperson wants the new order released today. What's correct?
options: Release it, sales is always right
Release only with documented approval per the credit policy
quiz.why: Policy-based approval, documented.

calc.problem: Credit limit €1,000,000. Open AR €700,000, unbilled work €150,000, new order €250,000. Will it block?
calc.answer: Yes, by €100,000; it needs credit review/approval.

lessons.title: Bad debt provision & write-off (ECL basics)
lessons.summary: Not every customer pays. Accounting makes you admit that early.

term.meaning: A bad-debt provision (under IFRS 9 / Ind AS 109, an expected credit loss allowance) is an estimate of receivables that may not be collected, booked as an expense in advance, and a write-off removes a receivable that is confirmed uncollectable.

sections.b: If you've lent money to ten friends, you know from experience one or two might never pay. A smart budget sets aside some money now for that likely loss instead of being shocked later. That's the provision. When a friend has clearly vanished, you strike his name off the list: that's the write-off. Under IFRS 9 you can't wait for a disaster; you estimate expected losses from day one.

• Build a provision matrix: loss rates by ageing bucket from historic data, adjusted for forward-looking info (simplified approach for trade receivables)
• Add specific provisions for known problem customers (insolvency, long disputes)
• Book: Dr Bad-debt expense, Cr Allowance for doubtful debts (contra-AR)
• Review monthly/quarterly with controllership and auditors
• Write-off with approval when recovery is exhausted: Dr Allowance, Cr AR
• Track recoveries of written-off amounts (credited to income)

Provision matrix for an entity: current 0.5%, 1-90 days 2%, 91-180 days 10%, 180+ days 50%. AR: $40M, $8M, $2M, $1M. ECL = 0.2 + 0.16 + 0.2 + 0.5 = $1.06M. A $300,000 customer in insolvency gets a specific 100% provision on top (excluded from the matrix to avoid double-counting).

• Loss rates are company-specific; never copy percentages from another company
• Don't double-count: customers with specific provisions should be excluded from the general matrix
• Write-offs need approval per delegation of authority; tax deductibility rules differ by country
• In India, Ind AS 109 governs; local GAAP entities abroad may use different rules - check with controllership

lessons.action: Ask controllership for the provision matrix percentages used this quarter and how they were derived.

quiz.q: Under IFRS 9 for trade receivables, companies often use…
options: No provision until the customer goes bankrupt
A simplified approach with a provision matrix
quiz.why: Lifetime ECL via a provision matrix.

quiz.q: The journal for creating a provision is…
options: Dr Bad-debt expense, Cr Allowance for doubtful debts
quiz.why: Expense now, contra-asset reduces AR.

quiz.q: Scenario: a customer already 100% specifically provided is also in the 180+ bucket of the matrix. Risk?
quiz.why: Exclude specifically provided balances from the matrix.

calc.problem: AR: current ₹50 crore (0.5%), 1-90 days ₹10 crore (3%), 90+ days ₹4 crore (25%). Compute ECL.

lessons.title: AR reconciliation: subledger vs GL and customer account recon
lessons.summary: AR recon proves what customers owe is what the books say.

term.word: AR reconciliation: subledger vs GL and customer account recon
term.meaning: AR reconciliation checks that the total of customer balances in the AR subledger equals the AR control account in the general ledger, and that individual customer accounts agree with the customer's own records and with bank receipts.

sections.b: Same idea as comparing notes with a friend, but now you're the lender. Your notebook (subledger) says the class owes you ₹10,000 in total; your main register (GL) should say ₹10,000 too. And when a friend says 'I paid you last week', you check your UPI history (bank) and your list. Any mismatch is a 'break' to explain.

• Subledger vs GL: AR customer totals vs AR reconciliation account; breaks from manual journals to the control account, interface timing, FX revaluation postings
• Customer account recon: compare our open items with the customer's AP ledger/confirmations (especially big clients, and for audit confirmations)
• Bank vs AR: receipts in bank not yet applied (unapplied cash), receipts applied but not in bank
• Typical breaks: unapplied cash, credit notes not processed on one side, deductions, FX differences, misapplied payments, invoices not received by the customer
• Document reconciling items with owners and ageing; sign off by preparer and reviewer
• Automation: match open items to customer statements/portals, auto-tag timing differences, propose cash matches

Year-end: auditor sends a balance confirmation to client NordBank. We show €1,250,000; NordBank confirms €1,180,000. Breaks: (1) invoice €100,000 dated 30 Dec not yet booked by NordBank (in transit), (2) payment €30,000 NordBank sent on 31 Dec that we received on 2 Jan. 1,250,000 − 100,000 + 30,000 = 1,180,000. Both are timing; no adjustment needed.

• An unreconciled difference between subledger and GL is a serious control issue
• Manual postings directly to the AR control account should be blocked in the ERP
• FX revaluation must hit both GL and subledger views consistently
• Long-standing credit balances on customers (overpayments) may need refund or reclass

lessons.action: Ask for last month's AR control-account recon and the oldest reconciling item on it.

quiz.q: AR subledger total should equal…
options: The AR control account in the GL
quiz.why: Subledger detail vs GL control.

quiz.q: Which is a timing difference in a customer recon?
options: An invoice we sent that the customer hasn't recorded yet
quiz.why: It'll resolve once the customer books it.

quiz.q: Scenario: subledger is ₹50,000 lower than GL; someone posted a manual journal directly to the AR control account. What's the fix?
options: Reverse/correct the manual entry and block direct postings to the control account
quiz.why: Control accounts should only be updated via the subledger.

calc.problem: GL AR control: $8,450,000. Subledger: $8,400,000. Found: manual GL journal +$70,000 with no customer; FX revaluation −$20,000 posted to GL only. Explained?
calc.answer: Yes, fully explained; fix the manual journal and align the FX revaluation posting.

lessons.title: Master data, explained
lessons.summary: Get the master wrong once and every transaction after it is wrong too.

term.meaning: Master data is the stable, reusable reference information in the ERP (vendors, customers, materials, GL accounts, cost centres, banks) that every transaction picks up automatically.

sections.b: Think of your phone contacts. You save a friend's number once, and every call, message and payment uses it. If you saved the wrong number, every message goes to a stranger. Master data is the company's contact list for vendors, customers, accounts and more. Transactions (invoices, payments, journals) are the calls and messages; they inherit whatever the master says.

• Receive create/change requests through a workflow tool or ERP (SAP MDG, Oracle, ServiceNow-style forms)
• Validate the request against documents and policy
• Create or change the record in the ERP (maker), then a second person approves (checker)
• Keep the audit trail: who requested, who changed, who approved, evidence
• Clean up duplicates and inactive records
• Run periodic quality checks and reconciliations

A new vendor 'Shakti Facilities Pvt Ltd' is created with payment terms Net 30 instead of Net 45 by mistake. For the next six months every invoice from that vendor falls due 15 days early, the payment run pays early and treasury loses float. One master field caused hundreds of wrong due dates.

• Master data errors are silent multipliers - they affect every downstream transaction
• Access to change masters (especially bank details) is one of the most sensitive in finance
• Master data teams are usually separate from transaction teams for segregation of duties
• In SAP S/4HANA, vendors and customers are both maintained as Business Partners (BP)

lessons.action: Ask the master data team to show you the request form for a new vendor and list the mandatory fields.

quiz.q: Which of these is master data?
options: A vendor's bank account and payment terms
quiz.why: Masters are reusable reference records.

quiz.q: In SAP S/4HANA, vendors and customers are maintained as…
quiz.why: The BP model replaced separate XK01/XD01 creation.

quiz.q: Scenario: a vendor's payment terms are wrong in the master. What is the downstream impact?
options: Every invoice gets a wrong due date until it's fixed
quiz.why: Transactions inherit master values.

lessons.title: Vendor master creation & KYC
lessons.summary: Before a supplier gets a single rupee, prove they are who they say they are.

term.meaning: Vendor master creation sets up a supplier in the ERP with legal name, address, tax IDs, bank details and terms, after KYC (know-your-vendor) checks verify the documents and bank account are genuine.

sections.b: Before you lend your bike to someone new, you'd want to see their ID and know where they live. Companies do the same before paying a supplier. The master data team checks the company is real, the tax numbers are valid, and the bank account really belongs to them, then creates the record so AP can pay.

• Receive request from procurement with supporting documents (registration certificate, PAN, GSTIN, cancelled cheque or bank letter, MSME certificate if any; W-9/VAT ID abroad)
• Validate PAN and GSTIN on government portals; check name matches legal name
• Validate bank account (penny-drop verification or bank letter) and check it isn't already used by another vendor or an employee
• Screen against sanctions/denied-party lists where required
• Set account group, reconciliation account, payment terms, withholding tax codes, MSME flag
• Maker creates; checker reviews against documents and approves

Procurement requests 'Bluewave IT Services LLP' in Hyderabad. The team checks PAN on the income-tax portal, GSTIN on the GST portal (status Active, legal name matches), does a ₹1 penny-drop test that returns 'BLUEWAVE IT SERVICES LLP', confirms Udyam (MSME) registration and sets the MSME flag so AP tracks the 45-day rule. A checker approves and the vendor code is released.

• Name mismatch between PAN, GSTIN and bank is a stop sign
• Missing or inactive GSTIN means ITC risk for every invoice
• Missing PAN means higher TDS on payments
• One-time vendors and employee-as-vendor setups need extra scrutiny

lessons.action: Ask for the vendor KYC checklist and see which checks are automated versus manual.

quiz.q: What does a penny-drop test check?
options: That the bank account exists and the name matches
quiz.why: A small credit returns the account holder's name.

quiz.q: Why set an MSME flag on an Indian vendor?
options: So AP can track the statutory payment deadline
quiz.why: MSME suppliers have a payment-time limit.

quiz.q: Scenario: GSTIN legal name is 'Sunrise Tech Pvt Ltd' but bank account name is 'R. Kumar'. What should the team do?
options: Change the GSTIN name to R. Kumar
Reject or hold until the mismatch is explained with evidence
quiz.why: Bank must belong to the vendor entity.

lessons.title: Customer master: sold-to, bill-to, ship-to, payer
lessons.summary: One customer can wear four hats: who orders, who's billed, who receives, who pays.

term.word: Customer master: sold-to, bill-to, ship-to, payer
term.meaning: A customer master holds a customer's legal, tax, address, contact, credit and payment-terms data, and partner functions define which party orders (sold-to), gets the invoice (bill-to), receives the service (ship-to) and pays (payer).

sections.b: Think of ordering a birthday gift online. You place the order (sold-to), the bill goes to your dad's email because he's paying (bill-to, payer), and the gift goes to your friend's address (ship-to). Same order, different people. Global companies do this all the time: a US parent signs, a German subsidiary receives the work, and a shared-services centre in Poland pays.

• Create customer BP with legal name, tax IDs (GSTIN, VAT, EIN), addresses and currency
• Set partner functions (SAP: SP sold-to, BP bill-to, SH ship-to, PY payer)
• Set payment terms per contract, reconciliation account, dunning procedure, credit segment
• Capture invoice delivery details: email, portal, PO requirements, e-invoicing IDs
• Validate tax IDs (e.g. EU VIES for VAT numbers, GST portal in India)
• Maker-checker approval and evidence of contract terms

Client 'Contoso Group' signs a master agreement in the US. Work is delivered to Contoso GmbH in Munich (ship-to), invoices must go to Contoso's AP portal in Poland (bill-to) and Contoso Finance Ltd pays (payer). The master team creates the partner functions accordingly, sets Net 60 per contract and adds the portal ID so billing invoices reach the right place.

• Wrong bill-to or email means invoices are never received and DSO rises
• Place of supply and GST/VAT depend on correct addresses and tax IDs
• Payment terms in master must match the contract; check against the signed document
• Duplicate customers split credit exposure and confuse cash application

lessons.action: Ask the master data team to show you a customer with different sold-to, bill-to and payer partners.

quiz.q: Which partner function receives the invoice?
quiz.why: Bill-to gets the invoice.

quiz.q: Where would you validate an EU VAT number?
quiz.why: VIES is the EU VAT validation system.

quiz.q: Scenario: invoices are going to an old email of the customer and remain unpaid. Root cause team?
quiz.why: Fix the master and all future invoices go right.

lessons.title: Material / service master & GL account master
lessons.summary: What you buy or sell, and where it lands in the books, is set by two masters.

term.word: Material / service master & GL account master
term.meaning: A material or service master describes items the company buys or sells (description, unit, category, default accounts), and the GL account master defines each ledger account in the chart of accounts and how it behaves.

sections.b: Think of a supermarket. Every product has a barcode card: name, unit, price group, which shelf. That's the material master. The GL master is the list of drawers in the cashier's desk: 'electricity', 'salaries', 'software'. Each card tells the system which drawer the money goes into. Put a laptop card on the 'stationery' drawer and your reports go wrong.

• Create material/service masters with type, unit of measure, material group and valuation class (SAP MM01), which drives account determination
• In services-heavy companies, many purchases use service masters or material groups instead of stock items
• GL master (SAP FS00): account number, type (P&L/balance sheet), currency, open-item and line-item flags, tax category, field status
• New GL requests usually come from controllership with justification and mapping to group reporting accounts
• Maker-checker approval; update the chart-of-accounts document
• Block obsolete accounts for posting

Controllership requests a new GL 'Cloud subscription expense - AI tools'. Master data creates it in the operating chart with P&L type, maps it to group account 'IT expenses', sets tax category to allow input tax, and the checker approves. Procurement then links material group 'Cloud SaaS' to this GL so future POs post correctly.

• Wrong valuation class or material group sends costs to the wrong GL
• Creating near-duplicate GLs fragments reporting
• Balance sheet accounts needing open-item management (like GR/IR, clearing) must have it switched on from the start - changing later is hard
• Group mapping must be maintained or consolidation breaks

lessons.action: Ask for the chart of accounts and find the GR/IR, AP and AR control accounts in it.

quiz.q: In SAP, which material master field strongly drives which GL a goods receipt posts to?
quiz.why: Valuation class feeds account determination.

quiz.q: Which GL setting is essential for clearing accounts like GR/IR?
quiz.why: Open items let entries be matched and cleared.

quiz.q: Scenario: two new GLs called 'Travel Exp' and 'Travel Expenses' exist. Problem?
quiz.why: Governance should stop near-duplicates.

lessons.title: Cost centre & profit centre master
lessons.summary: Cost centres say who spent it; profit centres say who earned it.

term.meaning: A cost centre is an organisational unit that collects costs (like a department), and a profit centre is a unit that tracks both revenue and costs so its profit can be measured (like a business unit or service line).

sections.b: Picture a college fest. Each committee (food, décor, sound) has its own expense sheet: those are cost centres. The whole fest, which sells tickets and spends money, is a profit centre - you can see if it made or lost money. In an IT company, 'Pune HR' could be a cost centre, while 'Banking & Financial Services vertical - Europe' could be a profit centre.

• Maintain the cost centre hierarchy (SAP KS01, standard hierarchy) and profit centre hierarchy (KE51)
• Assign each cost centre to a profit centre and company code
• Set validity dates, person responsible, category (admin, delivery, sales)
• Process reorganisation requests (new team, merger of units) with controllership approval
• Lock or close cost centres no longer needed; redirect postings
• Keep mapping to management reporting and allocations up to date

A new 'GenAI CoE' team is formed in Chennai. Controllership asks for cost centre CC-IN-CHN-4410 under profit centre 'Digital Services India', person responsible = CoE head, valid from 1 Oct 2026. Master data creates it, and payroll and AP are told to start coding the team's costs there.

• Costs posted to the wrong cost centre distort department budgets and allocations
• Changing profit centre assignment mid-year can break segment reporting - usually changes are dated
• Dormant cost centres still open for posting are a leak point
• Reorgs need coordination with payroll, procurement, billing and MIS

lessons.action: Ask MIS or controllership for the cost centre hierarchy of your own department.

quiz.q: A profit centre tracks…
quiz.why: So profit can be measured.

quiz.q: Which is a typical cost centre?
quiz.why: Departments collect costs.

quiz.q: Scenario: a team was dissolved but its cost centre is still open and getting expense postings. What should happen?
options: Lock it and redirect postings to the right cost centre
quiz.why: Block dormant objects.

lessons.title: Bank detail changes & call-back verification
lessons.summary: The single most dangerous field in finance: the vendor's bank account.

term.meaning: A bank detail change is an update to the account where a vendor (or employee) gets paid, and call-back verification is the control of phoning a known, independently sourced contact at the vendor to confirm the change before it's applied.

sections.b: Imagine you get a WhatsApp from your 'friend' saying 'new number, send money here'. You'd call his old number first. Fraudsters do this to companies: they hack or spoof a supplier's email and send a polished letter with 'new bank details'. If the company updates the master without checking, the next big payment goes to the fraudster. The call-back is the 'call his old number' step.

• Accept change requests only through approved channels with signed letter on letterhead and bank proof
• Call back the vendor using a phone number from the existing master or contract - never the number in the request email
• Record who was called, when, and what was confirmed
• Validate the new account (penny-drop / bank letter) and name match
• Maker-checker approval; flag the vendor for extra review in the next payment run
• Report suspicious requests to the fraud/security team

An email from 'accounts@globa1parts.com' (note the '1') asks to change Global Parts' bank to a new account before a ₹48 lakh payment. The master team calls Global Parts' finance contact on the number in the master; she says no change was requested. The request is rejected and the security team blocks the lookalike domain.

• Urgency, last-minute timing before payment runs and lookalike domains are classic signs
• Never trust contact details provided in the change request itself
• Sensitive-field change reports (SAP: change logs / S_ALR_87010039-style vendor change reports) should be reviewed regularly
• Changes to employee bank accounts for payroll need the same rigour

lessons.action: Ask the master data team to describe their call-back procedure and where the call evidence is stored.

quiz.q: Where should the call-back phone number come from?
options: The existing vendor master or contract, independently sourced
quiz.why: Independent source defeats spoofing.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag in a bank change request?
options: Sender domain slightly different from the vendor's real domain
quiz.why: Lookalike domains are a common trick.

quiz.q: Scenario: a 'CFO' emails demanding an urgent bank change today, skipping call-back. What do you do?
options: Skip the control because the CFO asked
Follow the call-back control anyway and escalate
Ask the requester to call you
quiz.why: Controls apply regardless of seniority; urgency is a red flag.

lessons.title: Duplicate masters & data governance (maker-checker)
lessons.summary: Two records for one vendor is how duplicate payments are born.

term.meaning: Duplicate masters are two or more ERP records for the same real-world vendor, customer or item, and data governance is the set of rules, roles and checks (like maker-checker) that keep master data accurate and controlled.

sections.b: If you save your best friend twice in your contacts, once as 'Rahul' and once as 'Rahul College', you might send the same message twice or miss one. In a company, a vendor saved twice can be paid twice for the same invoice, and duplicate checks won't catch it because they look within one vendor. Governance means: clear rules, a second person checks every change, and regular clean-ups.

• Search before create: check PAN/GSTIN/VAT, bank account and name similarity
• Run periodic duplicate reports (same tax ID, same bank, fuzzy name match)
• Merge or block duplicates; move open items to the surviving record
• Maker-checker: one person enters, another independent person approves
• Define data owners, naming conventions and mandatory fields
• Monitor access: no single person should create and approve

A duplicate scan finds 'Zenith Software Solutions Pvt Ltd' and 'ZENITH SOFTWARE SOLN PVT. LTD.' with the same PAN and bank account. One has open invoices. The team blocks the second for posting and payment, asks AP to check both for duplicate payments, and keeps one active record.

• Duplicates across company codes may be intended (same vendor extended to several entities) - distinguish 'extended' from 'duplicate'
• Maker-checker only works if the checker actually checks documents, not just clicks approve
• Self-approval access is a typical audit finding
• Fuzzy matching needs normalisation (remove punctuation, 'Pvt', 'Ltd', spaces)

lessons.action: Ask whether a duplicate vendor report exists and when it was last run.

quiz.q: Why are duplicate vendors dangerous?
options: The same invoice can be paid under both records
quiz.why: Duplicate checks work within a vendor, so cross-vendor duplicates slip through.

quiz.q: Maker-checker means…
options: One person enters a change, a different person approves it
The same person makes and checks
quiz.why: Two independent people.

quiz.q: Scenario: the same PAN appears on two vendor records in the same company code. First step?
options: Investigate, block the duplicate and check for duplicate payments
quiz.why: Control the risk, then clean up.

calc.problem: A vendor list has 8,000 records. A scan finds 240 sharing a tax ID with another record, of which 60 are legit 'extended to another entity' cases. What is the true duplicate rate?

lessons.title: Blocking, dormant records & mass updates
lessons.summary: Old records left open are unlocked doors; mass changes are power tools.

term.meaning: Blocking stops a master record from being used for postings, purchasing or payments; dormant records are masters with no activity for a long time; and mass updates change many records at once using approved templates or tools.

sections.b: Think of an old SIM card you no longer use but haven't cancelled. Someone could misuse it. Dormant vendors are the same: if no one has used them for 18 months, they should be blocked so nobody can quietly pay through them. Mass updates are like changing the Wi-Fi password on all your devices at once: very efficient, very dangerous if you type it wrong.

• Run a dormancy report (e.g. no transactions in 12-24 months, per policy) and propose blocks
• Confirm with procurement/business before blocking; set posting, purchasing and payment blocks (SAP: central block flags)
• Unblocking requires a request and re-validation (fresh KYC if long dormant)
• Mass updates (SAP MASS / LSMW / MDG mass change; Oracle FBDI) for things like payment-term changes or new tax codes
• Test mass updates on a small sample, get approval, keep before/after files
• Reconcile after the update that only intended records changed

A new e-invoicing field must be populated on 3,500 customer records. The team prepares an upload file, tests 20 records in the quality system, gets sign-off, runs the mass update in production, and then extracts all 3,500 to compare before vs after. 3 failed because of locked records and are fixed manually.

• Blocking is safer than deleting; history must remain for audit
• Reactivated dormant vendors are a fraud red flag; re-check bank and tax IDs
• Mass updates need the same maker-checker as single changes, plus evidence
• Always keep a rollback file

lessons.action: Ask how many vendors were blocked for dormancy in the last review and what the dormancy period is.

quiz.q: Why block dormant vendors?
options: To stop misuse of unused records for fraudulent payments
quiz.why: Unused but open records are a risk.

quiz.q: What should you always keep when doing a mass update?
quiz.why: Needed for audit and rollback.

quiz.q: Scenario: a vendor dormant for 3 years asks to be unblocked with new bank details. What applies?
options: Full re-validation including call-back and bank check
quiz.why: Dormant reactivation with bank change is high risk.

calc.problem: Policy: block vendors with no activity in 18 months. Of 12,000 vendors, 2,100 are dormant; business asks to keep 150 active. How many get blocked, and what % of the base?

lessons.title: Master data quality KPIs
lessons.summary: If you can't measure master data quality, you can't prove it's good.

term.meaning: Master data quality KPIs measure how accurate, complete, timely and controlled the master data process is, such as error rate, first-time-right, turnaround time and duplicate count.

sections.b: Like grades for your notes: are they complete (no missing pages), correct (no wrong formulas), and up to date? For master data, you check things like 'how many vendors are missing a GSTIN', 'how many requests were wrongly processed' and 'how fast we create a vendor'. These numbers tell leaders if the team is reliable.

• Track request volumes and turnaround time (TAT) against SLA (e.g. create within 1-2 working days, per your SLA)
• Track accuracy: changes found wrong on QC or later rework
• Track completeness: % records missing key fields (tax ID, email, bank)
• Track duplicates found and resolved
• Track control health: % changes with call-back evidence, % self-approved (should be 0)
• Publish a monthly dashboard and root-cause actions

In September the team processed 1,600 requests. QC on all records found 24 with errors (wrong payment term, typo in IFSC). Error rate = 1.5%, first-time-right = 98.5%. Average TAT was 1.2 days against an SLA of 2 days.

• Define error clearly (any field? critical fields only?) or numbers aren't comparable
• Sample-based QC gives an estimate, not certainty
• A great TAT with poor accuracy is not a win
• Critical fields (bank, tax, terms) deserve their own KPI

lessons.action: Ask for the master data team's monthly KPI pack and check how 'error' is defined.

quiz.q: First-time-right % equals…
quiz.why: Share processed correctly the first time.

quiz.q: Which is a completeness KPI?
quiz.why: Measures missing data.

quiz.q: Scenario: TAT improved from 3 to 1 day but error rate doubled. Assessment?
options: Speed came at the cost of quality; investigate
quiz.why: Balance speed and accuracy.

calc.problem: 2,000 requests processed; 30 had at least one error; of those, 12 had errors in critical fields (bank/tax). Compute overall error rate and critical error rate.

lessons.title: Master data reconciliation & periodic audit
lessons.summary: Prove that every change in the ERP was a change someone asked for and approved.

term.meaning: Master data reconciliation compares what actually changed in the ERP (from change logs) with approved requests, and checks master records against external sources like tax portals and bank validations.

sections.b: Imagine your bank statement versus your own spending notes: every debit should match something you remember buying. Master data recon is the same: every change in the ERP log should match an approved ticket. If the log shows a bank change with no ticket, someone changed it without permission - a huge red flag. Also, you check your contacts against the real world: are those GSTINs still active?

• Extract change logs for the period (SAP CDHDR/CDPOS-based reports; Oracle audit tables)
• Match each change to an approved request (ticket number, requester, approver, date)
• Breaks: change with no ticket, ticket with no change, changed by unauthorised user, approved after change, field changed differs from request
• Validate tax IDs in bulk (GSTIN status active/cancelled, PAN-name, VAT via VIES)
• Check bank accounts shared across vendors or with employees
• Report exceptions to controllership; fix and document; automation runs these matches every day instead of quarterly

Quarterly recon: 4,200 vendor changes in the log, 4,180 matched to tickets. 20 breaks: 14 were system-generated (e.g. archiving flags), 5 were mass updates linked to one approved change request, 1 bank change had no ticket. That one is escalated, the vendor is called, payments are held until verified.

• Unmatched sensitive-field changes (bank, terms, address) should be zero; treat any as an incident
• Exclude system/technical changes with documented rules, not by judgement each time
• GSTIN cancelled for a vendor means ITC risk; inform AP and tax
• Automation idea: daily log extract + ticket API match + exception queue
