lessons.action: Ask whether the team reconciles master data change logs to tickets, how often, and who reviews it.

quiz.q: What is master data reconciled against?
options: Approved change requests and external sources like tax portals
quiz.why: Log vs tickets, plus external validation.

quiz.q: Which break is most serious?
options: A vendor bank change with no approved ticket
A ticket for a description change
quiz.why: Unauthorised bank change is a fraud risk.

quiz.q: Scenario: GSTIN validation shows 12 active vendors' GSTINs are cancelled. Who should know?
options: AP and tax teams, because ITC on their invoices is at risk
quiz.why: Cancelled GSTIN affects input tax credit.

calc.problem: Change log: 5,000 entries. Matched to tickets: 4,940. Of the 60 unmatched, 45 are documented system changes. How many true exceptions, and what % of entries?
calc.answer: 15 exceptions, 0.3% of changes; each needs investigation.

lessons.title: Billing models: T&M vs fixed price vs milestone
lessons.summary: How a contract is priced decides how and when you can bill it.

term.word: Billing models: T&M vs fixed price vs milestone
term.meaning: In IT services, time-and-material (T&M) contracts bill for hours or days worked at agreed rates, fixed-price contracts bill an agreed total regardless of effort, and milestone billing raises invoices when defined deliverables are accepted.

sections.b: Think of hiring a tutor. T&M: you pay ₹800 per hour, however many hours. Fixed price: ₹20,000 for the whole exam prep, even if it takes more hours. Milestone: ₹5,000 after each completed chapter test. Each way changes who carries the risk (in T&M the client does; in fixed price the company does) and what billing needs as proof (timesheets vs acceptance certificates).

• Read the contract/SOW to identify the billing model, rates, caps and invoicing frequency
• T&M: collect approved timesheets, multiply by rate card, apply discounts/caps
• Fixed price: bill per agreed schedule (monthly instalments or %)
• Milestone: bill when milestone acceptance evidence (sign-off email, certificate) is received
• Set up billing plans in the ERP (SAP: billing plans on sales order / project, Oracle Project Billing)
• Hand over to AR once invoices are sent

Contract A (T&M): 4 consultants × 20 days × $600/day = $48,000 for March. Contract B (fixed price): $360,000 total, billed $30,000 monthly. Contract C (milestone): $200,000 split 30/40/30 on design sign-off, UAT sign-off and go-live; billing raises $60,000 when the design sign-off email arrives.

• Revenue recognition (Ind AS 115 / IFRS 15) is separate from billing: fixed-price revenue may be recognised on progress, not on invoicing
• T&M with a cap ('not to exceed') stops billing beyond the cap
• Milestone billing without documented acceptance is a dispute waiting to happen
• Many contracts are hybrids - read the actual SOW

lessons.action: Ask the billing team for one example contract of each type and what proof they need before invoicing.

quiz.q: In a T&M contract, billing is based on…
options: A fixed total regardless of effort
quiz.why: Time and material.

quiz.q: Which model puts most cost-overrun risk on the IT company?
quiz.why: The price is fixed even if effort overruns.

quiz.q: Scenario: a milestone is done but the client hasn't signed acceptance. Can you invoice the milestone?
options: Usually not until acceptance per contract terms
quiz.why: Contract terms decide the trigger; acceptance is usually required.

calc.problem: T&M contract: 3 consultants at $75/hour, 160 billable hours each in a month, with a monthly cap of $34,000. What do you bill?
steps: Cap = $34,000, so bill the lower amount
calc.answer: $34,000 (the cap applies; the extra $2,000 is not billable).

lessons.title: Billing triggers & timesheets
lessons.summary: No trigger, no invoice: billing waits for a signal.

term.meaning: A billing trigger is the event that allows an invoice to be raised (approved timesheets, a date in the billing plan, milestone acceptance), and timesheets are the records of hours each person worked on each project.

sections.b: Like a cab ride: the meter (timesheet) records the ride, and the trip ending (trigger) produces the bill. If the driver forgets to start the meter, there's nothing to charge. In IT services, if engineers don't submit timesheets on time or managers don't approve them, billing literally can't invoice the customer, and cash gets delayed.

• Engineers submit weekly timesheets in the time-tracking system against project/WBS codes
• Project managers approve; client approval may also be required for some contracts
• Approved hours flow to billing (SAP CATS → project billing / Oracle Projects)
• Billing checks billable vs non-billable hours, leave, holidays, overtime rules
• Raise invoices once triggers are met; chase missing or rejected timesheets
• Track 'unbilled due to missing timesheets' daily near month end

On 3 April, billing finds 12 consultants on a UK project haven't had March timesheets approved. That's 12 × 160 hours × £70 = £134,400 that can't be billed. The billing analyst escalates to the delivery manager; approvals arrive on 4 April and the invoice goes out the same day.

• Timesheet compliance % is a leading indicator of on-time billing
• Hours booked to the wrong project code bill the wrong customer
• Client-approved timesheets reduce disputes later
• Backdated timesheet changes after billing need a credit/debit note process

lessons.action: Ask billing for the 'pending timesheet approvals' report on the last day of the month.

quiz.q: Which is a typical billing trigger for T&M work?
quiz.why: Approved hours drive T&M billing.

quiz.q: Who usually approves timesheets first?
quiz.why: Delivery approves before billing uses them.

quiz.q: Scenario: hours were booked to the wrong customer's project and billed. Fix?
options: Correct the timesheet and issue credit/debit notes as needed
quiz.why: Correct source data and the invoices.

lessons.title: Invoice creation & e-invoicing (India IRN/QR, GST fields)
lessons.summary: In India, an invoice isn't fully valid until the government portal has seen it.

term.word: Invoice creation & e-invoicing (India IRN/QR, GST fields)
term.meaning: Invoice creation turns billing data into a legal invoice, and India's GST e-invoicing requires eligible businesses to report B2B and export invoices to the Invoice Registration Portal (IRP), which returns an IRN (Invoice Reference Number) and a signed QR code.

sections.b: Think of your exam hall ticket: it's only valid with the official stamp and barcode. E-invoicing is that stamp for invoices: your ERP sends the invoice data to the government portal, the portal checks it and gives back a unique number and QR code. Without it, the customer may not get its GST credit, and the invoice may be treated as invalid.

• Generate the invoice from the billing document (SAP VF01 / Oracle AR transactions)
• Check mandatory GST fields: supplier and recipient GSTIN, unique invoice number, date, HSN/SAC, taxable value, tax rate and CGST/SGST or IGST, place of supply
• For exports of services: zero-rated under LUT (or with IGST paid), with currency and foreign customer details
• Send JSON to IRP through GSP/ERP integration; receive IRN, acknowledgement and signed QR
• Print IRN/QR on the invoice PDF; deliver to customer portal/email
• Handle cancellations within the allowed window; otherwise use credit notes

The Pune entity bills an Indian client ₹10,00,000 for software services (SAC 9983xx), intra-state Maharashtra: CGST 9% ₹90,000 + SGST 9% ₹90,000 = ₹11,80,000. The ERP sends it to IRP, gets an IRN and QR code, and the PDF is emailed with the QR printed. For a US client, the same entity issues an export invoice in USD under LUT with zero GST, also reported to IRP.

• E-invoicing applies above a turnover threshold and has time limits for reporting old invoices - check current GST rules, as both have changed over time
• Wrong GSTIN or place of supply means wrong tax type (IGST vs CGST/SGST)
• Global entities have their own e-invoicing regimes (e.g. Italy SDI, Saudi ZATCA, EU rollouts); each country differs
• Invoice numbering must be unique and sequential per financial year and series

lessons.action: Ask billing to show you an Indian e-invoice PDF and point out the IRN and QR code.

quiz.q: What does IRP return after accepting an e-invoice?
options: IRN and a signed QR code
quiz.why: IRN + QR validate the e-invoice.

quiz.q: Intra-state supply in India generally attracts…
quiz.why: Same state → CGST + SGST; inter-state → IGST.

quiz.q: Scenario: an export of services invoice is issued under LUT. GST charged is…
quiz.why: Exports under LUT are zero-rated without paying IGST.

calc.problem: Inter-state services invoice: taxable value ₹4,50,000, IGST 18%. What's the invoice total?

lessons.title: Credit notes & debit notes
lessons.summary: You can't just edit a sent invoice; you issue a note.

term.meaning: A credit note reduces an amount a customer owes (for overbilling, discounts, returns or disputes), and a debit note increases it (for underbilling or extra charges), both linked to the original invoice.

sections.b: If you sent a friend a split-bill request for ₹1,000 but it should've been ₹800, you don't delete the message; you send 'sorry, ₹200 less'. That's a credit note. If you forgot to add ₹150 for drinks, you send 'add ₹150' - a debit note (or supplementary invoice). Accounting keeps the original invoice and adds a correction so the history is clear for auditors and tax.

• Receive request with reason (dispute, rate error, volume discount, service credit) and evidence
• Get approval per delegation of authority (often value-based)
• Create the note referencing the original invoice (SAP credit memo request → billing; Oracle credit memo)
• For India GST: report credit/debit notes in returns and through e-invoicing; GST credit notes have time limits - check current rules
• Apply the credit note against the invoice in AR
• Track volume and reasons as a billing-quality KPI

Invoice INV-7781 billed €120,000 to a German client at €600/day instead of the contracted €550/day for 200 days. The difference is 200 × €50 = €10,000. Billing raises credit note CN-0912 for €10,000 referencing INV-7781, gets manager approval, and AR applies it so the client's balance becomes €110,000.

• Credit notes reduce revenue; unusual volumes near quarter end can signal manipulation and attract audit attention
• Credit notes without approval or reason are an audit finding
• Avoid 'cancel and rebill' loops that confuse the customer and the ageing
• High credit-note % means upstream billing accuracy problems

lessons.action: Ask billing for last month's credit-note register and the top reasons.

quiz.q: A credit note…
options: Increases the amount a customer owes
Reduces the amount a customer owes
quiz.why: It's a downward correction.

quiz.q: A debit note is used when…
quiz.why: It increases the amount due.

quiz.q: Scenario: an invoice has the wrong rate and was already sent. Correct approach?
options: Issue an approved credit note (and rebill if needed) referencing the original
Edit the posted invoice amount directly
Ask the client to ignore it
quiz.why: Posted invoices are corrected through notes, keeping the audit trail.

lessons.title: Unbilled revenue vs billed (WIP)
lessons.summary: Work done but not invoiced yet is real money, and a real risk.

term.meaning: Unbilled revenue (often called WIP or, under Ind AS 115/IFRS 15, a contract asset or unbilled receivable) is revenue earned for work performed that has not yet been invoiced to the customer, while billed revenue has been invoiced and sits in AR.

sections.b: Like a tuition teacher who has taught the whole month but sends the bill on the 5th of next month. On the 31st, the money is earned but not yet billed. Finance must record it as revenue for that month (because the work happened), and show it as 'unbilled' until the invoice goes out. If unbilled keeps growing, something is stuck: missing timesheets, PO issues or unsigned milestones.

• At month end, calculate revenue earned from approved hours (T&M) or progress (fixed price)
• Compare with invoices issued; the gap is unbilled revenue
• Book: Dr Unbilled revenue (asset), Cr Revenue; reverse when invoiced
• Age unbilled balances and chase blockers (timesheets, PO, client approval)
• Report unbilled DSO with billed DSO
• Release billing as soon as triggers are met

March: a T&M project worked 2,000 approved hours at $50 = $100,000 revenue. Only $70,000 was invoiced by 31 March because the client PO ran out. Unbilled revenue = $30,000. In April, once the PO is extended, the $30,000 invoice is raised and unbilled is reversed to AR.

• Old unbilled (e.g. 90+ days) may never be billable; it may need provisioning
• Unbilled without a valid contract/PO is a red flag for revenue overstatement
• Classification differs: T&M unbilled is often an unbilled receivable; fixed-price progress before billing is a contract asset - follow your accounting policy
• Auditors test unbilled against timesheets and subsequent invoices

lessons.action: Ask for the unbilled revenue ageing for your largest client and the reason for its oldest item.

quiz.q: Unbilled revenue is…
options: Revenue earned but not yet invoiced
quiz.why: Work done, not yet billed.

quiz.q: When the invoice is raised, unbilled revenue is…
options: Reversed and moved to accounts receivable
quiz.why: It converts to billed AR.

quiz.q: Scenario: unbilled has grown 3 months in a row while billed revenue is flat. What's the likely issue?
options: Billing triggers are stuck (timesheets, POs, approvals)
quiz.why: Investigate blockers.

calc.problem: Quarter revenue recognised $9.0M; invoices raised in the quarter $7.8M; opening unbilled $1.1M, of which all was invoiced this quarter (included in the $7.8M). Closing unbilled?
steps: Closing unbilled = opening unbilled + revenue − invoices

lessons.title: Billing currency, exchange rates & invoice FX
lessons.summary: A dollar invoice from an Indian entity lives in two currencies at once.

term.word: Billing currency, exchange rates & invoice FX
term.meaning: Billing currency is the currency stated on the invoice per the contract, and the exchange rate converts it to the entity's local (functional) currency for booking, with later differences on collection or revaluation recorded as FX gains or losses.

sections.b: If you sell a used phone to a friend in the US for $200, you get paid in dollars but think in rupees. On the day of the deal $1 might be ₹83; when the money arrives it might be ₹85. You got ₹400 more than you expected - an FX gain. Companies record the invoice at the rate on the invoice date, then book the difference when cash arrives or at month-end revaluation.

• Bill in the currency stated in the contract (USD, EUR, GBP, etc.)
• ERP converts using the company's rate table (daily/monthly rates per policy, e.g. a reference rate source)
• Month end: revalue open foreign-currency AR at closing rate (SAP FAGL_FCV) - unrealised gain/loss
• On collection: difference between booked rate and receipt rate = realised gain/loss
• Check rate type, invoice currency and bank account currency before sending invoices
• Indian exporters must also track realisation of export proceeds within the RBI-permitted time - check current FEMA rules

Indian entity bills a US client $100,000 on 5 March at ₹83.00 = ₹83,00,000 AR. On 31 March closing rate is ₹83.50: unrealised gain ₹50,000. Cash arrives 20 April at ₹84.00 = ₹84,00,000. Total gain versus the original booking = ₹1,00,000: ₹50,000 shows up in March as unrealised, and the other ₹50,000 lands in April once the cash comes in. (If your ERP reverses the revaluation on 1 April, April shows a ₹1,00,000 realised gain less the ₹50,000 reversal, so the net is the same.)

• Invoicing in the wrong currency is a hard error that needs credit note and rebill
• Use the rate type defined in policy; manual rate overrides need approval
• FX on intercompany invoices must be mirrored on both sides or IC recon breaks
• Bank charges on foreign receipts are not FX loss; book separately

lessons.action: Ask billing which exchange-rate type and source your ERP uses for invoice conversion.

quiz.q: FX gain or loss when the customer pays at a different rate from the invoice is called…
quiz.why: Realised on settlement.

quiz.q: Month-end revaluation of open foreign AR produces…
quiz.why: Open items are revalued at closing rate.

quiz.q: Scenario: the contract says EUR but the invoice was issued in USD. Fix?
options: Credit note the USD invoice and rebill in EUR
quiz.why: Invoice currency must follow the contract.

calc.problem: Invoice €50,000 booked at ₹90.00/€. Customer pays when the rate is ₹91.20/€ (no revaluation in between). Realised gain or loss?

lessons.title: Rate cards & SOW/PO checks before billing
lessons.summary: Bill what the contract says, at the rate it says, against a PO that still has money.

term.word: Rate cards & SOW/PO checks before billing
term.meaning: A rate card lists the agreed rates per role, location or skill in a contract, and SOW/PO checks verify that each invoice matches the statement of work terms and the customer's purchase order (number, value remaining, validity) before it's sent.

sections.b: Like a salon price list: haircut ₹300, colour ₹1,200. If the stylist charges ₹1,500 for a haircut, you'll refuse. And if your gift voucher only has ₹500 left, you can't spend ₹800 on it. Rate cards are the price list; the customer's PO is the voucher with a balance and expiry date. Many big clients auto-reject invoices that don't quote a valid PO with enough balance.

• Maintain rate cards in the ERP/billing tool per contract (role, onsite/offshore, currency, validity)
• Before billing, check each resource's role and location against the rate card
• Check PO number, PO line, remaining value and expiry; request new PO/extension early
• Check SOW period, caps, discounts, rebates and invoicing instructions
• Flag rate changes (annual increases) that need a signed amendment
• Submit via customer portal (e.g. Ariba, Coupa) with matching PO data

A UK client's PO has £500,000 value, £60,000 remaining, valid till 31 Oct. October billing is £85,000. Billing raises £60,000 against the PO and asks the account manager for a PO extension for the remaining £25,000, which stays unbilled until the new PO arrives.

• Rate increases without signed amendments lead to disputes and credit notes
• Expired POs cause portal rejections and unbilled build-up
• Offshore resources billed at onsite rates (or vice versa) is a common error
• Track PO burn rate so you warn the client weeks in advance

lessons.action: Ask billing for a report of client POs with less than 20% balance remaining.

quiz.q: A rate card contains…
quiz.why: Contracted rates.

quiz.q: Why check PO balance before billing?
options: Customers often reject invoices exceeding the PO's remaining value
quiz.why: Over-PO invoices get rejected.

quiz.q: Scenario: the client agreed to a 5% rate rise verbally but no amendment is signed. Bill the new rate?
options: No, not until the amendment is signed per contract
quiz.why: Contract changes need documentation.

lessons.title: Billing cut-off at month end
lessons.summary: Which month does an invoice belong to? Cut-off decides.

term.meaning: Billing cut-off is the deadline and rules that decide which billing and revenue belong in the current month versus the next, so revenue, unbilled and AR are recorded in the right period.

sections.b: Like your exam result counting only assignments submitted before 11:59 pm on the last day. Work done before the cut-off counts this month; after, next month. Billing teams work fast in the last and first days of the month to invoice everything they can and to make sure nothing done in March is shown as April, or the other way round.

• Publish a month-end calendar (timesheet freeze, billing cut-off, unbilled calc, close)
• Freeze timesheets for the period; late timesheets go into unbilled calculation
• Raise all invoices whose triggers are met by the cut-off
• Calculate unbilled for work done but not invoiced
• Check invoice dates and posting periods (no March work posted in April without unbilled)
• Close the billing period in the ERP and lock postings

March close calendar: WD-1 timesheet freeze, WD+1 billing cut-off at 6 pm IST, WD+2 unbilled calculation, WD+3 revenue review. A milestone signed off on 31 March at 11 pm US time (1 April IST) - per policy, the acceptance date in the client's time zone is 31 March, so revenue and unbilled sit in March even though the invoice is dated 1 April.

• Pulling April invoices into March to hit targets is revenue manipulation
• Time zones matter for global clients; follow written policy
• Late timesheets mean revenue estimates; reverse and true-up next month
• Auditors test invoices around period end for cut-off errors

lessons.action: Ask for your organisation's month-end close calendar and find the billing cut-off time.

quiz.q: Billing cut-off ensures…
options: Revenue and billing are recorded in the correct period
quiz.why: Right period, right numbers.

quiz.q: Work done in March but invoiced on 2 April is shown in March as…
quiz.why: Earned in March, billed later.

quiz.q: Scenario: a manager asks to date April work as March to meet the quarter target. Response?
options: Refuse; it's a cut-off violation and should be escalated
quiz.why: That would misstate revenue.

lessons.title: Billing KPIs: on-time billing, billing accuracy, days-to-bill
lessons.summary: Fast, correct invoices = faster cash. Here's how billing is scored.

term.word: Billing KPIs: on-time billing, billing accuracy, days-to-bill
term.meaning: Billing KPIs measure how quickly and correctly invoices are produced, such as on-time billing % (invoices raised by the agreed date), billing accuracy % (invoices with no credit note or rework) and days-to-bill (time from billing trigger to invoice).

sections.b: Think of a restaurant that serves good food but brings the bill 40 minutes late, and gets it wrong half the time. Customers leave without paying properly. Billing KPIs check the 'bill' part: is it on time, is it right, and how long does it take? Every day of delay pushes DSO up.

• Measure on-time billing against the contract or internal SLA date
• Measure accuracy: invoices without credit notes, rejections or disputes in a period
• Measure days-to-bill: trigger date (timesheet approval, milestone) to invoice date
• Track portal rejection rate and unbilled ageing
• Root-cause analysis on misses (missing PO, wrong rate, late timesheets)
• Report monthly to finance and delivery leaders

September: 1,200 invoices due, 1,140 sent on time (95%). 36 needed a credit note or rebill (accuracy 97%). Average days-to-bill fell from 6 to 3 after automating timesheet-to-invoice for T&M contracts.

• Define 'accurate' precisely (credit notes only? portal rejections too?)
• Days-to-bill should be measured from the real trigger, not from when billing noticed it
• Targets differ by company - check your SLA
• A KPI looking great while unbilled rises means something is being excluded

lessons.action: Ask the billing lead for the last three months' KPI trend and the definition of each KPI.

quiz.q: Days-to-bill measures…
options: Time from billing trigger to invoice
quiz.why: Speed of invoicing.

quiz.q: Which suggests poor billing accuracy?
quiz.why: Corrections mean the original was wrong.

quiz.q: Scenario: on-time billing is 99% but portal rejections are 15%. Conclusion?
options: Invoices go out on time but many are wrong; fix accuracy
quiz.why: Speed without accuracy still delays cash.

calc.problem: 800 invoices due; 760 sent on time; 24 later needed a credit note or rebill. Trigger-to-invoice days total 2,400 across all 800. Compute on-time %, accuracy % and average days-to-bill.

lessons.title: Billing reconciliation: billed vs contract/timesheets & billing vs AR
lessons.summary: Billing recon proves we billed everything we should, and nothing we shouldn't.

term.word: Billing reconciliation: billed vs contract/timesheets & billing vs AR
term.meaning: Billing reconciliation compares what was invoiced against what should have been billed (approved timesheets, contract schedules, milestones) and checks that every invoice issued is correctly recorded in AR and the GL revenue accounts.

sections.b: Imagine a cab driver checking his trip log against fares collected and against what went into his bank. Trips with no fare = leakage. Fares with no trip = overcharging. Fares not in the bank = posting problem. Billing recon does all three checks for an IT company, and automation lets you do it every day instead of after a client complains.

• Billable vs billed: approved hours × rate card (or contract schedule) vs invoiced amount, per project and month
• Typical breaks: unbilled hours (missing PO, late timesheet), billed hours not in timesheets, wrong rate, wrong resource location, billing beyond cap, duplicate invoices
• Billing vs AR/GL: invoice register vs AR open items vs revenue GL; breaks from interface failures, manual invoices outside the system, cancelled invoices still in AR, FX differences
• Unbilled roll-forward: opening + revenue − invoices = closing, tied to the GL
• Document each break with owner and action (bill, credit, correct posting)
• Automation: pull timesheets, rate cards and invoices into a recon engine, match at project/resource/month level, and queue only exceptions

Project P-2231, March: approved hours 3,200; rate card average $45 → expected $144,000. Invoiced $139,500. Gap $4,500 = 100 hours of a new consultant not yet on the rate card (so not billed). Billing adds the role after the amendment is signed and bills $4,500 in April (shown as unbilled in March). The invoice register for March ($2.1M) ties to AR postings except one $12,000 manual invoice created outside the ERP, which is then posted properly.

• Revenue leakage (work done, never billed) is the most expensive break and often invisible without recon
• Overbilling causes disputes, credit notes and client trust issues
• Invoices outside the ERP break the billing-AR link; avoid them
• Recon evidence and reviewer sign-off are audit requirements

lessons.action: Ask billing whether they run a billable-vs-billed recon each month and what its biggest break category is.

quiz.q: Billable vs billed recon mainly detects…
quiz.why: Expected billing vs actual invoices.

quiz.q: A manual invoice created outside the ERP typically causes…
options: A break between the invoice register and AR/GL
quiz.why: It isn't in the system-generated AR.

quiz.q: Scenario: approved hours exceed billed hours for a consultant whose role is missing on the rate card. Correct action?
options: Get the rate added (with contract amendment if needed), show as unbilled, then bill
quiz.why: Fix the master/contract gap and bill properly.

calc.problem: Approved hours 1,500 at $40 = expected billing. Invoiced $57,600. What's the gap in $ and hours, and what might it be?
calc.answer: $2,400 (60 hours) unbilled: check for missing PO coverage, late approvals or a cap.

lessons.title: Payroll cycle & payroll calendar
lessons.summary: Every month, thousands of salaries must land on the right day, in the right amount, in 60+ countries. The payroll calendar is the timetable that makes it happen.

term.meaning: The payroll cycle is the repeating sequence of collecting inputs, calculating pay, checking it, paying employees and posting the cost to the books; the payroll calendar fixes the date of every step for every country.

sections.b: Think of a payroll cycle like a train timetable. The train (salary day) leaves at a fixed time no matter what, so every passenger (input: new joiners, leavers, bonuses, attendance) must reach the platform before the doors close (cut-off). If you are late you catch next month's train. The payroll calendar is simply the printed timetable for every country: when inputs close, when the draft run is ready, when it must be approved, when the bank file goes, and when the accounting entry is posted.

• Publish the yearly payroll calendar per country (input cut-off, draft run, approval, funding, pay date, GL posting) and share it with HR, managers and payroll vendors.
• Collect inputs: HR master changes (joiners, leavers, salary revisions, transfers), attendance/leave, one-time inputs (bonus, arrears, recoveries), tax declarations.
• Process the run in the payroll engine (in-house HRMS/ERP payroll or the in-country vendor's system).
• Validate: variance report vs last month, headcount reconciliation, exceptions (negative net pay, zero pay, huge jumps), maker-checker sign-off.
• Fund and pay: treasury funds the payroll account, bank/payment file is released so salaries credit on pay date.
• Post the payroll journal to the GL (salary expense, payables to employees, statutory liabilities like PF/TDS) and pay statutory dues by their due dates.
• Close: payslips released, payroll register archived, reconciliations and MIS prepared.

Priya in ES runs India payroll for ~40,000 employees with pay date on the last working day. Calendar: HR input cut-off on the 20th, draft run on the 22nd, variance review on the 23rd-24th, final approval on the 25th, bank file to the bank on the 27th, salary credit on the 30th, GL posting on the 30th. A sales head sends a joining-bonus approval on the 26th. Because the cut-off has passed, Priya does not re-open the run; it goes as a one-time input in next month's cycle (or as an off-cycle payment if the policy allows and the CFO approves).

• Late inputs after cut-off are the top reason for errors and off-cycle runs; track them as a KPI.
• Always compare this month's run with last month (headcount and amount variance) before approving; unexplained variance is an audit finding waiting to happen.
• Maker-checker: the person who processes the run should not be the one who approves and releases the bank file.
• Watch local holidays and weekends in each country; pay dates move and the calendar must say so.

lessons.action: Ask your ES colleagues for the payroll calendar of one country and note the input cut-off, approval date and pay date.

quiz.q: Why does payroll have an input cut-off date?
options: Because banks only work on the 20th
Because the GL closes on the 1st
To give the team time to calculate, validate, fund and pay before the fixed pay date
So employees cannot be paid bonuses
quiz.why: Processing and checks take days; the cut-off protects the pay date.

quiz.q: A manager sends a salary revision two days after the cut-off. What usually happens?
options: The whole run is re-done silently without approval
It goes into next month's run as arrears, unless an approved off-cycle is done
quiz.why: Late inputs roll to the next cycle (as arrears) or need an approved off-cycle.

quiz.q: Which step comes right before releasing the bank payment file?
options: Validation and approval of the payroll run
quiz.why: Pay only after the run is validated and approved.

lessons.title: Gross-to-net
lessons.summary: Your offer letter says one number, your bank account shows another. Gross-to-net is the maths in between.

term.meaning: Gross-to-net is the payroll calculation that starts with total earnings (gross pay), subtracts employee deductions such as tax and social security, and arrives at the net pay actually paid to the employee.

sections.b: Imagine you earn ₹100 for helping at a shop. Before you get it, ₹12 goes to your savings jar that you can't touch until later (PF), ₹8 goes to the government (income tax), and a tiny bit to the state (professional tax). You walk home with what's left; that's net pay. Gross is the whole ₹100. Your employer also pays some extra on top (their PF share) which never appears in your hand but is part of your CTC.

• Earnings: build gross from pay components (basic, HRA, special allowance, overtime, shift allowance, arrears, bonus).
• Pre-tax/statutory deductions: employee PF, ESI (if eligible), professional tax; in other countries social security, pension, health insurance.
• Income tax withholding: TDS on salary in India based on the chosen tax regime and projected annual income; PAYE in the UK, federal/state withholding in the US.
• Other deductions: loans, canteen, notice-pay recovery, voluntary deductions.
• Net pay = gross − all deductions; check no negative net pay.
• Employer contributions (employer PF, ESI, gratuity, social charges) are calculated separately; they are cost to company but not deducted from the employee.

Ravi in Bengaluru: basic ₹40,000, HRA ₹16,000, special allowance ₹24,000 → gross ₹80,000. Employee PF 12% of basic = ₹4,800 (this company computes PF on actual basic). ESI not applicable (gross above the ESI wage limit). Karnataka professional tax ₹200. TDS for the month ₹6,000 (projected annual tax ÷ remaining months). Net pay = ₹80,000 − 4,800 − 200 − 6,000 = ₹69,000. Employer separately pays PF ₹4,800, which shows in CTC, not in the net.

• Mixing up employee and employer contributions: employer PF is a cost, not a deduction from the employee.
• Tax regime: the employee's chosen regime (old vs new) changes TDS a lot; use the latest declaration.
• Rounding rules (statutory amounts are often rounded to the nearest rupee) and caps (PF wage ceiling, ESI wage limit) — check current rules.
• Validate gross-to-net on a sample of payslips every run, especially new joiners and leavers.

lessons.action: Open your own payslip and identify gross, each deduction, net pay, and which employer contributions are shown separately.

quiz.q: Gross pay ₹50,000; deductions PF ₹3,000, PT ₹200, TDS ₹2,800. What is net pay?
Employer's PF contribution is…
options: A cost to the company paid on top of salary, not deducted from the employee
Deducted from the employee's net pay
quiz.why: Employer PF is part of CTC, not a payslip deduction.

quiz.q: Which item is an earning, not a deduction?
quiz.why: Allowances add to gross; the rest reduce it.

calc.problem: Monthly: basic ₹40,000, HRA ₹16,000, special allowance ₹24,000. Employee PF 12% of basic, PT ₹200, TDS ₹6,000. Find gross and net pay.

lessons.title: Multi-country payroll & payroll vendors
lessons.summary: One company, 60+ countries, 60+ sets of tax rules. Nobody can know them all, so ES works with in-country payroll partners.

term.meaning: Multi-country payroll is running pay for employees in many countries, usually by combining a central team with in-country payroll providers who know local tax, social security, labour law and currency rules.

sections.b: Think of a food-delivery app that works in many cities. The app (the central ES team) sets the standard, tracks every order and checks quality, but in each city a local restaurant (the payroll vendor) actually cooks according to local taste (local tax law). The central team sends the inputs, the vendor calculates, the central team checks the output, funds it and books it in the ERP. Some vendors are aggregators that manage many local partners under one contract.

• Maintain a country matrix: vendor name, pay frequency (monthly, semi-monthly, bi-weekly in the US), pay date, currency, statutory filings and who files them.
• Send monthly inputs to each vendor in the agreed template (changes, hours, bonuses, leavers) through a secure channel/SFTP.
• Receive draft payroll outputs (payroll register, payslips, journal, funding request) and validate them against inputs and last month.
• Approve and arrange funding in local currency in time for pay date (often via treasury).
• Upload/post the vendor's GL file into the ERP with correct entity, cost centre and account mapping.
• Track vendor SLAs (accuracy, timeliness, query turnaround) and review their service controls report (e.g. SOC 1) annually.

The UK entity has 900 employees paid monthly in GBP through a UK provider who runs PAYE and National Insurance. The US entity pays bi-weekly in USD through a US provider that handles federal, state and local withholding. In month-end close, Arjun in ES gets both providers' journal files, maps vendor pay codes (e.g. 'NI_ER' for employer National Insurance) to ERP GL accounts and posts them into the respective company codes in local currency; the group books translate them to INR for consolidation.

• Pay-code mapping: one wrong mapping (e.g. employer tax posted as salary) breaks every month's GL until fixed.
• Data privacy: payroll data is personal data (GDPR in the EU, DPDP Act in India); use secure transfer and minimum access.
• Different pay frequencies mean month-end accruals for days worked but not yet paid (common in bi-weekly countries).
• Vendor errors are still the company's liability with the tax authority; always review, never just forward.

lessons.action: Ask ES which countries use which payroll vendor, and how the vendor's journal file is loaded into the ERP.

quiz.q: Why do global companies use in-country payroll providers?
options: They know local tax, social security and labour rules and file locally
Banks require them in every country
They remove the need for any internal review
quiz.why: Local expertise and filings are the main reason.

quiz.q: A US entity pays bi-weekly and the last pay date was 25 June. What is needed at 30 June month end?
options: Nothing, salary is only booked when paid
An accrual for salary earned 26-30 June but not yet paid
quiz.why: Days worked but unpaid at month end must be accrued.

quiz.q: Which is the central ES team's job, even when a vendor calculates pay?
options: Choosing employees' tax regime for them
Validating vendor output, funding, and posting the GL correctly
quiz.why: Accountability and review stay with the company.

lessons.title: Statutory compliances
lessons.summary: Salary is not just between employer and employee; the government takes its share, and missing a due date means interest and penalties.

term.meaning: Statutory compliance in payroll means correctly deducting, depositing and reporting the contributions and taxes the law requires, such as PF, ESI, professional tax and TDS in India, and social security and wage tax in other countries.

sections.b: Imagine your hostel rule: every month you must pay mess fees by the 15th, show the receipt, and once a year give a summary. Payroll compliance is like that, but with several authorities, each with its own form and deadline. The company collects money from your salary (and adds its own share) and must hand it over on time. If it is late, the 'hostel' charges interest and fines, and employees can lose benefits.

• India PF (EPFO): employee and employer contribute (12% each of PF wages is standard; part of employer share goes to pension, EPS); file the ECR and pay by the due date (15th of the following month).
• India ESI (ESIC): applies to employees below the wage threshold; employee and employer shares paid monthly — check current rates and limit.
• Professional tax: state-level tax (e.g. Karnataka, Maharashtra); rates and filing differ by state and some states have none.
• TDS on salary: deduct monthly on projected income, deposit by the 7th of the next month (March has a later date), file quarterly TDS returns (Form 24Q) and issue Form 16 annually. From 1 April 2026 the Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act and renumbers sections/forms — check current form names.
• Labour Welfare Fund, gratuity and bonus rules, and the new Labour Codes (in force from 21 Nov 2025, with state rules being notified) — check current rules.
• Other countries: e.g. UK PAYE/National Insurance via RTI, US federal/state withholding and Social Security/Medicare, Singapore CPF, Germany social insurance — each with its own filings, usually done by the in-country vendor.

October payroll for India: TDS deducted ₹42 crore, employee PF ₹18 crore and employer PF ₹18 crore, PT ₹0.6 crore. ES prepares challans: TDS deposited by 7 November, PF ECR uploaded and paid by 15 November, PT by the state due date. The GL statutory liability accounts (TDS payable, PF payable, PT payable) should become zero once paid. In January ES files Q3 Form 24Q; later, each employee gets Form 16.

• Late deposit = interest and penalties, and for PF/ESI possible prosecution and loss of deduction for employer; track a compliance calendar with owners.
• Employee-share deducted but not deposited is treated very seriously (it is the employee's money).
• Match the challan amount to the payroll register and the GL liability every month.
• Rates, wage ceilings and thresholds change (and Labour Codes changed the definition of wages); check current rules every year.

lessons.action: Ask for the statutory compliance calendar ES follows and see which challans are due this month.

quiz.q: What happens to the TDS payable GL balance after TDS is deposited correctly?
options: It should become zero for that month
quiz.why: Payment clears the liability created at payroll posting.

quiz.q: Which is a state-level payroll tax in India?
quiz.why: PT is levied by states, and not all states levy it.

quiz.q: ES finds employee PF was deducted in July but never paid. Why is this serious?
options: It is employee money held in trust; late payment brings interest, damages and legal risk
It only affects next year's bonus
It is not serious because PF is optional
PF can be paid any time without cost
quiz.why: Deducted-not-deposited statutory dues are a major compliance breach.

lessons.title: One-time inputs & cut-offs
lessons.summary: Bonuses, arrears, incentives, recoveries: anything that is not the regular monthly salary is a one-time input, and it is where most payroll mistakes hide.

term.meaning: One-time inputs are non-recurring pay items for a specific month (bonus, incentive, arrears, joining bonus, recoveries, deductions) that must be received, approved and loaded before the payroll cut-off.

sections.b: Your monthly salary is like your fixed mobile plan: same amount, auto-renewed. A one-time input is like a special top-up: someone must request it, someone must approve it, and it must be added before the billing cycle closes. Because it is manual and different every time, it needs extra checking — a wrong zero (₹1,00,000 instead of ₹10,000) is easy to make.

• Receive one-time inputs in a standard template from HR/business (employee ID, pay code, amount, month, approval reference).
• Check approvals against the delegation of authority (who can approve which bonus amount).
• Validate: employee active, pay code correct (taxable or not, PF-applicable or not), amount within reasonable limits, no duplicates.
• Load before cut-off; anything later goes to next month or an approved off-cycle run.
• Arrears: calculate back-dated differences (e.g. salary revision effective three months ago) including PF and tax impact.
• Recoveries: notice-pay shortfall, excess paid salary, advances; make sure net pay does not go negative.
• Reconcile total one-time inputs loaded vs total approved before final approval.

Appraisal letters effective 1 July are released on 10 September. In the September run, ES loads arrears for July and August: Neha's basic rose from ₹50,000 to ₹55,000, so arrears basic = ₹5,000 × 2 = ₹10,000 plus related allowances, with PF on the arrears basic (₹1,200 employee PF) and TDS recalculated. Separately, a quarterly sales incentive file of 2,300 rows arrives; ES's control check finds two employees listed twice and one leaver — both corrected before cut-off.

• Duplicates and decimal errors are classic; use control totals (row count and amount) from the approver.
• Wrong pay code = wrong tax and PF treatment; keep a pay-code master with tax/PF flags.
• Inputs after cut-off create off-cycle runs, extra bank files and more risk; measure on-time input %.
• Keep evidence of approval for every one-time payment; auditors sample these.

lessons.action: Look at one month's one-time input template and note which columns are mandatory and who approves.

quiz.q: Which is a one-time input?
quiz.why: Incentives are non-recurring items for a given month.

quiz.q: A bonus file total from HR is ₹2.4 crore but the loaded total is ₹2.6 crore. What should ES do?
options: Stop and investigate the ₹0.2 crore difference before approving
quiz.why: Control totals must match before release.

quiz.q: A revision effective two months ago is processed now. What is the extra payment called?
quiz.why: Arrears are back-dated pay differences.

lessons.title: Reimbursements & employee expense claims
lessons.summary: You spend from your pocket for work — a cab to the client, a hotel abroad — and the company pays you back. Simple idea, many rules.

term.meaning: Reimbursement is repaying employees for business expenses they paid personally, after checking receipts and policy, either through payroll or through an expense management tool and AP.

sections.b: Think of a group trip where you paid for everyone's tickets. You send the bill on the group chat, the organiser checks it's genuine and within the agreed budget, then pays you back. At work, the 'bill' goes into an expense tool (often linked to the ERP), your manager approves, finance checks the receipts and policy, and the money comes to your bank account. Some reimbursements (like certain allowances paid via payroll) have tax rules on whether they are taxable salary.

• Employee submits the claim in the expense tool with receipts, project/cost centre and expense category.
• Manager approves; finance/ES audits (policy limits per city/grade, valid tax invoice, no duplicates, correct currency rate).
• Approved claims are paid either via payroll (taxable or tax-free per rules) or through an AP/expense payment run.
• Corporate card transactions are matched to claims so the card bill is not paid twice.
• GL posting: expense by category and cost centre; GST input credit only if a proper tax invoice in the company's GSTIN is present.
• Advances given for travel are settled against claims; unsettled advances are chased.

Aman travels from Pune to Frankfurt for a client. He claims €1,200 hotel and €150 taxis. The expense tool converts at the policy rate to INR, his manager approves, and the auditor flags that one taxi receipt (€40) is a duplicate of one already claimed last week. €1,310 is approved and paid in the next reimbursement run; the €1,000 travel advance he took earlier is adjusted, so he receives the net €310 equivalent.

• Duplicate claims and claims without valid receipts are the top fraud/error risks; tools can auto-detect same amount/date/vendor.
• Taxability: some reimbursements are tax-free only with bills and for business use — check current rules.
• Old travel advances sitting open are a recon item and an audit concern.
• GST: claim input credit only on valid invoices billed to the company's GSTIN and eligible categories (food, for example, is often blocked).

lessons.action: Submit (or look at) one expense claim and follow its path: approval, audit, payment, GL account.

quiz.q: Why are corporate card transactions matched to expense claims?
options: To avoid reimbursing the employee for something the company already paid on the card
quiz.why: Matching prevents double payment.

quiz.q: An employee had a ₹20,000 travel advance and submits approved claims of ₹26,000. How much is paid?
When can GST input credit be taken on a hotel bill?
options: When it is a valid tax invoice in the company's GSTIN and the credit is not blocked
Whenever the employee paid by card
quiz.why: Valid invoice in the company's GSTIN and eligibility are required.

lessons.title: Leave balances & leave encashment provision
lessons.summary: Every unused leave day you carry is money the company may owe you later. Accounting must show that debt today.

term.meaning: A leave encashment provision is the liability the company books for unused leave that employees can carry forward and be paid for (on exit or as per policy), measured on current salary and, for long-term balances, actuarial valuation.

sections.b: Imagine a coffee shop loyalty card: each visit earns a stamp, and stamps can be swapped for coffee later. The shop must remember it owes those coffees even though nobody has claimed them yet. Leave works the same: each month you earn leave days; if policy lets you encash them, the company owes you money. Accounting (Ind AS 19 / IAS 19 'employee benefits') says book that obligation as you earn it, not when you leave.

• Maintain accurate leave balances in the HRMS (opening + accrued − availed − lapsed − encashed = closing).
• Identify encashable leave per policy and country (some countries require payout of accrued holiday on exit).
• Compute provision: encashable days × daily rate (basic or gross per policy); for long-term balances obtain an actuarial valuation (discount rate, salary growth, attrition) at quarter/year end.
• Book the monthly movement: Dr Leave encashment expense / Cr Provision for leave encashment (or reverse if lower).
• On payout (F&F or annual encashment) debit the provision, not expense again.
• Split current vs non-current portion for the balance sheet; disclose per Ind AS 19.

Kavya's basic is ₹60,000/month, so daily rate = ₹60,000 ÷ 30 = ₹2,000. Opening encashable balance 15 days (provision ₹30,000). This month she earns 1.5 days and takes 2 days off. Closing balance 14.5 days → provision ₹29,000. ES books a reversal of ₹1,000 (Dr Provision / Cr Expense). Multiply across 40,000 employees and leave provision is a big balance sheet number that auditors test.

• Leave balances in HRMS must be right; a wrong opening balance flows into provision and F&F.
• Use the correct base (basic vs gross) and divisor (30, 26 or actual days) per policy — keep it consistent.
• Tax: in India leave encashment may be deductible for tax only when paid, creating a deferred tax asset (see lesson 78) — check current rules.
• Actuarial assumptions must be reasonable and approved; reconcile the actuary's data file to HRMS headcount.

lessons.action: Check your own leave balance in the HR portal and estimate its value using your basic ÷ 30.

quiz.q: Why book a leave provision before anyone leaves?
options: It is optional and only for show
The obligation arises as employees earn leave, so the cost belongs to the period it is earned
quiz.why: Accrual accounting: book the obligation when earned.

quiz.q: On paying leave encashment in F&F, which account is debited?
quiz.why: The provision is used; expense was already booked.

quiz.q: Opening 20 days, accrued 2, availed 5, lapsed 1. Closing balance?

calc.problem: Basic ₹60,000/month (daily rate = basic ÷ 30). Opening 15 encashable days, accrued 1.5, availed 2. Find closing provision and the month's entry.
calc.answer: Closing provision ₹29,000; book a ₹1,000 reversal (Dr Provision, Cr Leave expense)

lessons.title: Benefit & bonus provisions / accruals
lessons.summary: Bonuses are paid once a year, but earned every month. Accruals spread the cost so no single month gets a shock.

term.meaning: A bonus or benefit accrual is a monthly provision for employee costs that are earned now but paid later (annual bonus, variable pay, gratuity, statutory bonus, medical benefits), trued-up when the actual amount becomes known.

sections.b: Suppose you plan a ₹12,000 trip in December. Instead of a big hit in December, you keep ₹1,000 aside each month. If in September you realise the trip will cost only ₹10,800, you adjust what's already saved. Companies do the same: they accrue 1/12 of the expected annual bonus each month and correct (true-up) when performance and payout percentages are clearer.

• Get the expected annual pool from HR/FP&A (target bonus × expected performance factor), split by entity and cost centre.
• Book monthly accruals: Dr Bonus expense / Cr Bonus provision.
• True-up each quarter when business performance changes; catch-up adjustments go in the current month.
• Long-term benefits (gratuity, long-service awards, pension in some countries) are measured by actuaries under Ind AS 19 / IAS 19; book service cost, interest cost and remeasurements (OCI for defined benefit plans).
• On payout, debit the provision; any excess/shortfall vs actual payout goes to expense.
• Reconcile provision balance roll-forward: opening + accrual − payout ± true-up = closing.

FY bonus pool estimate for the India entity: ₹1.2 crore, paid in May next year. ES accrues ₹10 lakh a month. After 9 months, ₹90 lakh is booked. In January the business forecasts a 90% payout, so the pool becomes ₹1.08 crore. Cumulative accrual should be ₹1.08 crore × 9/12 = ₹81 lakh, so ES reverses ₹9 lakh and accrues ₹9 lakh/month for the last 3 months, ending at ₹1.08 crore.

• Stale estimates: accruals that are never trued-up create big surprises at payout.
• Provisions with no supporting calculation are a classic audit finding; keep the working and approval.
• In India, statutory bonus (Payment of Bonus Act / Code on Wages) and gratuity have legal formulas — check current rules.
• Unused provisions must be reversed, not left sitting in the balance sheet.

lessons.action: Ask ES for the bonus provision roll-forward of one entity and see when the last true-up was done.

quiz.q: What is a 'true-up' of a bonus accrual?
options: Adjusting the accrued amount to the latest expected payout
quiz.why: True-up corrects cumulative accrual to the latest estimate.

quiz.q: Annual bonus estimate ₹24 lakh accrued evenly. How much provision after 4 months?
Bonus is finally paid ₹2 lakh less than the provision. What happens to the ₹2 lakh?
options: It is paid to the tax department
It stays in the provision forever
quiz.why: Excess provision is released.

calc.problem: Bonus pool ₹1.2 crore accrued evenly. After 9 months the estimate drops to ₹1.08 crore. Find the catch-up adjustment and new monthly accrual.
steps: Remaining = 1.08 crore − 81 lakh = ₹27 lakh over 3 months = ₹9 lakh/month
calc.answer: Reverse ₹9 lakh now; accrue ₹9 lakh per month for the last 3 months

lessons.title: Full & final settlement (F&F)
lessons.summary: When someone leaves, every rupee owed both ways must be settled once, correctly, and quickly.

term.meaning: Full and final settlement is the last payment to a leaving employee, combining unpaid salary, leave encashment, gratuity, bonus and reimbursements, minus recoveries (notice shortfall, advances, assets), with tax deducted.

sections.b: Think of moving out of a rented flat. You pay any remaining rent, the landlord returns your deposit minus damages, and you both sign that nothing more is owed. F&F is that for a job: salary up to the last day, money for unused leave, gratuity if eligible, minus anything you owe the company (notice period you didn't serve, a laptop not returned, an unadjusted advance).

• Receive the exit trigger from HR (last working day, notice served, reason) and clearances from IT, admin, finance (assets, advances, card dues).
• Calculate: salary for days worked, leave encashment, gratuity (eligibility per law/policy), pro-rata/statutory bonus, pending reimbursements.
• Recoveries: notice-pay shortfall (or waiver approval), advances, loans, asset recovery.
• Compute TDS on the final income and any tax exemptions (e.g. gratuity, leave encashment limits — check current rules).
• Approve, pay, issue F&F statement, Form 16 and relieving/experience letters; process PF exit (transfer/withdrawal is the employee's action on the EPFO portal).
• Post the GL: use leave and gratuity provisions, record recoveries; the Code on Wages expects payment within a short timeline (2 working days) — check current rules.

Rohit's last day is 20 June. Monthly gross ₹90,000 (basic ₹45,000). He worked 20 of 30 days, has 10 days encashable leave (on basic), 6 completed years (gratuity eligible), and served 45 of 60 notice days. F&F (before TDS/PT): salary ₹60,000 + leave ₹15,000 + gratuity ₹1,55,769 − notice shortfall ₹45,000 − employee PF on salary basic ₹3,600 = ₹1,82,169. Gratuity is often paid from the gratuity trust/insurer fund, so ES coordinates that leg separately.

• Delayed F&F creates employee complaints and legal risk; track ageing of pending F&Fs.
• Missing clearances (assets, advances) cause write-offs later.
• Gratuity formula and eligibility (15/26 × last drawn basic+DA × years; 5 years generally, shorter for fixed-term under the Labour Codes) — check current rules.
• After F&F, the employee's payroll and leave provision balances should be exactly zero.

lessons.action: Ask ES for an anonymised F&F statement and identify every earning and recovery line.

quiz.q: Which item is a recovery in F&F?
quiz.why: Notice shortfall is recovered unless waived.

quiz.q: After F&F is paid, what should the employee's leave provision balance be?
quiz.why: The provision is fully used or released.

quiz.q: An employee leaves without returning a laptop and clearance is pending. Best action?
options: Hold or recover per policy with approval, and document it
Ignore it and pay full F&F
quiz.why: Clearances drive recoveries; document approvals.

calc.problem: Basic ₹45,000, gross ₹90,000 (30-day month). Last day 20 June. 10 days leave on basic, 6 years service, notice shortfall 15 days on gross, employee PF 12% on salary basic earned. Compute F&F before TDS/PT.

lessons.title: Payroll reconciliation & payroll MIS
lessons.summary: Payroll is the biggest cost in an IT-services company. Reconciliation proves every rupee in the register reached the right place: the bank, the government, and the GL.

term.meaning: Payroll reconciliation compares the payroll register (what was calculated) with the GL (what was booked), the bank payout (what was paid) and statutory liability accounts (what was deposited), explaining every difference; payroll MIS reports the results to management.

sections.b: Imagine you organise a college fest: one list shows who should get paid how much (the register), your accounting notebook shows what you recorded (GL), your bank statement shows what actually went out (bank), and you also collected some money for the college fund that must be handed over (statutory dues). Reconciliation is ticking all four lists against each other until every line agrees, and writing a note for anything that doesn't.

• Register vs GL: total gross, each pay component and deduction vs the GL accounts posted, by entity and cost centre.
• Register net pay vs bank payout: total and employee-level match; investigate rejected/returned payments (closed accounts, wrong IFSC) and re-pay.
• Statutory liabilities: TDS, PF, ESI, PT payable in GL vs challans paid; balance should be zero after deposit.
• Salary payable / suspense: old unclaimed or returned salaries, holds and stops; age and clear them.
• Headcount recon: HRMS active employees vs paid employees (no ghost employees, no unpaid actives).
• Typical breaks: off-cycle runs not posted, pay-code mapping errors, FX on vendor-funded payroll, returned payments, timing (paid on 1st, booked on 30th).
• Automation (your area!): auto-load register, GL and bank files, match by employee ID/amount and by component totals, auto-clear exact matches, route exceptions with reason codes, and roll statutory liability recons forward each month.
• Payroll MIS: headcount, total cost by entity/vertical, variance vs last month and budget, overtime, attrition-driven F&F, compliance status — shared with FP&A and leadership.

October India payroll register net pay ₹210.40 crore. Bank shows ₹210.10 crore debited plus ₹0.25 crore returned later, and the GL salary payable account has ₹0.55 crore left. Breakdown: ₹0.30 crore withheld for employees on payroll hold (correct, documented) and ₹0.25 crore returned by the bank for 41 invalid accounts (to be re-paid after HR fixes bank details). The recon tool auto-matched 99.6% of employees; the analyst only works the 160 exceptions.

• A reconciliation with an unexplained 'other' bucket is not a reconciliation; every break needs a reason, owner and date.
• Ghost employees (paid but not in HRMS) and duplicate bank accounts are fraud red flags.
• Statutory liability accounts with old balances mean dues were missed or mis-posted.
• Prepare, review and sign off recons within the close calendar; keep evidence for SOX/internal audit.

lessons.action: Ask for last month's payroll-to-GL and payroll-to-bank recon and list the top three break types — they are your automation targets.

quiz.q: Payroll net pay ₹100 crore, bank paid ₹99.8 crore, ₹0.2 crore returned for invalid accounts. Where should ₹0.2 crore sit?
options: In salary payable as a liability until re-paid
quiz.why: Unpaid salary remains owed to employees.

quiz.q: Which check catches ghost employees?
options: Headcount recon: paid employees vs active HRMS employees
quiz.why: Anyone paid but not active in HRMS is a red flag.

quiz.q: What is the best first step to automate payroll-to-bank matching?
options: Only match totals once a year
Manually tick every employee each month
Match by employee ID and amount, auto-clearing exact matches and routing exceptions
quiz.why: Rule-based matching on keys and amounts with exception workflow.

lessons.title: Revenue recognition & the 5-step model
lessons.summary: Revenue is the top line every investor watches. Ind AS 115 / IFRS 15 says exactly when and how much you can call 'earned'.

term.meaning: Revenue recognition is the set of rules deciding when and how much revenue a company records; Ind AS 115 (India) and IFRS 15 use a 5-step model: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, determine the price, allocate the price, and recognise revenue when (or as) each obligation is satisfied.

sections.b: Imagine you're paid to tutor a student for 10 sessions for ₹10,000. You haven't earned ₹10,000 the day they sign up; you earn ₹1,000 each time you teach. If you also promised a free mock test, part of the ₹10,000 belongs to that test too. The 5-step model is just a disciplined way of asking: what did I promise, for how much, and how much of the promise have I delivered so far?

• Step 1 – Contract: confirm an enforceable agreement (MSA + SOW/PO), approved, with payment terms and collectability probable.
• Step 2 – Performance obligations (POs): list distinct promises (development, support, licence, managed service).
• Step 3 – Transaction price: fixed fees, T&M rates, variable consideration (rebates, penalties, bonuses), discounts.
• Step 4 – Allocate price to POs based on standalone selling prices.
• Step 5 – Recognise over time (most IT services: client benefits as you work) or at a point in time (e.g. some licences/hardware).
• CRT documents a revenue recognition memo per significant contract and configures the ERP/project system (billing plans, revenue recognition keys/methods).

A UK bank signs a ₹12 crore, 12-month deal with the company for application support (₹9 crore) and a one-time data migration (₹3 crore, delivered in month 3). CRT identifies two POs. Support is recognised over time, ₹75 lakh a month. Migration: if the client only benefits at completion and the company has no enforceable right to payment for work done to date, recognise ₹3 crore at completion in month 3; if over-time criteria are met, recognise as work progresses. Either way, the treatment is written into the contract memo before revenue is booked.

• No signed contract/SOW = no revenue (often called 'working at risk'); CRT must flag it, not book it.
• Bundled deals: allocate the price; don't just follow the invoice schedule.
• Billing ≠ revenue; the invoice date is not the recognition date.
• Keep memos for judgemental contracts; auditors will ask.

lessons.action: Ask CRT for one revenue recognition memo and map it to the 5 steps.

quiz.q: Which is step 2 of the 5-step model?
quiz.why: Step 2 lists the distinct promises.

quiz.q: Work started without a signed SOW. What should CRT do with revenue?
options: Not recognise until an enforceable contract exists; flag it
Book it anyway at full value
quiz.why: Step 1 requires an enforceable contract.

quiz.q: Most IT support services are recognised…
options: Only on the contract signing date
At the end of the financial year
Over time as the service is delivered
quiz.why: Client consumes the benefit as you perform.

lessons.title: Performance obligations
lessons.summary: A contract can hide several promises inside one price. Each distinct promise gets its own slice of revenue.

term.meaning: A performance obligation is a promise in a contract to transfer a distinct good or service (or a series of substantially the same services) to the customer; revenue is recognised separately for each.

sections.b: Think of a phone bundle: a handset, 12 months of data and a free case for one price. You get the phone today, data every month, and the case today. Each is a separate promise because you could buy them separately and use each on its own. If a contract says 'build, then support for 2 years', building and supporting are usually two obligations, so revenue for each follows its own timeline.

• Read the contract and SOWs; list every promise (build, test, deploy, support, licence, training, hardware).
• Test 'distinct': can the client benefit from it on its own or with readily available resources, and is it separately identifiable in the contract (not heavily integrated with other promises)?
• Combine non-distinct promises into one PO (e.g. design+build+integration delivered as one system).
• Identify 'series' (e.g. monthly managed service) treated as one PO satisfied over time.
• Estimate standalone selling price for each PO and allocate the total price.
• Set up each PO as a separate WBS element/revenue line in the ERP so revenue and unbilled are tracked separately.

A US retailer contract: ₹20 crore total for (a) building an e-commerce platform, (b) 2-year support, (c) training. CRT estimates standalone prices: build ₹15 crore, support ₹6 crore, training ₹1 crore (total ₹22 crore). Allocation of the ₹20 crore: build 15/22 × 20 = ₹13.64 crore, support ₹5.45 crore, training ₹0.91 crore. Build is recognised by progress, support evenly over 24 months, training when delivered.

• Splitting promises that are actually integrated (or combining distinct ones) changes timing — a key judgement.
• Free items (free training, free warranty beyond standard) are still promises and need a share of price.
• Standalone price evidence must be documented (price lists, rate cards, cost-plus-margin).
• Contract amendments may add new POs (see lesson 56).

lessons.action: Pick a contract summary in your ERP/project system and count how many performance obligations it has.

quiz.q: A managed-service contract delivers the same service every month for 3 years. How is it usually treated?
options: Revenue only at the end of 3 years
As a series: one performance obligation satisfied over time
quiz.why: Substantially similar services form a series.

quiz.q: Contract price ₹10 crore; standalone prices: A ₹8 crore, B ₹4 crore. Allocation to A?
Which suggests two promises are NOT distinct?
options: They are delivered at different times
The client can use each on its own
They are highly integrated into one combined output
They are sold separately on the price list
quiz.why: Heavy integration means one combined PO.

lessons.title: Revenue for T&M vs fixed-price
lessons.summary: Two pricing models dominate IT services. Time & material is like a taxi meter; fixed-price is like a pre-paid ride, and the accounting differs.

term.meaning: In time-and-material (T&M) contracts revenue follows billable hours/effort at agreed rates; in fixed-price (FP) contracts revenue is usually recognised over time by measuring progress, commonly with the input (cost-to-cost / effort) method.

sections.b: T&M is a taxi meter: every kilometre (hour) worked has a rate, so revenue = hours × rate, and the client usually pays for what was used. Fixed-price is a pre-paid cab: price is fixed whatever the traffic. To know how much of the ride you've 'earned', you check what share of the expected journey you've covered — measured by cost or effort spent so far versus the total you expect to spend. If the ride is going to cost you more than the fare, you must book the loss now.

• T&M: approved timesheets × rate card = revenue; often uses the 'right to invoice' practical expedient; accrue unbilled hours at month end.
• FP: project manager updates estimate-to-complete (ETC) every month; CRT computes % complete = cost (or effort) incurred to date ÷ total estimated cost.
• Cumulative revenue = % complete × contract value; this month's revenue = cumulative − already recognised.
• Compare with billing: excess revenue over billing = unbilled (contract asset); excess billing = unearned (contract liability).
• Onerous contracts: if total estimated cost exceeds price, provide for the full expected loss immediately (Ind AS 37).
• Review estimate changes (cumulative catch-up), especially big swings, with delivery and finance controllers.

Fixed-price project for a German insurer: contract ₹1 crore, estimated total cost ₹60 lakh. By Q1 end cost incurred ₹24 lakh → 40% → revenue ₹40 lakh; billed ₹30 lakh (milestone) → unbilled ₹10 lakh. In Q2 the estimate rises to ₹75 lakh and cost to date is ₹45 lakh → 60% → cumulative revenue ₹60 lakh, so Q2 revenue = ₹20 lakh. A T&M project next door: 160 hours × $50 = $8,000 for the month, booked from approved timesheets.

• Stale ETCs inflate % complete and revenue; ETC review is a key control.
• Costs that don't reflect progress (e.g. wasted effort, uninstalled hardware) should be excluded from the input measure.
• T&M: unapproved or rejected timesheets should not be revenue.
• Loss-making FP contracts must be identified early and provided for.

lessons.action: Ask CRT how often fixed-price ETCs are updated and who signs them off.

quiz.q: Contract ₹50 lakh, estimated cost ₹40 lakh, cost incurred ₹10 lakh. Cumulative revenue (cost-to-cost)?
A fixed-price contract is now expected to cost ₹1.2 crore against price ₹1 crore. What must be done?
options: Provide for the full expected ₹20 lakh loss now
quiz.why: Onerous contract losses are recognised immediately.

quiz.q: In T&M, revenue is mainly driven by…
quiz.why: T&M follows effort at agreed rates.

calc.problem: FP contract ₹1 crore. Q1: est. total cost ₹60 lakh, cost to date ₹24 lakh, billed ₹30 lakh. Q2: est. total ₹75 lakh, cost to date ₹45 lakh. Find Q1 revenue, Q1 unbilled, and Q2 revenue.
calc.answer: Q1 revenue ₹40 lakh (unbilled ₹10 lakh); Q2 revenue ₹20 lakh

lessons.title: Unbilled revenue & deferred revenue
lessons.summary: Revenue and invoices rarely move together. The gap shows up as unbilled revenue (earned, not billed) or deferred revenue (billed, not earned).

term.meaning: Unbilled revenue is revenue earned but not yet invoiced (shown as a contract asset, or as unbilled receivable when only time stands before billing); deferred/unearned revenue is amounts billed or received before the work is done (a contract liability).

sections.b: Picture a gym. If you trained a client all month but send the bill on the 5th of next month, you've earned money you haven't billed — unbilled. If the client paid a 3-month membership upfront, you have cash for months you haven't served yet — deferred. Unbilled is the company saying 'they owe us, the bill is coming'; deferred is 'we owe them service'.

• Month end: compute revenue per contract/PO, compare with billing to date.
• Revenue > billing → Dr Unbilled revenue / Cr Revenue; billing > revenue → Dr Revenue (or Receivable) / Cr Unearned revenue.
• Classify unbilled: unconditional (only time/invoice timing pending, e.g. T&M hours) = unbilled receivable; conditional on further performance (FP milestone not reached) = contract asset — check group policy.
• Age unbilled: old unbilled means billing delays, disputes or overstated revenue.
• Apply expected credit loss assessment to unbilled and contract assets as well.
• Release deferred revenue as service is delivered; reconcile the deferred balance contract by contract.

A Singapore client pays SGD 30,000 upfront on 1 April for 3 months of support. 30 April: revenue SGD 10,000, deferred revenue SGD 20,000. Meanwhile a T&M project worked 2,000 hours in April at $40, but the invoice goes out on 3 May: April revenue $80,000 booked against unbilled revenue; on 3 May the invoice moves it from unbilled to trade receivable.

• Unbilled older than 90 days is a key KPI and audit focus; ask why it isn't billed.
• Unbilled must reverse when invoiced; double counting (unbilled + receivable for the same work) is a common break.
• Deferred revenue mustn't be released faster than delivery.
• Presentation: contract assets/liabilities are shown per contract net, not offset across contracts.

lessons.action: Look at the unbilled ageing report and find the oldest bucket and its top three contracts.

quiz.q: Client paid ₹12 lakh upfront for 12 months. After 3 months, deferred revenue is…
quiz.why: 9 months of service still owed.

quiz.q: Hours worked in March, invoiced 4 April. What appears on 31 March?
quiz.why: Earned but not billed.

quiz.q: What happens to unbilled revenue when the invoice is raised?
options: It is cleared and becomes trade receivable
It stays and the receivable is added too
quiz.why: Unbilled moves to receivable on invoicing.

calc.problem: SGD 30,000 received 1 April for 3 months of support; also 2,000 T&M hours at $40 worked in April, invoiced 3 May. What is on the 30 April balance sheet?
calc.answer: Deferred revenue SGD 20,000 and unbilled revenue $80,000

lessons.title: Revenue accruals & reversals
lessons.summary: At month end the books must show what was earned, even if the invoice isn't out. Next month, those estimates are reversed and replaced by actuals.

term.meaning: A revenue accrual is a month-end entry recording revenue earned but not yet billed, usually set to auto-reverse on day 1 of the next month so the actual invoice can be booked without double counting.

sections.b: Imagine you're splitting a pizza bill with friends but the receipt hasn't come yet. You note in your notebook 'Rahul owes ~₹300'. When the actual receipt arrives showing ₹320, you cross out the ₹300 note and write ₹320. Accrual = the note; reversal = crossing it out; actual = the real receipt. Without crossing out, you'd think Rahul owes ₹620.

• Get unbilled effort (timesheets approved but not billed), milestones achieved, and FP % complete revenue by contract.
• Post accrual JEs (Dr Unbilled revenue / Cr Revenue) with support and approval; mark as auto-reversing.
• Day 1 next month: system reverses; invoices booked during the month replace the estimate.
• Track accrual accuracy: accrual vs actual invoice (a KPI); large differences mean poor estimates.
• Avoid 'evergreen' accruals that are reversed and re-booked month after month without ever being billed.
• Cost accruals (subcontractor costs) should match revenue accruals for margin accuracy.

On 31 July CRT accrues ₹4.8 crore for 600 T&M projects with approved but unbilled July hours. On 1 August the ERP auto-reverses the ₹4.8 crore. During August, billing raises July invoices worth ₹4.72 crore. Net effect in August from July work: −4.8 + 4.72 = −₹0.08 crore — an accrual accuracy of 98.3%. CRT investigates the ₹8 lakh gap (rate changes and rejected timesheets).

• Missing auto-reversal flag = double revenue next month; a classic error.
• Manual accruals need support (timesheets, milestone sign-off) and an approver other than the preparer.
• Accruals at quarter end are high-risk for audit (cut-off and management bias).
• Repeated accrual of the same item for months is a red flag for leakage or disputes.

lessons.action: Ask CRT for last month's accrual vs actual comparison and its accuracy %.

quiz.q: Why are revenue accruals set to auto-reverse?
options: So the actual invoice next month doesn't double-count the revenue
quiz.why: Reversal plus actual invoice = correct revenue.

quiz.q: Accrued ₹10 lakh; actual invoice ₹9.5 lakh. Net effect next month (from this work)?
quiz.why: −10 reversal + 9.5 invoice = −0.5.

quiz.q: An accrual has been reversed and re-booked for 6 months, never invoiced. What does it suggest?
options: A billing problem, dispute or possible revenue leakage to investigate
quiz.why: Evergreen accruals signal unresolved issues.

lessons.title: Contract modifications & variable consideration
lessons.summary: Deals change midway — scope grows, prices drop, rebates kick in. Revenue must follow the changed promise, not the old one.

term.meaning: A contract modification is an approved change in scope or price of a contract; variable consideration is any part of the price that can change (discounts, volume rebates, service-level credits, bonuses, penalties), estimated and included only to the extent a significant reversal is highly unlikely.

sections.b: Imagine a gym membership where the price drops 10% if you bring 5 friends this year. At the start the gym must guess: will you bring 5 friends? If very likely, it should record your fee at the lower price from day one. That's variable consideration. If halfway you upgrade to a premium plan, that's a contract modification — sometimes treated as a new contract, sometimes as part of the old one.

• Track change requests, amendments and new SOWs; only approved modifications count.
• Modification accounting: if it adds distinct services at their standalone price → treat as a separate contract; otherwise adjust the existing contract (prospectively or with cumulative catch-up).
• Variable consideration: estimate using expected value or most-likely amount; apply the constraint (don't book what might reverse).
• Volume rebates/discounts: book a refund liability/rebate accrual as revenue is recognised.
• SLA penalties/service credits: reduce revenue when probable.
• Review estimates every quarter and true-up.

A US client gets 5% rebate if annual hours exceed 10,000 at $100/hour. CRT expects 12,000 hours, so the rebate is likely. Q1: 3,000 hours billed at $100 = $300,000. Revenue booked at $95/hour = $285,000; refund (rebate) liability $15,000. If by Q3 hours look like only 8,000, the estimate changes and accumulated rebate liability is released to revenue.

• Booking full invoice value when a rebate/penalty is probable overstates revenue.
• Unapproved change requests are not modifications yet — don't book their revenue (though costs may be incurred).
• Document the estimation method and the constraint judgement.
• Credit notes issued later for discounts should hit the rebate liability, not current revenue.

lessons.action: Ask CRT which large contracts have volume rebates or SLA credits and how the accrual is tracked.

quiz.q: Billed $200,000; 5% rebate highly likely. Revenue to recognise?
A client adds a new distinct module at its standalone price. Usually this is…
options: Accounted for as a separate contract
A reduction of the old contract's revenue
quiz.why: Distinct goods at standalone price = separate contract.

quiz.q: What is the 'constraint' on variable consideration?
options: Always include the maximum possible bonus
Include it only if a significant revenue reversal is highly unlikely
Include only after cash is received
quiz.why: Prudence test under Ind AS 115 / IFRS 15.

calc.problem: Rate $100/hr, 5% volume rebate expected. Q1 hours 3,000. Compute billed amount, revenue and rebate liability.

lessons.title: Revenue cut-off & revenue leakage
lessons.summary: Revenue in the wrong month is a cut-off error; revenue that never gets billed at all is leakage. Both hurt.

term.meaning: Revenue cut-off means recording revenue in the period when it was earned, no earlier and no later; revenue leakage is revenue the company was entitled to but failed to bill or collect (missed hours, wrong rates, unbilled change requests, expired contracts still being served).
