sections.b: Cut-off is like dating your college assignment correctly: work done on 31 March belongs to March, even if you submit it on 2 April. Leakage is like doing extra tutoring sessions and forgetting to tell the parent — the work happened, but the money never came. For a big IT firm, tiny leaks across thousands of projects add up to crores.

• Cut-off: at period end, confirm effort up to the last day is included; invoices dated next period for this period's work are accrued; advance invoices are deferred.
• Test transactions around period end (last/first few days) for correct period.
• Leakage checks: timesheet hours vs billed hours, rate card vs invoice rate, approved change requests not yet billed, resources working on expired SOWs, unbilled expenses (travel re-billable to client).
• Fix root causes: rate master updates, SOW renewal alerts, timesheet compliance.
• Report leakage found and recovered as a KPI.

Leakage review for August: 1,20,000 billable hours in timesheets vs 1,18,600 billed. Of the 1,400-hour gap: 900 hours on a SOW that expired on 31 July (renewal pending — work at risk), 300 hours billed at the old rate (rate revision of $2/hour not updated), 200 hours timesheets approved late. CRT raises the late hours and rate-difference invoices, and escalates the expired SOW to the account manager.

• Quarter-end pressure leads to early revenue; auditors test cut-off heavily.
• Work without valid SOW: revenue not recognisable and leakage risk; track 'working at risk' hours.
• Rate masters must change with contract amendments — common leakage source.
• Re-billable expenses forgotten = pure leakage.

lessons.action: Ask CRT for the leakage tracker and the top root cause last quarter.

quiz.q: Work done 29-31 March, invoiced 3 April. Correct period for revenue?
quiz.why: Revenue follows the period earned.

quiz.q: 200 hours were billed at $48 instead of the new $50 rate. Leakage?
Which is a revenue leakage source?
quiz.why: Earned but unbilled = leakage.

lessons.title: Revenue by geography/vertical & revenue MIS
lessons.summary: Leadership doesn't just ask 'how much revenue?' but 'from where, from which industry, from which clients, and is it growing?'

term.meaning: Revenue MIS is management reporting that slices revenue by geography, industry vertical (BFSI, retail, manufacturing, healthcare), service line, client and contract type, compared with budget, forecast and prior periods.

sections.b: Think of a cricket team's scorecard. The total is nice, but the coach wants to know who scored, against which bowler, in which overs. Revenue MIS is the scorecard for the business: North America BFSI grew 4%, Europe retail fell 2%, top-10 clients are 30% of revenue. It helps leaders decide where to invest and which deals to chase.

• Ensure master data tags every contract/customer with geography, vertical, service line, delivery unit (profit centre/segment in the ERP).
• Run monthly revenue extracts after close; reconcile MIS total to GL revenue.
• Prepare views: actual vs budget vs last year, constant-currency growth (removing FX impact), top clients, T&M vs FP mix, offshore vs onsite mix.
• Explain variances with delivery/finance controllers (ramp-ups, project closures, FX).
• Feed segment reporting for published results (Ind AS 108 operating segments).
• Automate dashboards (Power BI/Tableau on ERP data) with drill-down.

Q2 revenue $1,000 million reported vs $970 million last quarter (+3.1%). Constant currency: USD strengthened, so revenue at last quarter's rates would be $1,010 million → constant-currency growth 4.1%. By vertical: BFSI $350m, Retail $180m, Manufacturing $150m, Others $320m. MIS ties to GL revenue exactly before release.

• MIS total must reconcile to GL; un-tagged revenue ('unassigned') signals master data gaps.
• Customer re-alignment between verticals needs approval; don't restate silently.
• Constant-currency method must be consistent quarter to quarter.
• Restricted, price-sensitive data for listed companies — handle per insider rules.

lessons.action: Open a revenue MIS deck and check if it shows constant-currency growth and how it ties to the GL.

quiz.q: Why report constant-currency growth?
options: To show business growth excluding exchange-rate movements
quiz.why: It separates real growth from FX effects.

quiz.q: MIS shows ₹5 crore revenue 'unassigned' to any vertical. Likely cause?
options: Missing vertical tags in customer/contract master data
quiz.why: Master data drives MIS slicing.

quiz.q: Revenue last quarter $500m, this quarter $520m. Growth?

lessons.title: Revenue controls & audit
lessons.summary: Revenue is the account auditors treat as presumed-risky. Controls prove the numbers are real, complete and in the right period.

term.meaning: Revenue controls are the checks (contract review, approvals, segregation of duties, system configurations, reconciliations, journal reviews) that ensure revenue is accurate and compliant; SOX-style internal controls over financial reporting test them every year.

sections.b: Imagine a school canteen where many students handle cash. The principal sets rules: two people count the cash, every sale is written in a register, the register is checked against the cash every evening. Nobody minds the rules, until money goes missing. Revenue controls are those rules for the company's top line. Auditing standards treat revenue as a presumed fraud risk, so auditors test these rules carefully.

• Contract review: CRT checks every new contract/SOW for performance obligations, pricing, variable terms, and signs a checklist before revenue setup.
• Master data controls: rate cards and billing plans entered by one person, approved by another.
• System controls (ITGC/application): revenue recognition methods configured and change-controlled in the ERP.
• Manual JE review: all manual revenue journals above a threshold reviewed by a manager with support.
• Period-end controls: cut-off review, unbilled ageing review, ETC review for FP contracts, onerous contract assessment.
• Reconciliations: revenue subledger vs GL, unbilled/deferred roll-forwards (see lesson 60).
• Provide audit evidence: contracts, timesheets, invoices, acceptance mails, memos; remediate deficiencies.

Statutory auditors sample 25 contracts from Q4. For contract #17, a $2 million FP deal, they ask for the signed SOW, the PO-identification checklist, the March ETC with project manager sign-off, and evidence that CRT's manager reviewed the % complete calculation. Everything is on the shared drive with sign-off dates before the close deadline — the control passes. For one manual JE, the reviewer signed after posting date by two weeks; this is logged as a control exception.

• Preparer and reviewer must be different people (segregation of duties).
• Evidence must be timely (review before close, not after audit asks).
• Top-side manual revenue entries at quarter end are high-risk; tight approvals.
• Automated controls (system-calculated revenue) reduce manual risk but need IT general controls to be reliable.

lessons.action: Ask CRT for the list of key revenue controls in the risk-control matrix (RCM) and who owns each.

quiz.q: Why is revenue a key audit focus?
options: It is not in the financial statements
Auditing standards presume a risk of fraud in revenue recognition
quiz.why: Revenue is a presumed fraud risk area.

quiz.q: A manual revenue JE was prepared and approved by the same person. What is the issue?
quiz.why: Maker and checker must differ.

quiz.q: Which is an IT-dependent revenue control?
options: System-configured revenue recognition method with change control
quiz.why: Automated controls rely on ERP configuration and ITGCs.

lessons.title: Revenue reconciliation
lessons.summary: Revenue, billing and unbilled are three views of the same work. The revenue reconciliation proves they agree — and that the subledger equals the GL.

term.meaning: Revenue reconciliation compares revenue recognised with billing raised and the movement in unbilled/deferred balances (revenue = billing + Δunbilled − Δdeferred), and ties the revenue subledger/project system to the general ledger.

sections.b: Imagine three friends each track the same cricket match: one counts runs scored (revenue), one counts runs announced on the scoreboard (billing), and one tracks runs 'scored but not yet on the board' (unbilled). At the end, runs scored should equal scoreboard runs plus the not-yet-shown runs. If not, someone miscounted. A revenue reconciliation forces those three counts to agree, contract by contract.

• Roll-forward per contract: opening unbilled + revenue − billing = closing unbilled (and the equivalent for deferred revenue).
• Subledger vs GL: revenue in the project/billing subledger vs GL revenue accounts by entity, profit centre, currency; check manual JEs posted directly to GL.
• Billing register vs AR: invoices in billing system vs receivables posted.
• Typical breaks: manual JEs posted directly to GL, invoices cancelled/credit notes not reflected in revenue, FX revaluation differences on unbilled, accrual not reversed, intercompany revenue mismatches, timing of invoice posting.
• Automation: pull subledger, GL and billing data daily, match on contract/WBS + period + amount, auto-explain known patterns (FX, reversals), flag contracts with negative unbilled or aged unbilled, and produce a roll-forward ready for review.
• Review and sign-off within close; carry open items with owners and target dates.

Contract C-2045 for June: opening unbilled ₹50 lakh, revenue ₹80 lakh, billing ₹1 crore → expected closing unbilled ₹30 lakh. The GL shows ₹38 lakh. The ₹8 lakh break: a credit note for a disputed May invoice was booked in billing but never reflected in revenue. CRT reduces revenue by ₹8 lakh (or confirms it was an invoicing error) and the recon clears. Across 5,000 contracts the matching engine auto-clears 92%; analysts work the rest.

• Negative unbilled for a contract (billing far ahead of revenue without deferred revenue) means a misclassification.
• GL-only manual revenue entries must be in the reconciliation as reconciling items with support.
• FX: unbilled in foreign currency is revalued; the recon must separate FX from real breaks.
• Unreconciled differences 'plugged' to a suspense account are an audit red flag.

lessons.action: Get one month's revenue-to-billing roll-forward and see which break types repeat — design matching rules for them.

quiz.q: Opening unbilled ₹20 lakh, revenue ₹60 lakh, billing ₹50 lakh. Closing unbilled?
Which is a common revenue recon break?
options: Credit note in billing not reflected in revenue
quiz.why: Credit notes often break the roll-forward.

quiz.q: A contract shows negative unbilled. What does it suggest?
options: Billing ahead of revenue booked wrongly instead of as deferred revenue, or a posting error
quiz.why: Excess billing belongs in deferred revenue.

calc.problem: Contract C-2045: opening unbilled ₹50 lakh, June revenue ₹80 lakh, June billing ₹1 crore. GL closing unbilled ₹38 lakh. Find expected closing and the break.
steps: Investigate: e.g. credit note in billing not reflected in revenue/unbilled
calc.answer: Expected ₹30 lakh; ₹8 lakh break to investigate

lessons.title: Treasury vs banking operations
lessons.summary: Treasury decides what to do with the company's money; banking operations make sure every rupee actually moves, gets recorded and reconciled.

term.meaning: Treasury is the strategic function managing liquidity, funding, investments, FX and financial risk; banking operations is the day-to-day processing of payments, receipts, bank statements, bank reconciliations and bank account administration.

sections.b: Think of a cricket team: treasury is the captain and coach deciding the strategy — when to attack, when to defend, which bowler to use (invest surplus, hedge dollars, borrow or not). Banking operations is the ground staff and scorers making sure the pitch is ready, every run is recorded and the scoreboard is right (payments released, statements loaded, entries posted, reconciliations done). Both are needed; one without the other fails.

• Treasury front office: cash forecasting, investment of surplus (FDs, liquid funds), borrowing, FX hedging decisions, bank relationships, policy limits.
• Middle office: risk limits, counterparty exposure, hedge effectiveness, treasury MIS.
• Back office/banking ops: confirmations of deals, settlement, accounting entries (interest, FX gains/losses), payment processing (vendor, payroll, tax, intercompany).
• Daily: load bank statements (MT940/camt.053), auto-post bank charges/interest, match receipts and payments, prepare cash position.
• Monthly: bank reconciliations for all accounts, FX revaluation of bank balances, confirm balances for audit.
• Bank account management: opening/closing accounts, signatory mandates, KYC.

Monday 9 a.m.: banking ops loads statements from 300+ bank accounts in 60 countries into the ERP. By 11 a.m. the cash position shows ₹480 crore across India accounts and $40 million overseas. Treasury decides to place ₹100 crore surplus in a 30-day FD and to sell $10 million forward for next month's receipts. Banking ops then books the FD placement, records the forward deal, and next month posts interest and settles the forward.

• Segregation: the person who decides a deal (front office) must not confirm and settle it (back office).
• Payments must be released only by authorised signatories with dual control.
• Unreconciled bank accounts are a fraud risk — every account, even dormant ones, needs a recon.
• Treasury actions must follow the board-approved treasury policy (limits, approved banks, instruments).

lessons.action: Ask who in your organisation prepares the daily cash position and who approves investment decisions.

quiz.q: Which is a treasury decision rather than a banking-ops task?
options: Deciding to hedge next quarter's dollar receipts
quiz.why: Hedging is a strategic risk decision.

quiz.q: Why separate deal-making and deal-confirmation?
options: To prevent unauthorised or fictitious deals going unnoticed
quiz.why: Front/back office segregation is a key control.

quiz.q: Daily bank statements usually arrive in which kind of format?
options: Electronic statements like MT940 or camt.053
quiz.why: SWIFT MT940 and ISO 20022 camt.053 are standard.

lessons.title: Bank reconciliation statement (BRS)
lessons.summary: Your books say one balance, the bank says another. The BRS is the bridge that explains why — line by line.

term.meaning: A bank reconciliation statement explains the difference between the bank balance per the company's books (cash book/GL) and per the bank statement on a date, by listing timing items (uncleared cheques/payments, deposits in transit) and items not yet booked (bank charges, interest, direct credits/debits) or errors.

sections.b: Imagine you track your spending in an app. You paid a friend by cheque yesterday — your app shows it, but your bank hasn't seen it. The bank cut ₹50 SMS charges — the bank shows it, your app doesn't. So the two balances differ, and both are 'right'. A BRS lists these reasons until the gap is fully explained. Anything left unexplained is a real problem.

• Get the GL bank balance and the bank statement balance for the same date.
• Identify items in books not in bank: payments issued not yet debited (unpresented cheques, in-process transfers), receipts recorded not yet credited (deposits in transit).
• Identify items in bank not in books: bank charges, interest, direct customer receipts, auto-debits, returned payments.
• Book the 'bank-only' items in the GL (charges, interest, direct receipts once identified).
• Prepare the BRS: adjusted book balance = adjusted bank balance.
• Age reconciling items; chase old ones (stale cheques, unidentified receipts) and clear them.

31 March, HDFC current account: GL balance ₹10,00,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹1,50,000; deposit in transit ₹80,000; bank charges not booked ₹2,000; interest credited not booked ₹5,000; customer direct credit not booked ₹40,000. Adjusted book = 10,00,000 − 2,000 + 5,000 + 40,000 = ₹10,43,000. Bank statement balance should be ₹11,13,000; adjusted bank = 11,13,000 − 1,50,000 + 80,000 = ₹10,43,000. Matched.

• Unexplained differences, however small, must not be 'plugged'.
• Stale reconciling items (e.g. cheques older than validity period) must be reversed/re-issued per policy.
• The preparer and reviewer must be different; sign off within close timelines.
• Direct credits sitting as 'unidentified receipts' affect customer ageing — clear them with the collections team.

lessons.action: Ask Banking for a recent BRS and count how many reconciling items are older than 30 days.

quiz.q: Bank charges appear in the bank statement but not in books. What should be done?
options: Ask the bank to reverse them always
Book the charges in the GL
quiz.why: Bank-only items are booked once validated.

quiz.q: A cheque issued on 30 March is cleared by the bank on 3 April. On the 31 March BRS it is…
quiz.why: Recorded in books, not yet in bank.

quiz.q: GL ₹5,00,000; deposit in transit ₹20,000; no other items. Bank balance?
quiz.why: The deposit is in books but not yet in bank: 5,00,000 − 20,000.

calc.problem: GL ₹10,00,000. Unpresented cheques ₹1,50,000; deposit in transit ₹80,000; bank charges ₹2,000 and interest ₹5,000 not booked; direct customer credit ₹40,000 not booked. Find adjusted book balance and bank statement balance.
steps: Bank = adjusted book + unpresented cheques − deposit in transit

lessons.title: Cash positioning & cash forecasting
lessons.summary: Knowing how much cash you have today (position) and will have next month (forecast) decides whether you invest, borrow or delay.

term.meaning: Cash positioning is the daily snapshot of available cash across all bank accounts after expected same-day flows; cash forecasting projects future inflows and outflows (collections, payroll, vendors, taxes, capex, dividends) over weeks or months.

sections.b: Like checking your wallet and UPI balance in the morning (position) and then planning the month: salary comes on the 1st, rent goes on the 5th, fees on the 15th (forecast). If you see a shortfall around the 15th, you plan ahead. For a company with 60+ countries, the same thing happens daily across hundreds of accounts and many currencies.

• Daily: aggregate opening balances from bank statements/APIs, add known receipts and payments for today → cash position by entity and currency.
• Collect forecast inputs: collections from O2C, AP payment runs, payroll from ES, tax payments from taxation, capex, intercompany settlements, debt service.
• Build 13-week rolling forecast and monthly/annual forecast; compare actual vs forecast (variance %) to improve accuracy.
• Decide: invest surplus, fund deficits (intercompany loans, credit lines), move cash between accounts.
• Keep a minimum cash buffer per policy.
• Report liquidity KPIs: forecast accuracy, idle cash, days cash on hand.

India entity, next month: opening ₹50 crore; collections ₹120 crore; payroll ₹80 crore; vendor payments ₹30 crore; GST/TDS/advance tax ₹15 crore. Closing = 50 + 120 − 80 − 30 − 15 = ₹45 crore. Minimum buffer per policy ₹40 crore → ₹5 crore can be invested short term. Last month the forecast missed collections by 8% because a large client paid late; treasury now asks collections for client-level commitments.

• Forecasts that are never compared with actuals don't improve; track accuracy.
• Trapped cash: some countries restrict moving money out (exchange controls); forecast by country.
• Payroll and tax dates are non-negotiable outflows; never plan to delay them.
• Use the same entity/currency master data as the ERP so position ties to GL.

lessons.action: Ask Treasury for this week's cash position report and the forecast accuracy for last month.

quiz.q: Opening ₹20 crore, inflows ₹30 crore, outflows ₹35 crore. Closing?
Forecast collections ₹100 crore, actual ₹92 crore. Forecast variance?
Which input does treasury typically get from the ES team?
quiz.why: Payroll is a major predictable outflow.

lessons.title: Payment channels & payment files
lessons.summary: Money moves through rails — NEFT, RTGS, SWIFT, host-to-host. Knowing which rail and which file format avoids failed or duplicate payments.

term.meaning: Payment channels are the systems used to transfer money (in India NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, UPI; cross-border SWIFT; local clearing systems abroad like ACH, SEPA, BACS), and payment files are the structured files the ERP sends to the bank (often via host-to-host/SFTP integration) to execute bulk payments.

sections.b: Think of sending parcels: a regular courier (NEFT, batch-processed but now 24x7), an express courier for big valuable parcels (RTGS, real-time, for high values), and an international courier (SWIFT, cross-border). Instead of going to the counter for each parcel, a big company sends one manifest with thousands of parcels — that's the payment file, sent through a secure direct line between the ERP and the bank (host-to-host).

• AP/ES/tax approve payment proposals in the ERP payment run; ERP generates the payment file (bank format or ISO 20022 pain.001).
• File is encrypted and sent host-to-host (SFTP/API) to the bank; dual authorisation on the bank portal if required.
• Bank returns acknowledgements and status (accepted, rejected, paid) — reverse files update the ERP.
• Domestic: NEFT (24x7, batch settlement), RTGS (real-time, high value — check current minimum), IMPS/UPI for small instant payments.
• Cross-border: SWIFT MT103/ISO 20022 pacs.008; beneficiary bank SWIFT/BIC, IBAN in Europe; FEMA documentation and Form 15CA/15CB where required.
• Rejected/returned payments go back to AP/ES for bank detail correction and re-payment.

Friday AP run: 4,200 vendor payments, ₹68 crore. The ERP creates one file for HDFC (NEFT/RTGS mix) and one SWIFT file for $1.2 million to 40 overseas vendors. Files go host-to-host; HDFC rejects 6 payments for invalid IFSC. The status file auto-updates the ERP, the 6 open items go back to the master data team, and the rest show 'paid' in the bank reconciliation the next morning.

• Never let anyone edit a payment file between ERP and bank; H2H with encryption and checksum prevents tampering.
• Vendor bank-detail changes are a major fraud channel; verify via call-back before change.
• Duplicate files (re-sent after a timeout) can cause double payment; use unique file/batch IDs.
• SWIFT is moving to ISO 20022 messages; formats and fields are changing — check current bank specifications.

lessons.action: Ask Banking which payment channels and file formats are used for India vs overseas payments.

quiz.q: Which channel is typically used for high-value real-time domestic transfers in India?
quiz.why: RTGS is real-time gross settlement for large values.

quiz.q: A payment file is re-sent after a network timeout. What is the risk?
options: Duplicate payment of the same batch
quiz.why: Use unique batch IDs and check status before re-sending.

quiz.q: What does a host-to-host connection do?
options: Directly and securely transfers files between the ERP and the bank
quiz.why: H2H automates secure file exchange.

lessons.title: FX exposure & hedging
lessons.summary: An Indian IT company earns in dollars, euros and pounds but pays salaries in rupees. A small rupee move can swing profit by crores — hedging limits that.

term.meaning: FX exposure is the risk that changes in exchange rates alter the value of foreign-currency receivables, payables, cash or future cash flows; hedging uses instruments like forward contracts and options to lock or limit the rate.

sections.b: Imagine you'll get $1,000 from a freelance client in three months. Today $1 = ₹88. If the rupee strengthens to ₹86, you get ₹2,000 less. A forward contract is like booking a fixed rate with the bank today: in three months you sell $1,000 at, say, ₹88.6 no matter what the market does. You lose the chance of extra gain if the rupee weakens, but you sleep peacefully.

• Identify exposures: transaction (receivables/payables), forecast (expected future revenue), translation (foreign subsidiaries' net assets).
• Hedge per policy: e.g. hedge a rolling % of forecast USD inflows over 12 months using forwards/options with approved banks.
• Book deals in the treasury system; confirm with bank; record notional, rate, maturity.
• Month end: revalue foreign-currency balances at closing rates (exchange gain/loss); mark-to-market derivatives.
• Hedge accounting (Ind AS 109 cash flow hedges): effective portion to OCI (hedge reserve), recycled to P&L when hedged revenue occurs; documentation needed.
• Settle at maturity and post realised gain/loss.

Invoice $1,00,000 booked at spot ₹88.00 = ₹88,00,000 receivable. Treasury sells $1,00,000 forward for 3 months at ₹88.60. At maturity spot is ₹87.50. The customer pays $1,00,000, sold under the forward for ₹88,60,000. Without the hedge the company would get ₹87,50,000. Accounting: FX loss on receivable (88.00 − 87.50) × 1,00,000 = ₹50,000; gain on forward (88.60 − 87.50) × 1,00,000 = ₹1,10,000; net gain ₹60,000.

• Over-hedging (hedging more than real exposure) turns hedging into speculation.
• Deals must be within board-approved limits and counterparties.
• Hedge accounting needs designation and documentation at inception; missing it pushes all MTM to P&L.
• Reconcile treasury system deals to bank confirmations and the GL every month.

lessons.action: Ask Treasury what % of next quarter's USD receipts are hedged and with which instruments.

quiz.q: An Indian IT exporter with USD receivables loses when…
options: The rupee weakens against the dollar
The rupee strengthens against the dollar
quiz.why: Fewer rupees per dollar received.

quiz.q: Forward sold at ₹84; spot at maturity ₹82; amount $10,000. Gain on forward?
Under cash flow hedge accounting, the effective portion of MTM goes first to…
quiz.why: It is recycled to P&L when the hedged item affects P&L.

calc.problem: Receivable $1,00,000 booked at ₹88.00. Forward sold at ₹88.60. Spot at maturity ₹87.50. Compute rupees received, loss on receivable, gain on forward, net.
calc.answer: ₹88,60,000 received; net gain ₹60,000 vs the booked ₹88,00,000

lessons.title: Bank guarantees & letters of credit
lessons.summary: Big clients and governments often want a bank's promise backing the company's promise. That's what BGs and LCs are.

term.meaning: A bank guarantee (BG) is a bank's promise to pay a beneficiary if the company fails to meet an obligation (e.g. bid bond, performance guarantee, advance payment guarantee); a letter of credit (LC) is a bank's undertaking to pay a seller on presentation of compliant documents, mainly used in trade.

sections.b: Imagine renting a flat where the landlord wants a guarantee. Your parent signs: 'If my child doesn't pay, I will.' A BG is the bank playing that parent for the company. An LC is like an escrow at an online marketplace: the bank promises the seller 'deliver as agreed, show me the proof, and I'll pay you', so the seller doesn't have to trust the buyer directly.

• Receive a BG request from business (tender, client contract) with format, amount, validity, claim period.
• Review wording with legal (avoid open-ended or on-demand terms beyond policy); get approval per delegation.
• Apply to the bank under sanctioned non-fund-based limits; margin/collateral if required; pay BG commission.
• Track BG register: number, beneficiary, amount, expiry, claim date, linked contract; renew or cancel on time.
• Get the original BG returned/discharge letter on completion to release limits and stop commission.
• Disclose BGs as contingent liabilities/commitments in financial statements as required.
• LCs: check documents (invoice, bill of lading, insurance) strictly against LC terms (UCP 600 rules) before presentation/payment.

A Middle East government bank awards a ₹40 crore project requiring a 10% performance guarantee. Treasury issues a ₹4 crore BG through an approved bank with 2-year validity plus a 3-month claim period, paying commission of, say, 1% a year (₹4 lakh/year — rates vary). The BG register sends alerts 60 days before expiry. After project acceptance, treasury obtains the discharge letter and cancels the BG, freeing the bank limit.

• Expired-but-not-returned BGs keep consuming limits and commission; chase discharge.
• Unlimited/open-ended wording creates unlimited risk — legal review is mandatory.
• Reconcile the BG register with bank statements of outstanding BGs quarterly.
• Commission is a period cost — amortise over BG validity if paid upfront.

lessons.action: Ask Treasury for the BG register and see how many guarantees expire in the next 60 days.

quiz.q: What is a performance bank guarantee?
options: A bank's promise to pay the client if the company fails to perform the contract
quiz.why: It protects the beneficiary against non-performance.

quiz.q: A project finished but the client never returned the BG. What should treasury do?
options: Obtain a discharge letter/return so limits are released and commission stops
Pay the BG amount to the client
quiz.why: Active BGs consume limits and cost commission.

quiz.q: In an LC, the bank pays the seller when…
options: Documents presented comply with the LC terms
quiz.why: LCs are document-based undertakings.

lessons.title: Working capital & cash pooling
lessons.summary: Working capital is the cash tied up in running the business. Cash pooling helps a group use its cash across entities efficiently.

term.meaning: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities (mainly receivables + unbilled − payables − accruals); cash pooling is a structure that concentrates or notionally combines balances of group entities to reduce idle cash and borrowing costs.

sections.b: Think of a family with three siblings, each with their own wallet. One has ₹5,000 spare, another is short ₹3,000 and borrows from a friend at high interest. Silly, right? Cash pooling is the family saying: put all spare money in one shared jar (physical pooling) or let the bank treat all wallets as one (notional pooling). Working capital is how much cash is stuck in 'people owe us' minus 'we owe others'.

• Measure working capital KPIs: DSO (days sales outstanding, including unbilled), DPO (days payables outstanding), cash conversion cycle.
• Work with O2C to cut DSO (faster billing, collections) and with AP on payment terms.
• Set up pooling where allowed: physical (zero-balancing sweeps into a header account) or notional (interest calculated on combined balances).
• Record intercompany loans created by sweeps, with interest at arm's length (transfer pricing!).
• Respect local regulations: India has exchange-control (FEMA) limits on cross-border pooling of rupee accounts, so pools are often regional (e.g. Europe, US) — check current rules.
• Reconcile pool balances and intercompany positions monthly.

Revenue ₹3,650 crore a year (₹10 crore/day). Receivables + unbilled = ₹800 crore → DSO = 80 days. If DSO falls to 70 days, ₹100 crore of cash is released. In Europe, the company's UK, Germany and Netherlands entities sweep balances to a header account in the Netherlands each evening; the German entity's €2 million overdraft is covered by the UK surplus instead of a bank loan, and intercompany interest is booked monthly.

• Sweeps create intercompany balances that must match on both sides (IC reconciliation).
• Notional pooling may face tax and regulatory limits in some countries.
• Include unbilled in DSO for IT services, otherwise the picture is too rosy.
• Interest on pool balances must be arm's length for transfer pricing.

lessons.action: Ask what the current DSO is and whether unbilled revenue is included.

quiz.q: Receivables ₹600 crore, annual revenue ₹3,650 crore. DSO?
In zero-balancing physical pooling, what happens to subsidiary accounts at day end?
options: Balances are swept to or from a header account, leaving zero
quiz.why: Sweeps move cash to the header account.

quiz.q: Why might an Indian entity not join a global cash pool easily?
options: Exchange-control rules restrict cross-border pooling of rupee balances
There is no cash in India
quiz.why: FEMA rules limit cross-border pooling.

lessons.title: Bank charges, interest & investment of surplus funds
lessons.summary: Banks charge for every service and pay for every deposit. Treasury makes surplus cash earn safely, and banking ops books it right.

term.word: Bank charges, interest & investment of surplus funds
term.meaning: Bank charges are fees for services (payments, SWIFT, BGs, account maintenance), interest is earned on deposits/investments or paid on borrowings, and surplus funds are invested in safe, liquid instruments like fixed deposits (FDs) or liquid mutual funds within treasury policy.

sections.b: Your savings account gives a little interest; an FD gives more but locks your money. Companies do the same with crores. Treasury's rule of thumb: Safety first, Liquidity second, Yield third (SLY). Meanwhile, every SWIFT transfer might cost a fee — small per payment but big across thousands, so banking ops checks the bank isn't overcharging versus the agreed rate card.

• Invest per policy: approved banks/funds, counterparty limits, tenors matched to cash forecast.
• Book FD placement: Dr Fixed deposit / Cr Bank; accrue interest monthly: Dr Interest accrued / Cr Interest income.
• On maturity: principal + interest credited; reverse accrual; TDS deducted by the bank (if any) is recorded as a tax receivable/credit — check current rules.
• Bank charges: auto-post from statement codes; compare monthly with the bank's agreed tariff (bank fee analysis); claim refunds for overcharges.
• Borrowings: accrue interest, track covenants.
• Report yield on investments and total bank cost per transaction.

Treasury places ₹5 crore in a 91-day FD at 7% (simple interest, illustrative). Interest = 5,00,00,000 × 7% × 91/365 = ₹8,72,603. At month ends banking ops accrues interest for the days elapsed. Also, the review of bank charges finds SWIFT fees charged at ₹1,000 per transfer instead of the negotiated ₹600 for 300 transfers — ₹1,20,000 overcharge claimed back.

• Interest accruals missed at month end understate income; ensure FD register drives accruals.
• Investments outside policy limits need prior approval; breaches are reported.
• TDS deducted on interest must be matched with Form 26AS/AIS for tax credit (see lesson 74).
• Bank charges posted to a suspense account and never analysed = silent leakage.

lessons.action: Ask Treasury for the FD register and check how interest accruals are calculated.

quiz.q: What does SLY stand for in treasury investing?
quiz.why: Safety first, then liquidity, then yield.

quiz.q: ₹1 crore FD at 8% for 1 year (simple). Interest?
Bank charges exceed the agreed tariff. Best action?
options: Analyse and claim the overcharge from the bank
quiz.why: Bank fee analysis recovers overcharges.

calc.problem: ₹5 crore FD for 91 days at 7% simple interest (365-day year). Find interest. Also: 300 SWIFT transfers charged ₹1,000 vs agreed ₹600 — find overcharge.

lessons.title: Bank account management & signatory controls
lessons.summary: Who can open a bank account, and who can move money out of it? These are some of the most important controls in a company.

term.meaning: Bank account management covers opening, maintaining and closing bank accounts with proper approvals, KYC documentation and a central register; signatory controls define who may authorise payments (mandates, limits, dual signatures) and keep that list up to date.

sections.b: Think of your family's joint account: you'd want to know every account that exists, who has the debit card, and require two people to approve big transfers. If someone leaves the family (an employee resigns), you'd take back their card immediately. Banks need KYC (know your customer) documents — board resolutions, IDs, address proof — before they let the company open or change an account.

• Account opening: business justification, approval per delegation (often CFO/board resolution), KYC pack to bank.
• Maintain a central bank account register: bank, entity, account, currency, purpose, signatories, e-banking users, status.
• Signatory matrix: panels (A/B), limits, dual authorisation; electronic banking roles (maker/checker).
• Update mandates on joiners/leavers promptly; quarterly review of signatories and e-banking users vs HR records.
• Close dormant/unneeded accounts after moving balances; ensure all accounts are reconciled until closure.
• Respond to periodic KYC refresh requests from banks; failure can freeze accounts.

During a quarterly review, Banking compares the e-banking user list for 120 accounts with HR data and finds two users who left the company three months ago still have authoriser access on a Singapore account. Access is revoked the same day, the bank confirms in writing, and the incident is reported to internal controls. They also find a dormant Brazil account with a small balance — it is reconciled, funds moved, and the account closed with board approval.

• Leavers with live signatory rights are a top fraud risk.
• Accounts not in the register (opened locally without approval) can hide fraud — get bank confirmations listing all accounts.
• No single person should be able to create and approve a payment.
• Expired KYC can freeze accounts on payroll day; track KYC renewal dates.

lessons.action: Ask how often the signatory and e-banking user list is reviewed and against what source.

quiz.q: An employee who was an authoriser has resigned. What should happen first?
options: Revoke their signatory and e-banking rights immediately
quiz.why: Leaver access must be removed promptly.

quiz.q: What is dual authorisation?
options: Two different authorised people must approve a payment
quiz.why: It prevents one-person fraud.

quiz.q: Why keep a central bank account register?
options: To know every account, its signatories and ensure all are reconciled
quiz.why: Completeness of accounts is a key control.

lessons.title: Bank reconciliation automation
lessons.summary: With thousands of transactions a day across hundreds of accounts, manual ticking is impossible. Matching engines do the heavy lifting; humans handle exceptions.

term.meaning: Bank reconciliation automation uses rule-based (and sometimes ML-assisted) matching of bank statement lines to GL/subledger entries, auto-posting known items, and routing unmatched open items to owners with ageing and reason codes.

sections.b: Imagine sorting 10,000 socks. A machine pairs all socks with the exact same colour and size instantly (one-to-one exact match), then pairs ones that are slightly different but obviously matching (fuzzy match), then bundles three small socks that match one big sock (many-to-one). Only the truly odd socks come to you. That's auto-matching: rules first, people for exceptions.

• Ingest bank statements (MT940/camt.053/BAI2/APIs) daily and GL/subledger items (payments, receipts, journals).
• Matching rules, in order: exact (amount + reference/cheque/UTR + date), tolerant (amount within tolerance, date window ± n days), one-to-many/many-to-one (one bank credit for many invoices; one payment file debit for many vendor payments), keyword rules (narration contains 'CHGS' → bank charges).
• Auto-post bank-only items (charges, interest) via rules to GL accounts.
• Exceptions workflow: unmatched items routed to AP, O2C, ES, treasury with reason codes; ageing buckets; SLA to resolve.
• KPIs: auto-match rate (%), number/value of open items, ageing > 30/60/90 days, time to reconcile.
• Continuous improvement: analyse exceptions monthly and add/tune rules; avoid over-loose rules that create false matches.

Before automation, 25 analysts reconciled 300 accounts in 6 days. Now the engine processes 1.8 lakh lines/month: exact rules match 78%, UTR-based many-to-one rules for customer receipts add 12%, and charge/interest keyword rules add 4% → 94% auto-match. The remaining 6% (≈10,800 lines) go to queues. Analysis shows 40% of exceptions are customer receipts with no invoice reference — the team adds a rule using remittance advice data and auto-match rises to 96%.

• Over-tolerant rules can match wrong items — sample-test auto-matches periodically.
• Rule changes need change control and documentation (they are controls in themselves).
• Unmatched items must not be force-cleared to suspense to hit KPIs.
• Bank statement completeness: check statement sequence numbers/opening balance = previous closing.

lessons.action: Ask for the auto-match rate by account and the top three exception reasons — pick one and propose a rule.

quiz.q: Which matching rule handles one customer payment that settles five invoices?
quiz.why: Group matching handles aggregated payments.

quiz.q: 180,000 lines, 169,200 auto-matched. Auto-match rate?
Why sample-test auto-matched items?
options: To catch false matches from rules that are too loose
quiz.why: Automation needs validation too.

lessons.title: Direct vs indirect tax
lessons.summary: Some taxes are on what you earn, some are on what you buy or sell. The tax team handles both, in India and abroad.

term.meaning: Direct tax is levied on income and paid by the person who earns it (corporate income tax, TDS as a collection mechanism, withholding tax); indirect tax is levied on supply of goods/services and collected from the customer by the supplier (GST in India, VAT in Europe, sales tax in the US).

sections.b: When you earn a salary, income tax comes from your own earnings — that's direct. When you buy a coffee for ₹118, ₹18 of it might be GST: you pay it, but the café collects and hands it to the government — that's indirect. A company pays direct tax on its profit and acts like the café for indirect tax on the services it sells.

• Direct tax: compute taxable income, pay advance tax, deduct/deposit TDS on payments, file the income-tax return, tax audit report, transfer pricing reports, handle assessments.
• Indirect tax: charge GST correctly on invoices, claim input tax credit, file GST returns, handle refunds (e.g. on exports), respond to notices.
• International: VAT/GST registrations and returns for foreign entities (often with local advisors), withholding tax on cross-border payments, foreign tax credits.
• Maintain tax GL accounts: income tax payable/advance tax, TDS receivable/payable, GST input/output, deferred tax.
• Monthly/quarterly tax provisioning and reconciliations with returns.
• From 1 April 2026 the Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act (with a 'tax year' concept and renumbered sections/forms) — check current names.

The India entity invoices a Bengaluru client ₹10 lakh + 18% GST = ₹11.8 lakh. GST of ₹1.8 lakh is indirect tax: collected from the client and paid to government (less input credit). At year end, the entity's profit of ₹500 crore attracts corporate income tax — a direct tax on its own income, paid via advance tax instalments. When the client pays, it deducts TDS (e.g. under the professional/technical services provisions) — that's direct tax collected in advance on the company's income.

• Mixing up GST payable and TDS receivable accounts is a common posting error.
• Indirect taxes are 'pass-through' only if collected and paid correctly; errors become real cost.
• Each country has its own registration thresholds and filing calendars; maintain a global tax compliance calendar.
• Law changes often (budgets, notifications); check current rules.

lessons.action: List the tax GL accounts in your entity's chart of accounts and classify each as direct or indirect.

quiz.q: Which is an indirect tax?
quiz.why: GST is levied on supplies.

quiz.q: A client deducts TDS when paying the company's invoice. For the company this is…
options: A credit against its own income tax (TDS receivable)
quiz.why: TDS deducted by customers is advance income tax of the company.

quiz.q: UK VAT is the equivalent of which Indian tax?
quiz.why: VAT and GST are both consumption taxes.

lessons.title: GST basics for services
lessons.summary: Every invoice the company raises needs the right GST: CGST+SGST, IGST, or zero. Place of supply decides which.

term.meaning: GST on services in India is charged as CGST+SGST for intra-state supplies and IGST for inter-state supplies, based on the place of supply; export of services is a zero-rated supply, which can be made without paying IGST under a Letter of Undertaking (LUT).

sections.b: Think of GST as a toll on services. If you sell within your own state, the toll is split half to the Centre (CGST) and half to the state (SGST). If you sell to another state, the Centre collects one combined toll (IGST) and shares it with the destination state. If you sell abroad (export), India doesn't want to tax its exports, so the toll is zero — and with an LUT you don't even need to pay first and claim back later.

• Determine place of supply (IGST Act rules; for most B2B services, the recipient's location).
• Same state as supplier's registration → CGST + SGST (e.g. 9% + 9% for 18% services); different state → IGST 18%.
• Export of services: supplier in India, recipient outside India, place of supply outside India, payment in convertible foreign exchange (or INR where RBI permits), and not between establishments of the same person → zero-rated.
• File the LUT (Form GST RFD-11) at the start of each financial year to export without paying IGST; claim refund of unutilised ITC.
• Ensure invoices carry GSTIN, HSN/SAC code (IT services mostly under SAC 9983), place of supply, tax breakup; e-invoicing (IRN/QR) for applicable taxpayers.
• Reverse charge (RCM): pay GST on certain imports of services (e.g. foreign vendor's services) and claim it as ITC.

The Karnataka-registered unit raises three invoices of ₹10,00,000 each: (1) Bengaluru client → CGST ₹90,000 + SGST ₹90,000; (2) Mumbai client → IGST ₹1,80,000; (3) US client, paid in USD, LUT filed → zero-rated, no GST charged, invoice marked 'supply meant for export under LUT without payment of IGST'. The foreign-currency proceeds (FIRC/e-BRC) must be tracked to prove export of services.

• Wrong place of supply (IGST charged instead of CGST+SGST) means paying again under the right head and claiming a refund — painful.
• Missing LUT renewal means exports need IGST payment and refund instead.
• Not receiving export proceeds in time can break the export-of-services condition — check current rules.
• Rates and SAC codes change; check current rules.

lessons.action: Look at one domestic and one export invoice and spot the GST breakup and the LUT declaration.

quiz.q: Karnataka supplier bills a Tamil Nadu client. Which GST?
quiz.why: Inter-state supply attracts IGST.

quiz.q: What is an LUT used for?
options: Exporting services without paying IGST upfront
quiz.why: LUT allows zero-rated exports without tax payment.

quiz.q: Indian entity bills a US client in USD for software development. Normally this is…
options: Export of services (zero-rated) if conditions are met
quiz.why: Meets the export of services conditions.

calc.problem: Karnataka unit bills ₹10,00,000 each to (a) a Bengaluru client, (b) a Mumbai client, (c) a US client under LUT. GST rate 18%. Compute GST on each.

lessons.title: GST returns & ITC matching
lessons.summary: GST is self-assessed through returns. Input tax credit is only as good as your vendors' filings — so matching is everything.

term.meaning: GSTR-1 reports outward supplies (sales invoices), GSTR-3B is the summary return where tax is paid after setting off input tax credit (ITC), and GSTR-2B is the auto-drafted statement of ITC available based on suppliers' filings, which must be matched with the purchase register before claiming ITC.

sections.b: Imagine a group project where you get marks only if your teammate also submits their part. ITC works like that: you can claim credit for GST you paid to a vendor only if the vendor reports that invoice in their GSTR-1, so it appears in your GSTR-2B. GSTR-1 is your list of what you sold; GSTR-3B is the final bill where you pay output tax minus eligible credit.

• Monthly: extract sales register from ERP → reconcile → file GSTR-1 (due around the 11th of next month for monthly filers — check current dates).
• Download GSTR-2B (generated mid-month) and reconcile with the purchase register by GSTIN + invoice number + amount; use the Invoice Management System (IMS) to accept/reject/keep pending supplier invoices.
• Claim ITC only if: tax invoice held, service received, tax paid by vendor, invoice in GSTR-2B, credit not blocked (Section 17(5) e.g. food, personal use), and vendor paid within 180 days.
• Prepare GSTR-3B: output tax − eligible ITC = cash payable; pay and file (around the 20th — check current dates).
• Follow up vendors whose invoices are missing in 2B; hold their payment or GST portion per policy.
• Annual return (GSTR-9) and reconciliation statement (GSTR-9C) where applicable.

April: purchase register ITC ₹12,00,000. ₹50,000 is blocked credit (employee food/catering). ₹80,000 relates to vendor invoices missing in GSTR-2B (vendor not yet filed). GSTR-2B also shows ₹30,000 for invoices not yet booked (investigate and book first). Eligible ITC = 12,00,000 − 50,000 − 80,000 = ₹10,70,000. Output tax ₹15,00,000 → cash payable in GSTR-3B = ₹4,30,000. The ₹80,000 is claimed in a later month once vendors file (within the time limit).

• Claiming ITC not in GSTR-2B leads to notices, interest and reversal.
• ITC must be claimed within the statutory time limit (generally by 30 November after the financial year — check current rules).
• GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B liability mismatches trigger system alerts/notices.
• Book GST input to separate GL accounts by type (IGST/CGST/SGST) for clean reconciliation.

lessons.action: Ask Taxation for last month's GSTR-2B vs books recon and the value of ITC on hold due to vendor non-filing.

quiz.q: Which return reports outward supplies invoice by invoice?
quiz.why: GSTR-1 is the outward supplies return.

quiz.q: A vendor's invoice is in your books but not in GSTR-2B. Best action?
options: Don't claim yet; follow up the vendor to file
quiz.why: ITC needs the invoice to appear in GSTR-2B.

quiz.q: Output tax ₹5 lakh, eligible ITC ₹3.5 lakh. Cash payable?

calc.problem: Books ITC ₹12,00,000; blocked credit ₹50,000; invoices missing in GSTR-2B ₹80,000; output tax ₹15,00,000. Find eligible ITC and cash payable.

lessons.title: TDS: deduction, deposit & returns
lessons.summary: When the company pays a vendor, landlord or employee, it often must keep back a slice of tax and give it to the government — that's TDS.

term.meaning: Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) requires the payer to deduct income tax at prescribed rates from specified payments (salary, professional/technical fees, contracts, rent, interest, payments to non-residents), deposit it by due dates, file quarterly TDS returns and issue TDS certificates; the deductee sees the credit in Form 26AS/AIS.

sections.b: Imagine your college collects exam fees and directly sends a part to the university on your behalf so you don't forget. TDS is the government asking every payer to do the collecting. The vendor gets paid a bit less but gets a credit for the tax already paid. If the company forgets to deduct or deposit, it pays interest and penalties — and can lose the expense deduction.

• At invoice/payment: AP system applies TDS based on vendor's section/nature code, PAN status and any lower-deduction certificate (higher rate if no valid PAN — check current rules).
• Deposit TDS by the 7th of the next month (March has a later due date — check current rules) via challan.
• File quarterly returns: 24Q (salary), 26Q (resident non-salary), 27Q (non-residents); 27EQ is for TCS.
• Issue certificates: Form 16 (salary, annual), Form 16A (non-salary, quarterly).
• Correct errors via revised returns; resolve defaults shown on TRACES.
• As deductee: customers deduct TDS on the company's invoices; reconcile with Form 26AS/AIS to claim credit in the income-tax return.
• From 1 April 2026 the Income-tax Act, 2025 renumbers TDS sections and forms — check current names.

AP books a ₹5,00,000 invoice from a Pune IT consultant (professional fees). Assume TDS at 10% under the professional-fee provision: AP pays ₹4,50,000 to the vendor and credits ₹50,000 to TDS payable. Taxation deposits ₹50,000 by 7 May for April deductions, reports it in Q1 26Q by 31 July, and issues Form 16A. The vendor sees the ₹50,000 in their Form 26AS and uses it against their tax.

• Wrong section/rate (e.g. contract vs professional) leads to short deduction and interest.
• Late deposit attracts interest per month or part; late filing has fees.
• PAN errors make the deductee's credit fail — validate PAN in vendor master.
• Check GST is excluded from the TDS base where shown separately on the invoice — check current rules.

lessons.action: Ask Taxation for the list of TDS sections most used in AP and their rates for this year.

quiz.q: Invoice ₹2,00,000; TDS 10%. Amount paid to vendor?
Which quarterly return covers TDS on payments to non-residents?
quiz.why: 27Q is for non-residents.

quiz.q: A customer deducted TDS but it is not in the company's Form 26AS. What should be done?
options: Ask the customer to deposit/correct their TDS return so the credit appears
quiz.why: Credit is allowed based on 26AS/AIS; the deductor must fix it.

lessons.title: Corporate income tax & advance tax
lessons.summary: Companies don't wait until year end to pay income tax. They estimate and pay in instalments during the year.

term.meaning: Corporate income tax is tax on a company's taxable profit; advance tax is the system of paying it in instalments during the year based on estimated income, with interest if instalments are short or late.

sections.b: It's like paying your annual gym fee in four instalments instead of one big shock. The government says: estimate your profit for the year, and pay 15% of the tax by mid-June, 45% (cumulative) by mid-September, 75% by mid-December and 100% by mid-March. If you under-estimate, you pay interest. At year end you calculate the actual tax and pay the balance (self-assessment) or claim a refund.

• Estimate annual taxable income: book profit ± adjustments (disallowances, depreciation difference, provisions not deductible until paid, exempt income).
• Compute tax at the applicable rate (many Indian companies opt for the concessional regime; effective rate including surcharge and cess ≈ 25.17% — check current rules).
• Reduce by TDS/TCS credits and MAT credit (if applicable) to get advance tax payable.
• Pay instalments by due dates: 15 June (15%), 15 September (45%), 15 December (75%), 15 March (100%) cumulative — check current rules under the new Act.
• Book: Dr Advance tax (asset) / Cr Bank; at period end compute current tax provision, net advance tax against provision.
• File return, tax audit report and transfer pricing report; track refunds and demands.

Estimated FY tax liability ₹40 crore; expected TDS credit from customers ₹4 crore → net advance tax ₹36 crore. Cumulative: June 15% = ₹5.4 crore; September 45% = ₹16.2 crore (pay ₹10.8 crore); December 75% = ₹27 crore (pay ₹10.8 crore); March 100% = ₹36 crore (pay ₹9 crore). In December the estimate is revised up because of a large one-off gain; the December instalment is increased to avoid interest for shortfall.

• Under-estimating income → interest on shortfall (check current rules); re-estimate every quarter with FP&A.
• Keep working papers for each instalment (estimate basis, approvals).
• Global entities pay corporate tax under their own country's rules and calendars (e.g. quarterly estimates in the US/UK large companies).
• Reconcile advance tax paid (challans) with the GL and with Form 26AS/AIS.

lessons.action: Ask Taxation for this year's advance tax working and see what was paid by 15 September.

quiz.q: Cumulative advance tax due by 15 September for a company (as per the traditional schedule)?
What happens if advance tax paid is lower than required?
options: Interest becomes payable on the shortfall
quiz.why: Shortfall attracts interest.

quiz.q: Net advance tax ₹20 crore; paid ₹3 crore by June. Cumulative due by December?

calc.problem: Estimated tax ₹40 crore, TDS credit ₹4 crore. Compute instalment amounts using cumulative 15%/45%/75%/100%.
calc.answer: Instalments: ₹5.4 cr, ₹10.8 cr, ₹10.8 cr, ₹9 cr (check current rules)

lessons.title: Transfer pricing basics
lessons.summary: When the Indian parent does work for its own US subsidiary, what price should it charge? Tax authorities on both sides care deeply.

term.meaning: Transfer pricing is the pricing of transactions between related entities of the same group (intercompany services, loans, royalties), which must follow the arm's length principle — the price unrelated parties would agree in similar circumstances — supported by documentation and benchmarking.

sections.b: Imagine two brothers running shops in different towns. If the elder sells goods to the younger at a silly-low price, one town's tax office loses tax. Tax authorities say: charge each other what you'd charge a stranger. In an IT-services group, the US subsidiary often signs the client contract and subcontracts delivery to the Indian entity; the price for that subcontract must be arm's length (commonly cost plus a markup, tested using the TNMM method).

• Map all intercompany transactions: services (delivery, support, management), cost recharges, loans/guarantees, cash pool interest, royalties.
• Agree intercompany agreements and pricing policy (e.g. Indian delivery centre at cost + x% markup; front-end subsidiaries earn a routine margin).
• Benchmark with comparable companies (TNMM, cost-plus, CUP methods) and document in local file, master file and country-by-country report (CbCR) where thresholds apply.
• Monitor actual margins during the year; make year-end true-up adjustments to stay within the arm's length range.
• Ensure intercompany invoices, GST/withholding tax and IC reconciliation are aligned with TP.
• In India: accountant's report (Form 3CEB) and TP documentation; options like safe harbour and advance pricing agreements (APA) — check current rules.

The Indian entity provides software services to its US subsidiary at cost + 15%. Indian costs for the year: ₹800 crore → intercompany revenue ₹920 crore. Benchmarking shows comparable IT companies earn 12-20% on cost. At Q4, actual markup has drifted to 11% because of higher costs; Taxation and CRT raise a true-up invoice to bring it to 15% before year end, and the US side books the matching cost — so both IC ledgers still match.

• Year-end TP adjustments must be invoiced and reflected on both sides (and with GST/WHT impact) — otherwise IC recon breaks.
• Missing documentation leads to adjustments and penalties.
• Different countries may challenge the same transaction from opposite sides (double taxation) — APAs and MAP help.
• Keep TP policy consistent with what actually happens (substance).

lessons.action: Ask Taxation which intercompany transactions your entity has and what markup policy applies.

quiz.q: What does the arm's length principle mean?
options: Related parties should price as unrelated parties would in similar conditions
quiz.why: That's the core TP rule.

quiz.q: Indian entity costs ₹500 crore; policy cost + 12%. Intercompany revenue?
A year-end TP true-up invoice is raised by India but not booked by the US entity. What breaks?
options: The intercompany reconciliation (and possibly TP compliance)
quiz.why: Both sides must reflect the adjustment.

lessons.title: Withholding tax on cross-border payments & DTAA
lessons.summary: Paying a foreign vendor or receiving money from a foreign client? Tax may be withheld at the border — and tax treaties decide how much.

term.word: Withholding tax on cross-border payments & DTAA
term.meaning: Withholding tax (WHT) is tax deducted by the payer on payments to non-residents (fees for technical services, royalties, interest, dividends); a Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) between two countries can reduce the rate or exempt the income, provided the recipient proves treaty eligibility (e.g. Tax Residency Certificate).

sections.b: Imagine earning prize money in another country's quiz show: that country keeps some tax before paying you, and then your home country also wants tax on the same money. A DTAA is the two countries agreeing: 'we won't both fully tax the same income'. To use it you must prove you are a resident of the treaty country (Tax Residency Certificate) and usually that you don't have a permanent establishment (PE) there.

• Payments abroad (India entity pays a foreign vendor): determine taxability in India, nature (FTS/royalty/business income), apply lower of domestic rate or DTAA rate (if TRC, Form 10F and other documents obtained), deduct and deposit TDS, report in 27Q; Form 15CA/15CB for remittance where required — check current rules.
• Receipts from abroad (foreign client pays India entity): client may withhold tax under its own law/treaty; collect the withholding certificate to claim foreign tax credit in India (Form 67) — check current rules.
• Maintain a vendor/customer tax master: country, TRC validity, PE declarations, treaty rate.
• Gross-up clauses: if the contract says the payer bears the tax, compute the grossed-up amount.
• Review for PE risk when employees work onsite at client countries for long periods.

The India entity pays a US consulting firm $50,000 for technical services. Taxation checks the India-US DTAA (fees for included services, generally 15% with a 'make available' condition — check current treaty terms). The vendor provides a valid TRC, Form 10F and no-PE declaration. If taxable, WHT at 15% = $7,500 is deposited in India and the vendor receives $42,500 and a certificate to claim US credit. Without a TRC, the higher domestic rate would apply.

• No TRC = no treaty benefit; track TRC expiry dates (usually per financial/calendar year).
• Wrong characterisation (royalty vs business income) changes taxability completely.
• Foreign tax credits are lost if certificates and Form 67 aren't filed on time.
• Treaty rates and conditions differ by country and change via protocols/MLI — check current rules.

lessons.action: Ask Taxation for a list of foreign vendors and whether their TRCs are valid for the current year.

quiz.q: Which document proves a foreign vendor is resident of a treaty country?
quiz.why: TRC is needed for treaty benefits.

quiz.q: Payment $20,000; treaty rate 10%. WHT amount?
A US client withheld tax from the India entity's invoice. How does the India entity avoid double tax?
options: Write it off as bad debt only
Claim foreign tax credit in India with the withholding certificate and required form
quiz.why: Foreign tax credit relieves double taxation.

lessons.title: Deferred tax
lessons.summary: Accounting profit and taxable profit differ because of timing. Deferred tax keeps the tax expense honest across years.

term.meaning: Deferred tax is the future tax effect of temporary differences between the book value of assets/liabilities and their tax base (Ind AS 12 / IAS 12): a deferred tax liability (DTL) when more tax will be payable later, and a deferred tax asset (DTA) when tax will be saved later.

sections.b: Imagine your parents count your pocket money monthly but the bank counts it yearly. Over a year both totals match, but month by month they differ. Accounting and tax are like that: tax law lets you depreciate a laptop faster, or deducts leave provision only when paid. The total over the years is the same — only timing differs. Deferred tax records 'we've paid less tax now, we'll pay more later' (DTL) or the reverse (DTA).

• Identify temporary differences: depreciation (book vs tax), provisions deductible on payment (leave, bonus, gratuity, statutory dues under payment-basis rules), lease accounting, unrealised FX/derivative MTM, tax losses carried forward.
• Compute: temporary difference × applicable tax rate (enacted/substantively enacted).
• DTL for taxable differences; DTA for deductible differences, recognised only if future taxable profit is probable.
• Book movement each quarter: Dr/Cr Deferred tax expense (P&L) or OCI (for items in OCI, e.g. hedge reserve).
• Effective tax rate (ETR) reconciliation: statutory rate vs actual tax expense with explanations.
• Disclose DTA/DTL by nature in financial statements.

Year 1: laptop fleet book depreciation ₹10 lakh, tax depreciation ₹16 lakh → asset's book value exceeds tax base by ₹6 lakh → DTL = 6 lakh × 25.168% = ₹1,51,008. Also, leave encashment provision ₹20 lakh is not deductible until paid → DTA = 20 lakh × 25.168% = ₹5,03,360. Net DTA = ₹3,52,352 (if recoverable and allowed to offset).

• Use the right rate (new regime vs old; changes in rate need remeasurement).
• DTA on losses needs strong evidence of future profits — auditors challenge it.
• Items booked in OCI carry their deferred tax in OCI too.
• Rebuild the ETR reconciliation every quarter; unexplained ETR moves are red flags.

lessons.action: Ask Taxation for the deferred tax schedule and find the largest DTA item.

quiz.q: Tax depreciation is higher than book depreciation. This creates…
quiz.why: Less tax now, more later → DTL.

quiz.q: Leave provision ₹10 lakh is deductible only when paid; tax rate 25%. Deferred tax?
quiz.why: Future deduction → DTA = 10 × 25%.

quiz.q: When can a DTA on tax losses be recognised?
options: When future taxable profits are probable to use them
quiz.why: Recoverability test under Ind AS 12.

calc.problem: Book depreciation ₹10 lakh, tax depreciation ₹16 lakh; leave provision ₹20 lakh (deductible on payment). Tax rate 25.168%. Compute DTL, DTA and net.

lessons.title: Tax audits, assessments & notices
lessons.summary: Filing a return is not the end. Tax authorities review, ask questions and sometimes disagree — and the company must answer with evidence.

term.meaning: A tax audit (in India, the tax audit report by an accountant for income tax, and GST audits by officers) checks compliance; an assessment is the authority's examination of a return to determine the correct tax; notices are formal requests for information or demands, which must be answered by deadlines with documentation.

sections.b: It's like submitting a college project and later getting a mail from the examiner: 'Explain why you used this formula, attach your sources by Friday'. If you've kept your notes and sources neat, it's an easy reply. If not, you lose marks (here: tax demand, interest, penalty). Most of a tax team's defence work is about keeping that 'evidence folder' ready long before the mail arrives.

• Maintain a documentation repository: returns, computations, reconciliations, invoices, contracts, TP studies, TRCs, LUTs, challans.
• Prepare and file tax audit report (with the statutory tax auditor) and TP report on time.
• Track all notices (income tax portal, GST portal, foreign authorities) in a register with deadlines and owners; acknowledge quickly.
• Prepare responses with legal/tax advisors; submit data reconciliations (e.g. GSTR-3B vs books, 26AS vs books).
• Faceless assessments in India mean online submissions — make answers complete and clear.
• Appeals: if you disagree with an order, file appeals within time limits; provide for or disclose contingent liabilities based on assessment of probability.

A GST notice asks the India entity to explain why ITC claimed in GSTR-3B (₹48 crore) exceeds GSTR-2B (₹46.5 crore) for FY. The tax team pulls its monthly 2B vs books recon: ₹1.2 crore relates to invoices that appeared in 2B in later months (timing, already claimed then — shown with month-wise mapping), and ₹0.3 crore is from a vendor who never filed. The team reverses ₹0.3 crore with interest and submits the reconciliation; the notice is closed.

• Missed notice deadlines can lead to ex-parte orders (decided without your side).
• Undocumented positions are hard to defend years later — document at the time of filing.
• Keep monthly reconciliations; they are your best defence.
• Assess each dispute for provision vs contingent liability disclosure (Ind AS 37) with auditors.

lessons.action: Ask Taxation for the notice tracker and see the most common reason for notices last year.

quiz.q: What is the best defence against tax notices?
quiz.why: Evidence wins assessments.

quiz.q: A notice's reply deadline is tomorrow and data is incomplete. Best approach?
options: Submit what's available and request an adjournment formally, per process
quiz.why: Never miss deadlines; seek time formally.

quiz.q: A tax dispute where outflow is possible but not probable is usually…
quiz.why: Ind AS 37 treatment for possible obligations.

lessons.title: Tax reconciliation
lessons.summary: Tax returns are built from books, and the government sees your data from other people's filings. Reconciliation makes sure all three stories match.

term.meaning: Tax reconciliation compares tax data across sources: GSTR-2B vs books ITC (purchase register), GSTR-1 vs sales register/revenue, GSTR-3B vs GL tax accounts, and Form 26AS/AIS vs TDS receivable in books — explaining every difference before filing and before authorities ask.

sections.b: Imagine three diaries of the same week: yours (books), your friend's about you (vendor/customer filings visible in 2B and 26AS), and the official attendance register (returns filed). If your diary says you attended 5 lectures, your friend's says 4 and the register says 3, someone must explain. Tax recon is matching these diaries every month so the tax authority never finds a gap before you do.

• GSTR-2B vs purchase register: match by supplier GSTIN + invoice number + date + taxable value + tax; categorise breaks: in books not in 2B (vendor not filed), in 2B not in books (not yet booked/not ours), value mismatch, wrong GSTIN, blocked credit.
• GSTR-1 vs sales register: invoices, credit notes, export (LUT) invoices, e-invoice (IRN) data vs ERP billing; ties to revenue after adjusting unbilled/deferred.
• GSTR-3B vs GL: output tax and ITC claimed vs GST GL accounts; cash ledger payments vs bank.
• 26AS/AIS vs books TDS receivable: by customer TAN and amount; chase customers who deducted but didn't deposit or report under wrong PAN.
• Typical breaks: invoice number formatting (INV/001 vs INV-001), timing (different months), credit notes, FX conversion on export invoices, wrong GSTIN/PAN.
• Automation: normalise invoice numbers, fuzzy match on GSTIN + amount + date window, auto-generate vendor follow-up mails, month-wise roll-forward of open items, dashboards of ITC at risk and TDS credit not reflected.

September 2B vs books: 18,500 invoices. Automated matching: 16,900 exact, 1,050 after normalising invoice numbers ('INV/23/001' vs 'INV-23-001'), 300 within ₹10 tolerance. Remaining 250 invoices (ITC ₹62 lakh): 180 vendors not filed (auto-mail sent), 50 booked under wrong GSTIN (corrected in ERP), 20 not ours (rejected in IMS). TDS side: 26AS shows ₹14.2 crore vs ₹14.8 crore TDS receivable in books — ₹0.6 crore from 12 customers who deducted but haven't filed their TDS returns; collections team chases them with Form 16A requests.

• Claiming ITC before matching = notices and interest; reversing late is costly.
• Unreconciled TDS receivable becomes a write-off when the return is filed without credit.
• Keep month-wise recon evidence — it answers future notices (lesson 79).
• Rule changes (IMS, auto-populated returns, new forms under the Income-tax Act, 2025) affect recon design — check current rules.

lessons.action: Pull one month's GSTR-2B vs books recon and measure the auto-match rate — then list the top break type you could automate.

quiz.q: Books show ITC ₹10 lakh, GSTR-2B shows ₹9.4 lakh. First step?
options: Identify invoice-level breaks (vendor not filed, mismatch, wrong GSTIN)
quiz.why: Investigate breaks invoice by invoice.

quiz.q: 26AS shows less TDS than books. Common cause?
options: Customer deducted but didn't deposit/report it correctly against the company's PAN
quiz.why: The deductor's filing drives 26AS.

quiz.q: 'INV/23/001' in books vs 'INV-23-001' in 2B. What automation rule helps?
options: Normalise invoice numbers by removing special characters before matching
quiz.why: Normalisation fixes format-only breaks.

lessons.title: MIS (Management Information System)
lessons.summary: The numbers leadership actually reads every month come from this team.

term.meaning: MIS is the set of regular management reports (P&L, margins, headcount, cash, KPIs) that turns raw accounting data into decisions.

sections.b: Accounting records every rupee; MIS tells the story of those rupees. Think of the ERP as your phone's raw photo gallery and MIS as the curated highlights reel your parents actually watch. The CFO, business unit heads, account leaders and the board do not want 2 lakh journal lines; they want 'Which client is losing money? Which region is growing?'. MIS slices the same accounting data by business unit, client, geography, service line and project so each person sees the view that helps them act.

• Extract the closed trial balance and sub-ledger data (revenue, cost, headcount) from the ERP after close
• Map GL accounts to MIS line items (revenue, direct cost, SG&A, EBITDA) using a maintained mapping table
• Slice by dimensions: entity, business unit, vertical, client, geography, cost centre, project
• Add non-financial data: headcount, utilisation, billable hours, pipeline from HR and delivery systems
• Prepare the monthly MIS pack, flash report and commentary on key movements
• Answer ad-hoc questions from leadership (why did BFSI margin drop 2%?)

On WD+4, the MIS team releases the monthly pack. Page 1 shows group revenue of Rs 1,250 cr, EBITDA 21.4%. Page 6 shows the Europe BFSI unit at 14% margin vs 19% last month. The commentary explains: two large fixed-price projects had extra effort (cost overrun Rs 6 cr) and a client discount of Rs 2 cr was booked. The BU head now asks delivery for a recovery plan.

• A wrong GL-to-MIS mapping (a new GL account not mapped) silently drops cost from the report
• Different teams using different versions of the same number destroys trust; one published version only
• MIS is management reporting, not statutory reporting, but it should still reconcile to the books
• Access control: client-level margins and salaries are confidential

lessons.action: Ask a colleague for last month's MIS pack index and note which five pages leadership looks at first.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of MIS?
options: To turn accounting data into management decisions
quiz.why: MIS reshapes accounting data into views that help managers decide.

quiz.q: A BU head asks why her unit's margin fell. Which team typically answers first with data?
quiz.why: MIS owns the management view by BU, client and geography and writes the commentary.

quiz.q: A new GL account for cloud costs was created but not added to the MIS mapping. What happens?
options: The cost may be missing or misclassified in MIS
quiz.why: Unmapped accounts are a classic cause of MIS not tying back to the GL.

lessons.title: Month-end close calendar (WD+1, WD+2...)
lessons.summary: Close runs on a countdown clock, and MIS is near the end of it.

term.meaning: The close calendar is the day-by-day schedule of who must finish which close task by which working day (WD) after month end.

sections.b: Month end is like a relay race. AP must hand the baton (all invoices booked) before accruals, accruals before the trial balance freezes, and the TB before MIS can publish. WD+1 means the first working day after the month ends, WD+2 the second, and so on (weekends and holidays don't count). If one runner is late, everyone after them is late, so the calendar exists to make every hand-off visible.

• WD-2 to WD0: cut-off reminders, open PO review, unbilled revenue estimates
• WD+1: sub-ledger close (AP, AR, FA), bank recon, payroll accruals posted
• WD+2: revenue recognition, provisions, intercompany cross-charges, FX revaluation
• WD+3: TB frozen, period closed in ERP for most entities; MIS flash numbers
• WD+4/5: full MIS pack, variance commentary, CFO review
• MIS tracks the calendar daily and chases late tasks (exact days vary by company)

Calendar for September close: Sep 30 is a Tuesday. WD+1 = Wed Oct 1, WD+2 = Fri Oct 3 (Oct 2 is a holiday, Gandhi Jayanti), WD+3 = Mon Oct 6 (weekend skipped). The flash revenue to the CFO is due WD+3, so it lands on Oct 6, not Oct 3 as someone counting calendar days might assume.

• Counting calendar days instead of working days, or forgetting local holidays in different countries
• Late manual journals after the TB freeze cause MIS vs GL differences
• Track task status with owners and timestamps; auditors like evidence of review
• Reopening a closed period should need approval and be logged

lessons.action: Find your company's close calendar and note which WD your reconciliation outputs are needed by.

quiz.q: What does WD+2 mean?
options: Two calendar days after month end
Second working day after month end
quiz.why: Working days skip weekends and holidays.

quiz.q: Why can't MIS publish before the trial balance is frozen?
options: Numbers could still change, so the pack would not tie to books
quiz.why: MIS should reflect final closed numbers.

quiz.q: Month ends on a Friday; Monday is a public holiday. When is WD+1?
quiz.why: Saturday, Sunday and the holiday are skipped, so WD+1 is Tuesday.

lessons.title: P&L, gross margin & EBITDA in MIS
lessons.summary: Three numbers every leader asks about: revenue, gross margin, EBITDA.

term.word: P&L, gross margin & EBITDA in MIS
term.meaning: Gross margin is revenue minus direct delivery cost; EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, i.e. operating profit before non-cash and financing items.

sections.b: Imagine you run a tiffin service. Revenue is what customers pay. Gross margin is what's left after food and cook's wages (direct cost). EBITDA is what's left after rent, marketing and admin too, but before loan interest, tax, and the wear-and-tear on your van. In IT services, direct cost is mostly delivery employee salaries plus subcontractors and travel billed to projects.

• Map GL accounts into P&L lines: revenue, direct cost (cost of revenue), SG&A, other income
• Compute gross margin % and EBITDA % by BU, client and geography
• Exclude or show separately one-offs (restructuring, legal settlements) as per policy
• Compare with last month, last year and budget
• Write commentary on drivers: pricing, utilisation, wage hikes, FX

BU 'Retail' in October: revenue Rs 100 cr, delivery salaries Rs 55 cr, subcontractors Rs 8 cr, project travel Rs 2 cr. SG&A (sales, admin, allocated overheads) Rs 15 cr. Depreciation Rs 3 cr. See the calculation.

• Classify costs consistently (is a delivery manager direct or indirect?) or margins jump around
• EBITDA is a non-GAAP measure; definition must be documented and stable
• FX movements can change INR revenue without any real business change; show constant-currency too
• Depreciation and interest must not leak into EBITDA lines

lessons.action: Look at one BU's P&L in the MIS pack and identify which line holds subcontractor cost.

quiz.q: Gross margin is revenue minus...
options: Direct cost of delivering the service
quiz.why: Gross margin covers only direct cost.

quiz.q: Which item is NOT deducted to arrive at EBITDA?
quiz.why: EBITDA is before depreciation and amortisation.

quiz.q: Revenue Rs 50 cr, direct cost Rs 35 cr. Gross margin %?

calc.problem: Retail BU: revenue Rs 100 cr; direct cost = 55 + 8 + 2 cr; SG&A Rs 15 cr; depreciation Rs 3 cr. Find gross margin % and EBITDA %.
