lessons.title: Budget vs actual & variance analysis
lessons.summary: Plan vs reality, and the story of why they differ.

term.meaning: Variance analysis compares actual results with budget (or forecast) and explains each difference as favourable or unfavourable.

sections.b: At the start of the month you budgeted Rs 8,000 for food; you spent Rs 9,500. The Rs 1,500 gap is the variance, and the interesting part is why: more eating out (volume) or prices went up (rate)? Companies do the same at a massive scale. Revenue above budget is favourable; cost above budget is unfavourable. MIS doesn't just show the gap; it explains the drivers so leaders know what to fix.

• Load the approved annual budget (by month, BU, account) into the reporting tool
• Compare actuals after close; compute absolute and % variance
• Set thresholds (for example, explain any variance above Rs 50 lakh or 5%; thresholds vary by company)
• Get explanations from BU finance / delivery; split into volume, rate, mix, FX, timing
• Publish variance commentary in the MIS pack

Cloud BU, October: budget revenue Rs 50 cr, actual Rs 46 cr; budget cost Rs 30 cr, actual Rs 28 cr. Explanation: a client project start slipped by a month (timing), so revenue and related staff cost both came in lower.

• A timing variance (will reverse next month) is different from a permanent one; label it
• Compare like with like: same exchange rates or show FX impact separately
• Watch the sign convention: cost under budget is favourable
• Explanations need evidence, not 'business as usual'

lessons.action: Pick one large variance in the latest MIS pack and read how it was explained.

quiz.q: Actual cost is higher than budget. The variance is...
quiz.why: Spending more than planned reduces profit.

quiz.q: A project started one month late, so October revenue missed budget but November will catch up. This is a...
quiz.why: It shifts between periods rather than disappearing.

quiz.q: Budget revenue Rs 20 cr, actual Rs 22 cr. Variance %?
quiz.why: (22-20)/20 = +10%, revenue above plan is favourable.

calc.problem: Cloud BU: budget revenue Rs 50 cr, actual Rs 46 cr; budget cost Rs 30 cr, actual Rs 28 cr. Compute variances and profit impact.
steps: Cost variance = 30 - 28 = Rs 2 cr below budget (6.7%), favourable
Budget profit = 50 - 30 = Rs 20 cr; actual profit = 46 - 28 = Rs 18 cr
calc.answer: Profit Rs 2 cr below budget (revenue -4, cost +2)

lessons.title: Forecasts & rolling forecasts
lessons.summary: The budget is the plan from last year; the forecast is today's best guess.

term.meaning: A forecast is an updated estimate of future results; a rolling forecast always looks a fixed number of months ahead (for example 12 or 18), adding a new month as each month closes.

sections.b: The budget is like the route Google Maps showed when you started; the forecast is the updated arrival time after traffic. A rolling forecast keeps the horizon fixed: it's always showing you the next 12 months, not just 'until 31 March'. Leaders use it to decide hiring, cash needs and what to tell investors.

• Collect inputs: revenue by client from account managers, pipeline, headcount plans from HR
• Start from actuals to date, then add the forecast months (often called a 3+9 or 6+6 forecast)
• Apply assumptions: FX rates, wage hike month, utilisation, attrition
• Consolidate, review with BU heads, challenge unrealistic numbers
• Track forecast accuracy (forecast vs actual) to improve over time

In October (after 6 months of an April-March year), MIS builds a 6+6 forecast: 6 months actual revenue Rs 2,400 cr + 6 months forecast Rs 2,550 cr = full year Rs 4,950 cr vs budget Rs 5,100 cr. The gap is flagged early, so sales and delivery can act before year end.

• Forecasts drift into 'hope'; compare them with pipeline and signed contracts
• Use the same FX rate assumption across BUs or note differences
• Keep versions (V1, V2) and lock the approved one
• Forecast accuracy is a KPI; repeated optimism should be called out

lessons.action: Ask which forecast version is currently approved and what FX rate it assumes for USD/INR.

quiz.q: What makes a forecast 'rolling'?
options: It is redone every year only
It always covers a fixed number of months ahead
quiz.why: Each month a new month is added at the end.

quiz.q: A '6+6' forecast means...
quiz.why: Actuals to date plus forecast for the rest of the year.

quiz.q: BU heads forecast 15% growth but signed contracts show 5%. What should MIS do?
options: Challenge the assumption with pipeline evidence
quiz.why: MIS challenges inputs to keep forecasts realistic.

lessons.title: Cost allocation & chargebacks
lessons.summary: Shared costs get sliced up and charged to whoever benefits.

term.meaning: Cost allocation spreads shared costs (IT, rent, HR, finance) to business units using a fair driver such as headcount or area; a chargeback is the internal charge that results.

sections.b: Four flatmates share a Rs 20,000 Wi-Fi-plus-electricity bill. Splitting by 'who used how much' is fairer than splitting equally. Companies do the same: IT support is shared by all BUs, so each BU gets a share based on headcount, laptops or tickets. Without allocation, BU margins look better than reality because someone else is paying their shared costs.

• Collect shared cost pools from cost centres (IT, facilities, HR, finance)
• Pick a driver for each pool: headcount, seats, square feet, revenue, tickets
• Get driver data (from HR, facilities) as of the agreed date
• Run allocation cycles in ERP (assessment/distribution) or in the MIS tool
• Review results, publish driver logic so BUs can see why they were charged
• If allocation crosses entities, it becomes an intercompany charge (see IC team)
October IT support cost Rs 12 lakh is shared by headcount: BFSI 300, Retail 150, Healthcare 50 (total 500). See the calculation.

• Drivers must be documented and stable; changing them mid-year distorts trends
• Allocated total must equal the cost pool exactly (no leakage)
• Cross-entity allocations have tax/transfer pricing impact
• BUs will dispute; keep driver evidence ready

lessons.action: Find one allocation cycle in the ERP or MIS model and note which driver it uses.

quiz.q: Why allocate shared costs to BUs?
options: To show each BU's true profitability
quiz.why: BUs that consume shared services should bear their cost.

quiz.q: Which is a sensible driver for office rent?
quiz.why: Rent relates to space used.

quiz.q: After allocation, the BU totals add to Rs 11.8 lakh but the pool was Rs 12 lakh. What does this suggest?
options: Some cost leaked or a driver was missing
quiz.why: Allocated amounts must equal the pool.

calc.problem: Allocate Rs 12,00,000 IT cost by headcount: BFSI 300, Retail 150, Healthcare 50.
steps: Total headcount = 500; cost per head = 12,00,000 / 500 = Rs 2,400
calc.answer: BFSI 7.2 lakh, Retail 3.6 lakh, Healthcare 1.2 lakh

lessons.title: Headcount, utilisation & revenue per employee
lessons.summary: In IT services, people are the product, so people metrics are money metrics.

term.meaning: Utilisation is billable hours divided by available hours; revenue per employee is revenue divided by average headcount.

sections.b: An IT services firm earns money mostly by billing people's time. If an engineer sits 'on bench' (not on a project), the company pays salary but earns nothing. Utilisation tells you what share of available time is billed, like how full a bus is. Revenue per employee shows how productive the whole organisation is. These are as important to leadership as profit itself.

• Get headcount from HR (opening, joiners, leavers, closing) by BU and location
• Get billable and available hours from timesheets / project systems
• Compute utilisation (with and without trainees), bench %, attrition %
• Compute revenue per employee and cost per employee
• Reconcile headcount between HR, payroll and MIS (they often differ: contractors, notice period)
Engineer pool in Pune, October: 100 employees x 180 available hours = 18,000 hours; 15,300 hours billed. Annual revenue Rs 500 cr, average headcount 10,000. See the calculation.

• Define headcount clearly: employees only, or include contractors? Closing or average?
• Timesheet gaps (unfilled timesheets) understate utilisation and revenue
• Use average headcount for per-employee ratios, not closing
• Personal data: keep employee-level data restricted

lessons.action: Ask MIS which headcount definition (closing/average, with or without contractors) the pack uses.

quiz.q: Utilisation equals...
quiz.why: It measures how much available time is billed.

quiz.q: Bench means employees who are...
options: Not currently assigned to billable work
quiz.why: Bench staff cost money without generating revenue.

quiz.q: Revenue Rs 300 cr, average headcount 6,000. Revenue per employee?
quiz.why: 300 cr / 6,000 = Rs 5 lakh.

calc.problem: Pune pool: 18,000 available hours, 15,300 billed. Company: revenue Rs 500 cr, average headcount 10,000. Find utilisation and revenue per employee.
calc.answer: Utilisation 85%; revenue per employee Rs 5 lakh

lessons.title: Dashboards & single source of truth
lessons.summary: One number, one source, everyone sees the same thing.

term.meaning: A single source of truth is one agreed, governed dataset (usually from the ERP via a data warehouse) that all dashboards and reports read from.

sections.b: If five friends each keep their own Excel of who owes what for a trip, you'll get five different answers. A shared Splitwise is the single source of truth. In finance, numbers flow from the ERP (SAP, Oracle) into a data warehouse, and BI tools like Power BI or Tableau show them as dashboards. If someone builds a private Excel with tweaks, leadership gets conflicting numbers, which is worse than no numbers.

• Define the data pipeline: ERP tables -> data warehouse/lake -> semantic model -> dashboards
• Maintain master mappings (GL to MIS line, cost centre to BU, customer to vertical)
• Schedule refreshes after close and control who can publish
• Build dashboards: revenue trend, margin by BU, DSO, headcount, utilisation
• Retire shadow Excel reports and point users to the governed source

The CFO sees revenue of Rs 412 cr on a Power BI dashboard but Rs 415 cr in a BU's Excel. Investigation: the Excel included Rs 3 cr of a manual adjustment that was later reversed in the ERP. Fix: the BU uses the dashboard, and the dashboard shows a 'data as of' timestamp.

• Every dashboard should show data refresh time and source
• Changes to mappings or logic need change control and testing
• Row-level security: BU heads should see only their BU if policy requires
• A pretty chart on bad data is still bad data

lessons.action: Open one finance dashboard and find its 'last refreshed' time and source system.

quiz.q: What does 'single source of truth' mean?
options: Every team keeps its own Excel
One governed dataset all reports use
quiz.why: Everyone reads from the same agreed data.

quiz.q: Which is a BI tool?
quiz.why: Power BI and Tableau visualise data.

quiz.q: Dashboard and a BU Excel show different revenue. What is the best first step?
options: Trace both to the ERP source and find the difference
quiz.why: Trace back to source to find the cause.

lessons.title: Data validation & sign-offs before publishing
lessons.summary: Check, check again, get a signature, then hit send.

term.meaning: Validation is the set of checks run on MIS data before release; sign-off is the documented approval by the preparer, reviewer and owner.

sections.b: Before you post a group trip budget on the WhatsApp group, you double-check the totals, because once 20 people see it, a wrong number spreads. MIS packs go to leadership and sometimes investors, so errors are expensive and embarrassing. Validation catches errors; sign-off makes it clear who checked what, so accountability is real.

• Run completeness checks: all entities loaded, all periods closed, no unmapped GLs
• Run accuracy checks: MIS totals = TB totals, revenue = revenue sub-ledger
• Run reasonableness checks: month-on-month swings above threshold flagged
• Get BU finance to confirm their numbers and commentary
• Preparer, reviewer and approver sign off (in a tool or checklist) with date/time
• Publish only the signed-off version; log any later revisions

Validation report on WD+4 flags: Healthcare BU gross margin jumped from 28% to 41%. Check finds a Rs 4 cr salary accrual posted to the wrong cost centre (in Retail). The entry is corrected before release, and the pack is signed off by the MIS lead and Head of FP&A.

• Never publish 'draft' numbers casually in emails; they get forwarded
• Keep the validation checklist evidence for internal audit / SOX-type reviews
• If a number changes after publishing, issue a formal revision note
• Reviewer should not be the preparer (segregation of duties)

lessons.action: Ask to see the MIS checklist and count how many checks are automated vs manual.

quiz.q: Which is a completeness check?
options: All entities and periods are loaded
quiz.why: Completeness means nothing is missing.

quiz.q: Why should preparer and reviewer be different people?
quiz.why: An independent review is a key control.

quiz.q: A margin jumps 13 points in a month with no business reason. What is the right action?
quiz.why: Unusual swings often reveal misposted entries.

lessons.title: MIS reconciliation (MIS vs GL / trial balance)
lessons.summary: Management numbers must tie back to the books, to the rupee.

term.word: MIS reconciliation (MIS vs GL / trial balance)
term.meaning: MIS reconciliation proves that totals in the MIS pack agree with the general ledger / trial balance, and explains any difference.

sections.b: MIS reshuffles accounting data into new buckets (BU, client, EBITDA). Reshuffling should never change the total, like rearranging books on shelves doesn't change how many books you own. The reconciliation checks that total revenue, cost and profit in MIS equal the trial balance, and that every adjustment between them is listed and approved. This is exactly where reconciliation automation shines.

• Compare: MIS revenue/cost/EBITDA per entity vs TB balances for mapped GL groups
• Also compare MIS sub-totals vs sub-ledgers (revenue system, payroll, headcount from HR)
• Typical breaks: unmapped new GL accounts, late journals after MIS extract, wrong cost centre/BU mapping, MIS-only adjustments (management overlays), FX rate differences for consolidation, reclassifications
• Document every reconciling item with owner and evidence
• Automation: scheduled extracts of TB and MIS, rule-based matching by entity/GL group, auto-flag unmapped accounts, variance thresholds, and a reconciling-items log that carries forward

October: TB total operating cost Rs 820.0 cr; MIS shows Rs 818.5 cr. Breaks: (1) new GL 'SaaS subscriptions' Rs 1.2 cr unmapped; (2) a Rs 0.3 cr journal posted after the MIS extract. After mapping and refresh, difference is zero. The automation tool now raises an alert whenever a GL with balance has no MIS mapping.

• A difference of zero at total level can still hide offsetting errors at BU level; reconcile by entity and BU too
• Management overlays must be approved and shown separately
• Lock the extract timestamp so you know which version you reconciled
• Keep the recon as audit evidence each month

lessons.action: Ask MIS how they currently tie the pack to the TB and whether it is manual Excel; this is a candidate for your automation.

quiz.q: What does MIS reconciliation compare?
options: MIS totals vs GL / trial balance
quiz.why: Management numbers must tie to the books.

quiz.q: Which is a common MIS-vs-TB break?
options: A new GL account not mapped to an MIS line
quiz.why: Unmapped accounts drop out of MIS.

quiz.q: Totals match but BU-level numbers are wrong. Why still reconcile at BU level?
options: Offsetting errors can hide at total level
quiz.why: Misallocations between BUs cancel out in totals.

calc.problem: TB operating cost Rs 820.0 cr; MIS Rs 818.5 cr. Known items: unmapped SaaS GL Rs 1.2 cr, late journal Rs 0.3 cr. Is the recon fully explained?

lessons.title: Intercompany (IC) transactions
lessons.summary: When one group company does business with another group company.

term.meaning: An intercompany transaction is any sale, service, loan or cost recharge between two legal entities of the same group.

sections.b: Think of a family where the elder sibling lends money to the younger one. Inside the family it's still real money, but if you count the family's total wealth, the loan cancels out. A global IT company has many entities: India Pvt Ltd does the work, US Inc signs the client contract. The US entity buys services from India, and that's an IC transaction. Each entity books it separately in its own books, and both sides must match.

• Maintain the list of entities, IC agreements and IC trading partner codes in ERP
• Raise IC invoices / cross-charges (services, cost recharges, royalties, management fees)
• Ensure both sides book the same amount, currency and period
• Track IC loans and interest
• Settle balances (netting or bank payments) and support eliminations at consolidation

US Inc wins a $1 million project from a bank. India Pvt Ltd delivers it. India invoices US Inc $850,000 for services. India books IC receivable and revenue; US books IC payable and cost. In group accounts, only the $1 million external revenue remains.

• Use the trading partner field on every IC posting, or matching becomes impossible
• IC charges need a written agreement and arm's length pricing (transfer pricing)
• Withholding tax, GST and FX apply to IC like any third-party deal
• Long-unsettled IC balances raise questions under FEMA for cross-border entities

lessons.action: Ask for the list of group entities and which ones India entity invoices most often.

quiz.q: Which is an intercompany transaction?
options: India Pvt Ltd paying an electricity bill
India Pvt Ltd invoicing its US subsidiary
A client paying the US entity
quiz.why: Both parties are group entities.

quiz.q: In group consolidated accounts, IC sales are...
quiz.why: The group cannot earn revenue from itself.

quiz.q: India books IC receivable of $850k from US; US books payable of $800k. What is this?
quiz.why: Both sides should agree; a difference must be reconciled.

lessons.title: IC invoicing & cross-charges (cost-plus mark-up)
lessons.summary: The India entity bills its sister companies cost plus a margin.

term.meaning: A cross-charge is an IC invoice for services or costs; under cost-plus, the charge equals the cost incurred plus an agreed mark-up percentage.

sections.b: If you cook dinner for your cousin's party, charging only the grocery cost leaves you with nothing for your effort. A small mark-up pays you fairly. Tax authorities insist group companies charge each other like strangers would (arm's length), so Indian entities providing IT services to group companies usually charge cost plus a mark-up. Some charges are pure pass-through recharges (e.g., a software licence bought centrally) with no mark-up, depending on policy.

• Collect the cost base per service (salaries, overheads, depreciation) from the cost centres
• Apply the mark-up as per IC agreement and transfer pricing policy
• Raise IC invoices in ERP in the agreed currency, with correct tax treatment (export of services from India, LUT, etc.)
• Send to the counterparty entity, which books the payable in the same period
• Track true-ups at quarter / year end if actual margin differs from target

India Pvt Ltd provides back-office support to UK Ltd. October cost: salaries Rs 70 lakh, rent and IT Rs 10 lakh. Mark-up as per agreement 10% (illustrative; real rate comes from the TP study). See the calculation.

• Cost base must exclude items the agreement excludes (e.g., pass-through costs)
• Invoice currency and FX rate must follow policy so both sides agree
• GST: export of services is zero-rated if conditions are met; check place-of-supply rules
• Missing or late IC invoices create mismatches at month end

lessons.action: Look at one IC invoice: find cost base, mark-up %, currency and the IC agreement reference.

quiz.q: Cost-plus pricing means the charge is...
options: Cost incurred plus an agreed mark-up
quiz.why: Cost base times (1 + mark-up).

quiz.q: Why do group entities add a mark-up to IC services?
options: To meet arm's length / transfer pricing expectations
quiz.why: Tax rules expect related parties to price like independent ones.

quiz.q: Cost base Rs 50 lakh, mark-up 8%. IC invoice?
quiz.why: 50 x 1.08 = Rs 54 lakh.

calc.problem: Cost base = salaries Rs 70 lakh + rent/IT Rs 10 lakh; mark-up 10%. Compute IC invoice.
steps: Margin on cost = 8/80 = 10%; margin on revenue = 8/88 = 9.1%

lessons.title: IC netting & settlement
lessons.summary: Don't send money both ways; pay only the difference.

term.meaning: Netting offsets amounts that group entities owe each other so only the net balance is paid; settlement is the actual payment that clears IC balances.

sections.b: You owe your friend Rs 500 for movie tickets; she owes you Rs 300 for pizza. Instead of two transfers, you pay her Rs 200. Large groups do this monthly across dozens of entities, often through a netting centre, saving bank charges and FX conversion costs. But cross-border netting involving Indian entities must follow FEMA/RBI rules, so check what is permitted before netting.

• Confirm IC balances with each counterparty (matched and agreed)
• Prepare a netting statement showing gross payables/receivables and net position
• Get approvals and check regulatory permissions for cross-border entities
• Execute settlement payments on the netting date
• Post clearing entries so IC open items are closed in both books

UK Ltd owes India Pvt Ltd GBP 50,000 for services; India owes UK GBP 30,000 for a software licence recharge. If netting is permitted, UK pays India GBP 20,000 net. Both entities clear the gross open items against the settlement.

• Only net balances that both sides have agreed; disputes first
• Indian exports must still be realised and reported; set-off of export receivables against import payables needs regulatory compliance (check current RBI rules)
• Clear open items at gross level so ageing reports stay correct
• FX rate used for netting should follow policy

lessons.action: Ask whether your group uses a netting centre and how India entities settle (gross or net).

quiz.q: What is IC netting?
options: Offsetting mutual balances and paying only the net
quiz.why: Only the difference moves.

quiz.q: Which benefit does netting bring?
options: Fewer payments and lower FX/bank costs
quiz.why: Fewer transactions mean lower costs.

quiz.q: A owes B Rs 80 lakh; B owes A Rs 50 lakh. Net settlement?
quiz.why: 80 - 50 = 30, paid by A.

calc.problem: UK owes India GBP 50,000; India owes UK GBP 30,000. Net settlement?
calc.answer: UK pays India GBP 20,000 (if netting is permitted)

lessons.title: IC eliminations in consolidation
lessons.summary: In group accounts, the group can't sell to itself.

term.meaning: Eliminations are consolidation entries that remove IC revenue/cost, receivables/payables, investments and profits so group accounts show only dealings with outsiders.

sections.b: If you move Rs 1,000 from your left pocket to your right, you're not richer. Group consolidation adds up all entities, then removes these 'pocket-to-pocket' moves. If both sides recorded the same amount, elimination is clean. If they didn't, the difference is stuck in the group accounts and someone has to explain it. That's why IC matching before consolidation matters so much.

• Collect IC balances by trading partner from each entity's ledger
• Match receivable vs payable and revenue vs cost per pair
• Post elimination entries in the consolidation tool (e.g., group reporting module)
• Eliminate unrealised profit if one entity holds assets bought from another
• Report and resolve unmatched differences before group sign-off

India revenue from US Inc: Rs 70 cr; US cost from India: Rs 70 cr (after translation). Elimination: Dr IC revenue Rs 70 cr, Cr IC cost Rs 70 cr. Group revenue = external revenue only. Balance sheet: India IC receivable Rs 12 cr eliminated against US IC payable Rs 12 cr.

• Translation differences (different FX rates) create small mismatches; policy should define treatment
• Missing trading partner codes break automatic elimination
• Unrealised profit in inventory/assets is easy to forget
• Auditors test that eliminations are complete

lessons.action: Ask who runs consolidation and which tool posts eliminations.

quiz.q: Why are IC sales eliminated?
options: Group can't earn revenue from itself
quiz.why: Only external transactions remain in group results.

quiz.q: Which field helps automatic eliminations?
quiz.why: It identifies the counterpart entity.

quiz.q: India shows IC receivable Rs 12 cr, US shows IC payable Rs 11.5 cr. On elimination...
options: Rs 0.5 cr difference remains to explain
quiz.why: Mismatches leave a residual that must be resolved.

lessons.title: Transfer pricing link for IC charges
lessons.summary: Tax authorities in every country check that IC prices are fair.

term.word: Transfer pricing link for IC charges
term.meaning: Transfer pricing (TP) is the set of tax rules requiring related-party transactions to be priced at arm's length, as independent parties would.

sections.b: If you sell your bike to your brother for Rs 1 to avoid paying something, the authorities would say 'that's not a real price'. Countries worry groups shift profit to low-tax places by setting IC prices artificially. India's Income Tax Act has TP rules, and other countries have similar rules. The finance team's IC charges must match the TP policy and agreements, or the company faces adjustments and penalties.

• TP team (tax/advisers) sets policy: method (often TNMM for IT services), target margin range
• IC team applies the policy in monthly cross-charges
• Track actual margin vs target; book true-ups before year end
• Keep documentation: IC agreements, invoices, benchmarking study
• Support the accountant's report (Form 3CEB in India) and any TP audits

TP policy for India captive: operating margin on cost of 15% (illustrative). By December actual margin is 12% because costs rose. The team raises a true-up invoice to the US entity to bring the year to target, after checking tax and FEMA implications.

• Mid-year mark-up changes without agreement amendments are risky
• True-ups must be documented and timely; year-end surprises cause tax issues on both sides
• Safe harbour rules exist in India for some IT services; check current thresholds and rates
• IC agreements must match how charges are actually computed

lessons.action: Ask the tax team what TP method and target margin apply to your entity's IC services.

quiz.q: Arm's length price means...
options: The price unrelated parties would agree
quiz.why: It mimics independent pricing.

quiz.q: Which method is commonly used for Indian IT service captives?
quiz.why: TNMM tests net margin against comparables.

quiz.q: Actual margin is below the TP target near year end. A typical fix is...
quiz.why: True-ups align actual results to policy.

lessons.title: Softex form
lessons.summary: Software exports leave no customs trail, so India asks for a declaration.

term.meaning: A Softex form is the export declaration for software/IT services exported from India (typically delivered electronically), filed by the exporter and certified by STPI or the SEZ authority so export proceeds can be tracked.

sections.b: When goods are exported, customs sees a container and a shipping bill. When code is sent over the internet, nothing passes customs. So the government asks exporters to declare 'we exported services worth X to client Y' on a Softex form. The certified Softex is like a shipping bill for software: RBI and the bank use it to check that the foreign money actually comes back to India.

• Identify export invoices raised by STPI/SEZ units (often via the Softex/billing data)
• Prepare Softex form(s) with invoice details, client, currency, amount (often in bulk/periodic format as allowed)
• File online with STPI or the SEZ authority within the prescribed time (check current rules)
• Obtain certification / Softex number; submit details to the AD bank as required
• Track the Softex in EDPMS until realisation is matched

India Pvt Ltd (STPI unit, Bengaluru) raises October export invoices to US, UK and Germany clients worth USD 4.2 million. The Softex team files the form on the STPI portal with all invoice details. Once certified, the Softex number appears in the bank's EDPMS records, waiting for incoming payments to be tagged against it.

• Filing deadlines and formats are set by FEMA/RBI rules and STPI/SEZ procedures; check current rules
• Invoice amounts in Softex must match ERP invoices; credit notes need corresponding handling
• Late filing can attract penalties / caution listing issues
• Keep certified copies; auditors and banks ask for them

lessons.action: Ask the Softex team how many Softex forms were filed last month and their filing turnaround.

quiz.q: Why is a Softex form needed for software exports?
quiz.why: It replaces the customs trail for electronic exports.

quiz.q: Who certifies the Softex form?
quiz.why: The designated STPI/SEZ officer certifies it.

quiz.q: Softex shows USD 4.2m but ERP export invoices total USD 4.3m. What should you do?
options: Reconcile; find the missing invoice or credit note
quiz.why: Softex and invoices should agree.

lessons.title: Export realisation, EDPMS & FIRC / e-BRC
lessons.summary: Exported? Now prove the dollars came home.

term.meaning: Export realisation is receiving the export payment in India; EDPMS is RBI's system that tracks each export until realised; FIRC/FIRA is the bank's proof of inward remittance and e-BRC is the DGFT electronic realisation certificate.

sections.b: Imagine lending your bike out with a register entry. The register stays 'open' until the bike is returned. EDPMS is RBI's register: each export (shipping bill or Softex) stays open until the bank tags incoming foreign money to it. FEMA requires export proceeds to be realised and repatriated within the period allowed under FEMA/RBI rules (check current limit). Unrealised items appear on the bank's overdue list and can create compliance trouble.

• Receive foreign inward remittances in the bank; identify which invoice/Softex they settle
• Give the bank the mapping so it can tag the remittance to the Softex in EDPMS
• Obtain FIRC/FIRA or bank advice; e-BRC is generated on the DGFT system as applicable
• Track open Softex/invoices ageing vs the permitted realisation period
• Apply to the AD bank for extension or write-off if needed (as per current RBI rules)
• Resolve short realisations (bank charges, discounts) with documentation

Softex 2026-OCT-118 covers invoice to client ABC Corp for USD 100,000. Payment arrives as USD 99,950 (USD 50 deducted by intermediary bank). The team tells the bank to tag it fully against the Softex and records the USD 50 as bank charges with documents, so the EDPMS entry is closed.

• Exact realisation period and extension rules: within the period allowed under FEMA/RBI rules; check current limit
• Lump-sum client payments covering many invoices need clear remittance advice to tag correctly
• Open EDPMS entries can block future benefits or trigger bank follow-ups
• e-BRC data supports export incentive and GST refund claims

lessons.action: Ask for the EDPMS outstanding report and how many entries are past the allowed period.

quiz.q: What does EDPMS track?
quiz.why: It's RBI's export monitoring system.

quiz.q: A FIRC/FIRA is...
options: Bank proof of foreign inward remittance
quiz.why: It evidences the incoming foreign currency.

quiz.q: Client pays USD 99,950 against a USD 100,000 invoice due to intermediary charges. Best handling?
options: Tag remittance and document the USD 50 as bank charges
quiz.why: Small charges are documented so the export entry can close.

lessons.title: STPI / SEZ units & export benefits
lessons.summary: Special schemes that let Indian IT companies export more easily.

term.meaning: STPI (Software Technology Parks of India) and SEZ (Special Economic Zone) are government schemes under which registered units export software/IT services with procedural and tax/duty benefits, subject to conditions.

sections.b: Think of SEZ like a 'special lane' at an airport: faster, fewer checks, some charges waived, but only if you follow the lane's strict rules. STPI units mainly get single-window clearance, duty-free import of equipment and help with exports; the old STPI income tax holiday (section 10A) ended years ago. SEZ units historically got income tax deductions (section 10AA, only for units that started before a sunset date) plus GST zero-rating and duty benefits.

• Maintain unit registrations (Letter of Approval/permission) and renewals
• Track each unit's exports and file Softex/returns to STPI or the SEZ Development Commissioner
• File periodic performance reports (e.g., SEZ annual performance reports) as required
• Ensure imports/procurements claim duty/GST benefits correctly and are used for approved purposes
• Keep unit-wise books/profit tracking where tax deductions depend on unit profits

A company has an STPI unit in Pune and an SEZ unit in Chennai. Chennai's employees work on approved services; its exports are filed through the SEZ online system. Laptops bought for the SEZ unit are procured without GST as a zero-rated supply, but they must stay with that unit unless the move is approved.

• Benefit rates, sunset dates and conditions change; check current rules before quoting them
• Moving assets or employees between SEZ and non-SEZ units has compliance steps
• Net foreign exchange (NFE) positive conditions apply to SEZ units; check current requirements
• Unit-wise records are audited by authorities

lessons.action: Find out which units (STPI / SEZ / domestic) your entity has and which unit your team's invoices belong to.

quiz.q: What does STPI stand for?
quiz.why: STPI is the scheme for software export units.

quiz.q: Which benefit is typical for SEZ units?
options: Zero-rated GST supplies and duty benefits
quiz.why: Supplies to SEZ units are zero-rated under GST.

quiz.q: An SEZ unit wants to send laptops to a domestic office. What should you do first?
options: Check the SEZ approval/procedure for removal
quiz.why: Duty-free assets in SEZ need approved movement.

lessons.title: Foreign currency invoices & realisation gains/losses
lessons.summary: The rupee moves between invoice day and payment day; that's a gain or loss.

term.meaning: Foreign currency invoices are booked at the exchange rate on the invoice date; when paid at a different rate, the difference is a realised exchange gain or loss (and open balances are revalued at month end as unrealised gains/losses).

sections.b: You sell a phone to a US friend for $100 when $1 = Rs 83, so you expect Rs 8,300. He pays a month later when $1 = Rs 83.60, so you get Rs 8,360: Rs 60 extra, a gain. If the rupee had strengthened, you'd get less, a loss. Indian IT exporters bill mostly in USD/EUR/GBP, so these differences are large and are reported separately from revenue.

• Book invoice at the rate type set in ERP (e.g., daily rate)
• Month end: revalue open foreign currency receivables/payables at closing rate (unrealised gain/loss)
• On receipt: clear invoice; ERP posts realised gain/loss for the difference
• Reverse prior unrealised entries as per ERP setup to avoid double counting
• Report FX gain/loss and hedging impacts to Treasury and MIS
Invoice to ABC Corp: USD 10,000 on 1 Sep at Rs 83.00. Payment received 15 Oct at Rs 83.60. Bank charges ignored. See the calculation.

• Using the wrong rate type (buying vs mid) creates small recurring differences
• Partial payments: gain/loss is on the cleared portion only
• Unrealised revaluation must be reversed or handled so realised gain isn't double counted
• Hedges (forwards) are accounted separately as per policy

lessons.action: Look at one customer receipt in foreign currency and find the realised FX gain/loss posting.

quiz.q: Realised FX gain arises when...
options: Payment is received at a better rate than booked
quiz.why: More INR received than booked.

quiz.q: What happens at month end to open USD receivables?
quiz.why: Revaluation shows the current INR value.

quiz.q: Invoice EUR 5,000 at Rs 90; paid at Rs 89. Result?

calc.problem: USD 10,000 invoice booked at Rs 83.00; received at Rs 83.60. Find realised gain/loss.
steps: More INR received, so it is a gain

lessons.title: IC & Softex reconciliation
lessons.summary: Both sides of IC must agree, and every export must be filed and paid.

term.meaning: IC reconciliation matches IC receivables/payables and revenue/cost between entity pairs; Softex tracking reconciles export invoices vs Softex filings vs realisations in EDPMS.

sections.b: IC recon is like checking your Splitwise with your flatmate: you say she owes Rs 2,000, she says Rs 1,800; find the Rs 200. Softex recon is a three-way check: did every export invoice get a Softex (filed), and did every Softex get its money (realised)? Both are high-volume matching problems, which makes them perfect for automation.

• IC: extract IC balances by trading partner, currency and invoice reference from both entities; match pairwise
• Typical IC breaks: invoice booked by one side only (timing/cut-off), FX rate differences, wrong trading partner, disputed amounts, GST/withholding tax booked differently, manual journals without reference
• Softex: match ERP export invoices -> Softex lines -> EDPMS entries -> bank remittances (FIRC)
• Typical Softex breaks: invoice missing from Softex, credit notes not reflected, short receipts (bank charges), lump-sum payments untagged, wrong Softex number tagged
• Automation: rule-based matching on invoice number/amount/currency, tolerance for FX and bank charges, ageing buckets vs permitted realisation period, auto-generated query emails to counterparties

October IC: India shows receivable from UK GBP 250,000; UK shows payable GBP 238,000. Breaks: GBP 12,000 invoice raised 31 Oct by India, booked by UK on 2 Nov (timing). Softex: 412 export invoices; 409 in Softex filings; 3 missing (raised after filing cut-off) go in next filing; EDPMS shows 37 entries unrealised, 5 approaching the allowed period, escalated to collections.

• Agree a cut-off rule: IC invoices must be booked by both sides in the same period
• Compare in transaction currency first, then in INR, to separate FX noise from real breaks
• Keep evidence for each reconciling item; unexplained differences go to consolidation as 'IC difference'
• Overdue export realisations are a regulatory risk, not just an accounting break

lessons.action: Ask for the IC mismatch report by entity pair and the EDPMS outstanding list; see how they are matched today.

quiz.q: Which is a typical IC break?
options: Invoice booked by one entity in October, by the other in November
quiz.why: Cut-off timing is the most common cause.

quiz.q: Softex tracking reconciles which chain?
quiz.why: Every export must be filed and realised.

quiz.q: IC balances agree in USD but differ in INR. Most likely reason?
quiz.why: Matching in transaction currency isolates FX differences.

calc.problem: India receivable from UK GBP 250,000; UK payable GBP 238,000; one India invoice of GBP 12,000 dated 31 Oct not yet booked by UK. Unexplained difference?

lessons.title: Fixed assets & capex vs opex
lessons.summary: Is it something you use for years, or something you use up now?

term.meaning: A fixed asset (property, plant & equipment) is a tangible item used in the business for more than one year; capex is spending to buy or improve such assets, opex is day-to-day running cost expensed immediately.

sections.b: Buying a laptop you'll use for 3 years is capex; paying the monthly internet bill is opex. Capex goes on the balance sheet as an asset and is expensed slowly through depreciation, while opex hits the P&L straight away. Getting this wrong changes profit: capitalising a repair inflates profit now; expensing a server understates assets.

• Review purchase invoices / POs flagged as capital (asset GL, asset class)
• Apply the capitalisation policy (threshold amount, useful life over one year)
• Create asset master records and post acquisition
• Review repairs and maintenance for items that should be capitalised (major upgrades)
• Report capex vs budget to MIS

Company buys 200 laptops at Rs 70,000 each (Rs 1.4 cr) and pays Rs 3 lakh for annual software support. Laptops are capitalised (asset class 'Computers'); annual support is opex (or prepaid and expensed over 12 months).

• Capitalisation threshold is set by company policy; low-value items may be expensed (check policy)
• Repairs that only maintain an asset are opex; upgrades that extend life or capacity can be capex
• Misclassification affects EBITDA (capex is outside EBITDA via depreciation)
• Each asset needs supporting invoice and approval

lessons.action: Ask for your company's capitalisation policy and its threshold amount.

quiz.q: Which is capex?
quiz.why: It benefits multiple years.

quiz.q: Capex reaches the P&L through...
quiz.why: The cost is spread over useful life.

quiz.q: A Rs 2 lakh AC repair keeps the AC working as before. Treatment?
quiz.why: It maintains, not improves, the asset.

lessons.title: Capitalisation & CWIP (capital work in progress)
lessons.summary: Assets under construction wait in CWIP until ready to use.

term.meaning: CWIP holds costs of assets not yet ready for use (e.g., office fit-out under construction); capitalisation moves them to fixed assets when ready, starting depreciation.

sections.b: Building a new office floor is like building a house: you pay contractors for months, but you can't live in it yet. Those payments sit in CWIP. When the floor is ready to use, the total moves to 'Buildings/Leasehold improvements' and depreciation starts. If you forget to move it, profit is overstated (no depreciation) and assets look 'in progress' forever.

• Create CWIP / project (e.g., AuC, asset under construction) for each capex project
• Collect costs: contractor bills, materials, directly attributable costs
• Get completion certificate / ready-for-use confirmation from facilities/IT
• Settle CWIP to final asset(s) with correct asset class and capitalisation date
• Review CWIP ageing every month and chase stuck projects

Chennai office fit-out: Jan-Jun contractor bills Rs 2.2 cr, electricals Rs 50 lakh, furniture Rs 30 lakh, all in CWIP. Ready for use on 1 July. CWIP of Rs 3 cr is split: leasehold improvements Rs 2.7 cr, furniture Rs 30 lakh; depreciation starts from 1 July.

• Depreciation starts when asset is available for use, not when the last invoice is paid
• Old CWIP items may be ready assets not capitalised, or abandoned projects needing write-off
• Companies Act Schedule III asks for CWIP ageing disclosure (check current format)
• Only directly attributable costs can be capitalised

lessons.action: Pull the CWIP ageing report and find the oldest open project.

quiz.q: When does depreciation start?
options: When the asset is available for use
quiz.why: Use-readiness triggers depreciation.

quiz.q: CWIP stands for...
quiz.why: It holds incomplete capital projects.

quiz.q: An IT room was ready in March but is still in CWIP in October. Impact?
quiz.why: Missing capitalisation skips depreciation.

lessons.title: Asset register & asset tagging
lessons.summary: Every asset gets an ID, a location, and an owner.

term.meaning: The fixed asset register is the detailed list of every asset (ID, description, cost, date, location, custodian, depreciation); a tag is the physical label (barcode/QR/RFID) linking the item to its register entry.

sections.b: It's like your college library: every book has a barcode and an entry saying where it is and who borrowed it. Companies may have lakhs of laptops, monitors and chairs across cities. Without tags, you can't prove assets exist, and auditors want proof. The register in ERP is the 'sub-ledger'; its total must equal the fixed asset GL.

• Create asset master in ERP: class, description, cost centre, location, serial number, custodian
• Print/attach tag with asset number when received
• Link IT assets to the IT asset management (ITAM) tool
• Update register on transfers, employee exits, disposals
• Maintain the register as the basis for depreciation and physical verification

Laptop received in Hyderabad: asset 100045231, class Computers, cost Rs 72,000, serial 5CD1234XYZ, custodian employee 45821, cost centre HYD-BFSI-01. QR tag is stuck on it; scanning it in a verification shows the same details.

• Missing serial numbers make physical verification very hard
• Employee exits without laptop return leave 'ghost' assets
• Register cost must equal GL; differences mean manual GL postings bypassed the asset module
• Grouping many items in one asset record makes partial disposal hard

lessons.action: Check whether your own laptop has an asset tag and ask how to look it up in the register.

quiz.q: What is the fixed asset register?
options: A list of all assets with details
quiz.why: It's the detailed sub-ledger of assets.

quiz.q: Why tag assets physically?
options: To link physical items to records for verification
quiz.why: Tags let you prove existence.

quiz.q: An employee resigns and the laptop is not returned. What should happen?
options: Recover or record loss/write-off per policy
quiz.why: The register must reflect reality.

lessons.title: Depreciation: straight-line vs WDV
lessons.summary: Two ways to spread an asset's cost across its life.

term.meaning: Depreciation allocates an asset's cost (minus residual value) over its useful life; straight-line (SLM) charges equal amounts each year, written-down value (WDV) charges a fixed percentage of the reducing balance.

sections.b: A Rs 3 lakh server loses value as you use it. Straight-line: same slice every year, like paying equal EMIs. WDV: big slice early, smaller later, like a new phone losing value fastest in year one. Companies choose a method under accounting standards; Indian tax law uses its own WDV block rates separately.

• Set depreciation key/method and useful life per asset class in ERP
• Run depreciation each month (depreciation run), check the log for errors
• Post to depreciation expense and accumulated depreciation GLs by cost centre
• Review assets with zero or negative net book value
• Report depreciation to MIS (below EBITDA)
Server cost Rs 3,00,000, residual value Rs 15,000 (5%), useful life 3 years. SLM vs WDV at 40% (illustrative rate). See the calculation.

• Pro-rata from capitalisation date; check ERP period control
• Changing method or life is a change in estimate and needs approval and disclosure
• Depreciation run errors (missing cost centre) leave assets undepreciated
• Book depreciation and tax depreciation are different; don't mix them

lessons.action: Ask which depreciation method your entity uses in books and view one month's depreciation run log.

quiz.q: Straight-line depreciation charges...
quiz.why: Cost less residual, divided by life.

quiz.q: Under WDV, depreciation in later years is...
quiz.why: It's a % of a shrinking balance.

quiz.q: Asset Rs 1,00,000, no residual, 5-year SLM. Annual depreciation?

calc.problem: Server Rs 3,00,000, residual Rs 15,000, life 3 years. Compute SLM per year and WDV at 40% for 3 years.

lessons.title: Useful life: Companies Act Schedule II vs Income Tax blocks
lessons.summary: Two rulebooks: one for your accounts, one for your tax return.

term.word: Useful life: Companies Act Schedule II vs Income Tax blocks
term.meaning: Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013 gives indicative useful lives for book depreciation; the Income Tax Act gives depreciation rates on blocks of assets (WDV) for tax computation.

sections.b: It's like two scoreboards for the same match: the accounting scoreboard (books) and the tax scoreboard (income tax). For books, Schedule II says, for example, laptops/desktops about 3 years and servers/networks about 6 years; a company can use a different life with technical justification. For tax, assets are grouped in blocks (e.g., computers, furniture, plant & machinery) with fixed WDV rates. The difference creates deferred tax.

• Maintain book depreciation area (Companies Act) and tax depreciation area in ERP
• Apply Schedule II lives (or justified different lives) per asset class
• Compute tax depreciation by block, including half-rate rule for assets used less than 180 days in the year of acquisition
• Provide data to tax team for the return and tax audit
• Compute deferred tax on book vs tax differences

Laptop Rs 90,000 bought in May. Books: SLM over 3 years = about Rs 30,000 per year (pro-rata in year 1). Tax: computers block at 40% WDV (check current rate), used over 180 days, so full-rate Rs 36,000 in year 1. Difference of timing creates deferred tax.

• Schedule II lives are indicative; using a different life needs justification and disclosure
• Tax rates and block rules change; check current Income Tax rules before relying on any rate
• Common Schedule II references: end-user computers 3 years, servers & networks 6 years, furniture 10 years, office equipment 5 years (verify)
• Tax depreciation is per block, not per asset; disposal proceeds reduce the block

lessons.action: Ask the FA team for the useful life table by asset class used in your ERP.

quiz.q: Which law gives indicative useful lives for book depreciation in India?
quiz.why: Schedule II covers book depreciation.

quiz.q: Income Tax depreciation is computed on...
options: Blocks of assets using WDV rates
quiz.why: Tax uses block-wise WDV.

quiz.q: An asset is used for less than 180 days in the year of purchase. Tax depreciation that year is...
quiz.why: The half-rate rule applies.

lessons.title: Asset transfers between entities & locations
lessons.summary: When laptops move from Pune to Chennai, or from one company to another.

term.meaning: An asset transfer moves an asset's record to a new location/cost centre within the same entity, or to another legal entity (an intercompany sale/transfer with tax implications).

sections.b: Moving your bicycle from your room to your brother's room at home is a location change. Selling it to your cousin (another household) is a different thing, with a price and paperwork. Within an entity, only the cost centre/location changes. Between entities, it's a sale: invoice, GST (if applicable), and both entities update registers.

• Receive transfer request with asset numbers, from/to location, approvals
• Intra-entity: update location/cost centre in ERP (intra-company transfer), depreciation follows new cost centre
• Inter-entity: raise invoice/delivery challan, apply GST as applicable, retire in sending entity, capitalise in receiving entity
• Check SEZ/STPI restrictions for duty-free assets before moving
• Update tags, ITAM tool and custodian

50 laptops move from Pune STPI unit (entity A) to Bengaluru office of entity B (a different legal entity). NBV Rs 15 lakh. Entity A raises an invoice at agreed value with GST as applicable, retires the assets; entity B capitalises them at the transfer price and starts depreciation.

• Moving duty-free imported/SEZ assets without the required approval is a compliance breach
• Inter-entity transfer price should be arm's length (transfer pricing)
• Mismatch: sending entity retires, receiving entity forgets to capitalise
• Physical movement without ERP update breaks verification

lessons.action: Ask how many asset transfer requests the FA team processed last month and which approvals are needed.

quiz.q: A laptop moves from one floor to another in the same entity. What changes in ERP?
quiz.why: Same entity, just a location change.

quiz.q: A transfer between two legal entities is treated like...
quiz.why: Different entities need invoice and tax.

quiz.q: Entity A retired the asset but entity B never capitalised it. Which recon finds it?
quiz.why: Matching transfers across entities catches this.

lessons.title: Disposal, sale & write-off (gain/loss on sale)
lessons.summary: When an asset leaves, compare what you get with what it's worth in the books.

term.meaning: Disposal removes an asset from the register when sold, scrapped or lost; gain or loss = sale proceeds minus net book value (cost minus accumulated depreciation).

sections.b: You bought a bike for Rs 50,000; after using it, its 'book value' is Rs 15,000. If you sell for Rs 12,000, you've lost Rs 3,000 versus the books; at Rs 18,000 you've gained Rs 3,000. Companies sell old laptops to e-waste vendors, scrap broken furniture, or write off lost items. Each needs approval and an ERP retirement entry.

• Receive approved disposal request (asset numbers, reason, method)
• Get quotes/vendor (e.g., authorised e-waste recycler) for sale
• Raise sale invoice with GST as applicable
• Retire asset in ERP: remove cost and accumulated depreciation, post gain/loss
• Keep evidence: approval, invoice, e-waste certificate, data-wipe certificate
Old servers: cost Rs 5,00,000, accumulated depreciation Rs 3,50,000, sold to a recycler for Rs 1,20,000. See the calculation.

• Data wiping certificates are essential for IT assets
• Lost assets: write-off needs investigation and approval, maybe insurance claim
• Fully depreciated assets still in use stay in register; scrapped ones must be retired
• Tax: sale proceeds reduce the tax block (no separate tax gain unless block rules say so; check)

lessons.action: Ask for the last disposal file and see the evidence attached.

quiz.q: Gain/loss on sale equals...
quiz.why: Compare proceeds to NBV.

quiz.q: Which document is critical when selling old laptops?
quiz.why: It proves confidential data was destroyed.

quiz.q: Cost Rs 2,00,000, accumulated depreciation Rs 1,50,000, sold for Rs 60,000. Result?

calc.problem: Servers cost Rs 5,00,000, accumulated depreciation Rs 3,50,000, sold for Rs 1,20,000. Find gain/loss.
steps: Entry: Dr Bank 1,20,000, Dr Acc. dep 3,50,000, Dr Loss 30,000, Cr Asset 5,00,000

lessons.title: Impairment
lessons.summary: When an asset is worth less than the books say, write it down.

term.meaning: Impairment is a write-down when an asset's carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount (the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use), under Ind AS 36 / IAS 36.

sections.b: You bought a fancy gaming PC for your café; a new rule bans gaming cafés nearby, so the PC can't earn what you expected. Its book value says Rs 1 lakh but it's really worth Rs 60,000. Accounting says: don't pretend; write it down. For IT companies, triggers include a data centre being shut, software that's abandoned, or a client contract lost for which assets were bought.

• Look for impairment indicators (idle assets, closed sites, obsolete tech, losses in a unit)
• Get carrying amount (NBV) from register
• Estimate recoverable amount: fair value less costs of disposal, and value in use (discounted future cash flows)
• Book impairment loss for the excess; reduce future depreciation base
• Document assumptions; goodwill is tested annually by the consolidation/technical team

A dedicated data centre setup for a client has NBV Rs 10 lakh. The client contract ends early. Fair value less costs of disposal Rs 6 lakh; value in use (remaining cash flows) Rs 7 lakh. See the calculation.

• Recoverable amount is the HIGHER of the two measures, not the lower
• Idle assets in the register are a common audit finding
• Assumptions (discount rates, cash flows) need review and evidence
• Reversal of impairment is allowed for most assets but not goodwill under Ind AS 36

lessons.action: Ask whether any assets are flagged idle or in closed locations in the register.

quiz.q: Recoverable amount is...
options: Higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use
quiz.why: Ind AS 36 uses the higher of the two.

quiz.q: Which is an impairment indicator?
quiz.why: Idle or obsolete assets signal impairment.

quiz.q: NBV Rs 5 lakh; recoverable amount Rs 5.5 lakh. Impairment?
quiz.why: No write-down if recoverable amount exceeds carrying amount.

calc.problem: NBV Rs 10 lakh; fair value less costs of disposal Rs 6 lakh; value in use Rs 7 lakh. Find impairment loss.
steps: Recoverable amount = higher of 6 and 7 = Rs 7 lakh
Carrying amount Rs 10 lakh > Rs 7 lakh, so impaired
New carrying amount Rs 7 lakh; depreciate over remaining life

lessons.title: Leases & right-of-use (ROU) assets
lessons.summary: Renting an office? On the balance sheet, that's an asset and a liability.

term.meaning: Under Ind AS 116 / IFRS 16, a lessee recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability (present value of lease payments) for most leases, then depreciates the asset and charges interest on the liability.

sections.b: Earlier, renting an office was just a monthly rent expense. Now, signing a 5-year lease is treated like buying the 'right to use' the office for 5 years with borrowed money. So you show an ROU asset (the right) and a lease liability (what you owe). Rent payments reduce the liability; the P&L shows depreciation plus interest instead of rent. Short-term leases (12 months or less) and low-value assets can be exempted.

• Collect lease contracts from facilities/legal: term, rent, escalations, options
• Compute lease liability = PV of payments at incremental borrowing rate
• Recognise ROU asset (liability + initial direct costs etc.)
• Monthly: depreciation on ROU, interest on liability, record rent payments
• Handle modifications (extensions, rent changes) and remeasure
• Many companies use a lease module or tool for calculations
Office lease: Rs 1,00,000 per year paid at year end for 3 years; incremental borrowing rate 10%. See the calculation.

• EBITDA increases under Ind AS 116 because rent becomes depreciation + interest; MIS must explain this
• Missing leases (not given to finance) understate liabilities
• Discount rate choice drives the numbers; document it
• Tax treatment of rent differs from Ind AS 116 accounting; check current rules

lessons.action: Ask how many leases are in the lease register and who updates it when a lease changes.

quiz.q: Under Ind AS 116 a lessee recognises...
quiz.why: Most leases go on the balance sheet.

quiz.q: The lease liability is measured at...
quiz.why: Payments are discounted.

quiz.q: A 6-month lease for a temporary project room. Possible treatment?
quiz.why: Leases of 12 months or less can use the exemption.

calc.problem: Lease Rs 1,00,000/year, paid at year end, 3 years, rate 10%. Find lease liability, year-1 interest and year-1 ROU depreciation.
calc.answer: Liability about Rs 2,48,685; year-1 interest Rs 24,869; depreciation Rs 82,895

lessons.title: FA reconciliation (register vs GL, physical verification, CWIP ageing)
lessons.summary: Do the books, the register and the actual assets all agree?

term.word: FA reconciliation (register vs GL, physical verification, CWIP ageing)
term.meaning: FA reconciliation ties the asset register (sub-ledger) to the fixed asset and depreciation GL accounts, compares the register to physical verification results, and reviews CWIP ageing.

sections.b: Three lists should tell the same story: the GL (total value), the register (item-by-item), and what's physically in the office. If the GL says Rs 50 cr, the register should add up to Rs 50 cr, and the laptops listed should actually exist. Stuck CWIP is a fourth check: costs waiting too long to become assets.

• Register vs GL: compare cost, accumulated depreciation and depreciation expense by asset class/entity
• Typical breaks: manual journals posted directly to asset GLs, depreciation run not posted, disposals retired in register but not GL (or vice versa), wrong asset class-GL mapping, FX translation of foreign entity assets
• Physical verification (PV): scan tags, compare to register; list missing, untagged and extra items; investigate and adjust after approval. CARO requires reporting on PV at reasonable intervals (check current requirements)
• CWIP ageing: bucket by age (<1, 1-2, 2-3, >3 years), chase capitalisation or write-off
• Automation: monthly auto-extract of register and GL balances, rule-based matching by class, flags for direct GL postings, PV scan matching on serial/tag, CWIP ageing alerts

October: GL computers cost Rs 48.6 cr; register Rs 48.2 cr. Breaks: Rs 30 lakh manual accrual posted to asset GL without an asset record, Rs 10 lakh disposal retired in register but GL posting failed. PV in Pune: 5,000 tagged items in register, 4,930 found, 70 missing (40 with exited employees). CWIP: Rs 1.1 cr older than 1 year flagged.

• Block direct manual postings to asset GL accounts in ERP where possible
• Missing assets need approval before write-off; repeated losses signal control weakness
• Reconcile accumulated depreciation, not just cost
• Keep PV reports signed by counting team and reviewed by finance

lessons.action: Ask for the last FA register-vs-GL recon and the last physical verification report; note which steps are manual.

quiz.q: FA register-vs-GL recon compares...
options: Asset sub-ledger totals vs asset GL balances
quiz.why: Sub-ledger must equal GL.

quiz.q: A manual journal posted directly to the asset GL causes...
quiz.why: No asset record is created, so only GL increases.

quiz.q: Physical verification finds 70 laptops missing. Best next step?
quiz.why: Investigate before adjusting the register.

calc.problem: GL computers cost Rs 48.6 cr; register Rs 48.2 cr. Items: manual accrual in GL Rs 0.3 cr; disposal not posted in GL Rs 0.1 cr. Unexplained?
steps: Manual accrual in GL only = +0.3 cr
Disposal retired in register, not GL = +0.1 cr
